articles.title: Iran's quest for its own Monroe Doctrine
articles.body:
Iran’s quest for its own Monroe Doctrine
- November 24, 2026
- Meir Javedanfar
- Themes: Geopolitics, Iran, Middle East
The Islamic Republic aims to drive the United States from the Middle East – and then assert its regional supremacy.
President Trump is looking for a new nuclear deal with Iran. But what the leadership of the Islamic Republic of Iran is looking for is something beyond that: its own version of the Monroe Doctrine.
Outlined in 1823 by President James Monroe, the doctrine asserted that the United States would not accept any new European colonisation or military intervention in the Americas. Today, Iran wants an equivalent agreement, one that declares the Middle East ‌off limits to American forces. This is why the withdrawal of US troops from the Middle East, which Iran refers to as ‘West Asia’, has been one of Iran’s preconditions for an agreement. Iran uses this term to refer to the Middle East because it sees the latter as a Eurocentric definition, created by the imperialist powers.
The leadership of the Islamic Republic sees the current conflict as an unmissable opportunity to establish a new sphere of influence for itself in the region. Powerful figures, such as Rezaei and Ali Akbar Velayati, adviser to Iran’s supreme leader on international affairs, call this the ‘emerging West Asian order’. In this new order, the US will no longer have any bases in the region, while any new regional arrangement must include Iran’s concerns and considerations.
Fulfilling this goal will not be easy and Iran’s leadership realises this; accordingly, it has moved beyond rhetoric towards action to fulfil its ambition, pursuing a two-pronged strategy.
First, it has attacked regional countries that host American military bases on their soil. This is why Iran has targeted all the Arab Gulf states and Jordan during the recent war. Iran hopes that this will force the host countries to view these bases on their soil as a liability, and conclude that US bases attract insecurity and conflict, rather than security and stability. As the speaker of Iran’s Parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, stated in May this year: ‘some governments in the region believe that the presence of America will bring them security. But recent events [i.e. attacks against US bases in Gulf countries] have illustrated that such a presence does not create security, rather, it creates insecurity for them’.
Second, it has sought to establish control over the Strait of Hormuz through attacks against ships that wish to pass through it without Iran’s permission. This is in addition to insisting that Iran retains control over this important waterway as part of a future agreement with the US. The Strait is a vital economic artery for the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries. Controlling it gives Tehran immense leverage to pressure these nations into downgrading or expelling American forces.
This strategy risks pushing the Gulf countries further towards the US. However, Iran believes that, ultimately, these countries will reach the conclusion that Washington is an unreliable partner. Just as it abandoned Afghanistan and left its Kurdish allies in Syria high and dry, it will also abandon its Persian Gulf partners for the simple reason that it does not have the stomach or incentive to pursue a prolonged conflict far away from its own borders.
One of the key challenges faced by the Monroe Doctrine was enforcement. On numerous occasions, European powers defied the doctrine by intervening militarily in the Americas, including Britain seizing the Falkland Islands in 1833 and the French intervention in Mexico in 1861. Originally underwritten by British naval supremacy, Washington’s claims over the Western Hemisphere were only truly enforced when the United States emerged as a major military and naval power during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
By insisting on formal control over the Strait of Hormuz as part of a final deal with Washington, Iran wants to ensure that, unlike with the original Monroe Doctrine, it has the means to enforce its own version. The Islamic Republic’s missile and drone arsenal, generated by the regime’s domestic production capabilities, have already inflicted heavy military and economic costs on its adversaries. Securing total control over the Strait, backed by Iran’s armed forces, would provide Tehran with credible deterrence against both foreign powers seeking to deploy forces to the region and regional states that consider hosting them.
Iran’s current strategy has been shaped by several developments since 7 October 2023, many of which have been against Iran’s interests. Chief among them has been the weakening of Iran’s ‘Axis of Resistance’. This has been through the loss of the Assad regime in Syria, and Iran’s Hamas and Hezbollah allies becoming militarily weakened. Iran believes that the best time to compensate for these losses is now by using the leverage afforded by its hold over Hormuz and attacks against Persian Gulf countries.
The emphatic defeat suffered by President Trump’s Republican Party in the US midterm elections has emboldened Iran’s decision-makers. The Islamic Republic’s leaders believe that the American people have shown that they are unwilling to pay the price of war against Iran, owing to the costs imposed by Iran through attacks against oil and gas installations and transport networks, which have driven up the price of energy. As the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, General Rezaei stated the day after the midterms, ‘the great people of Iran imposed a strategic defeat on the US on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz, and a political defeat against Trump’.
The Iranian leadership’s resolve is further strengthened by the belief that a US departure from the region would strengthen its standing at home, allowing the regime to present itself as victorious in its conflict against a mighty foe and vindicating its claim to be the region’s greatest power. Ultimately, the Islamic Republic wants the Trump administration to recognise it as the main power in the Middle East, just as it has recognised China as the superpower of the Far East, and Russia as a major European regional power. The regime’s leaders believe that Iran deserves a seat at the table of great powers and should be invited to diplomatic conferences, such as the trilateral summit between Xi, Putin and Trump that took place on 19 November in China. They do not expect their Russian and Chinese allies to negotiate on their behalf.
History has taught Iran’s leaders that despite warm words of friendship, the leaders of China and Russia put their own interests above those of Iran. They are even willing to use their influence over Iran as a bargaining chip in their dealings with the US at Iran’s expense.
The leadership of the Islamic Republic regards the ongoing war as a convergence of opportunities that must be leveraged to reshape the regional balance of power in its favour. To do so, it needs to push the US out, and to make sure it stays out. The leverage it has gained through recent events is one it believes it can use to redraw the map of the region, assert local supremacy, and exclude hostile foreign forces. In short, it wants to secure for itself in the Middle East what President Monroe proclaimed for the United States in the Western Hemisphere in 1823.

articles.title: Russia May Launch Nuclear Weapon Into Orbit As Soon As Next Month
articles.body:
Russia May Launch Nuclear Weapon Into Orbit As Soon As Next Month (arstechnica.com) 158
			
		 	
				Western intelligence agencies reportedly believe Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit as early as December, "suggesting the country's development of a satellite-killing weapon of mass destruction is more advanced than previously thought," reports Ars Technica, citing German media reports. Such a launch would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, while a detonation could create radiation belts that damage satellites for years. From the report:  The orbiting nuclear weapon would threaten thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit, including military and commercial communications networks like Starshield and Starlink. A nuclear-armed satellite would also put at risk Western military surveillance satellites and human spaceflight platforms like the International Space Station. A nuclear detonation in orbit would be indiscriminate, also knocking out Russia's own spacecraft and Chinese satellites.
Reporting from three German news outlets -- public broadcasters NDR and WDR and the Munich-based newspaper Suddeutsche Zeitung -- indicates Russia's launch of a nuclear-armed satellite could be imminent. The report says Western intelligence agencies, including the German Armed Forces and Federal Intelligence Service, believe Russia is preparing to deploy the weapon in space this year. Several NATO countries have exchanged their findings on the matter.
The nuclear-armed satellite, designated Sputnik-S, has been in storage in the greater Moscow area for years, the German news report said. German Space Command believes the satellite could be launched as early as December. Once in orbit, a nuclear weapon could loiter for months or years, ready for detonation on the command of Russian military forces. The Kremlin dismissed the report. "Given the number of qualifiers like 'allegedly' and 'possibly' -- not to mention the fact that the claims are attributed to some unspecified source -- they are hardly worth taking seriously," said Dmitry Peskov, spokesperson for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Spy Story Is a Hoax
articles.body:
U.S. intelligence never concluded that Alice Huang was a spy, sources tell me.
How, then, did the media get so spun up over a made-for-Hollywood story about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang getting honeypotted by a Chinese spy?
Blame Marco Rubio. He cooked the intelligence until it was charred beyond recognition, then served it to the press — just ahead of Pulitzer season.
Rubio, a China hawk and longtime foe of Huang’s, took creative liberties in describing preliminary intelligence and sent the media on a wild goose chase that ended with Huang ousted from Nvidia.
Now the chatter in Washington is that the New York Times will win a Pulitzer for taking down the CEO of Nvidia and a powerful ally of President Trump’s. Never mind that its reporting was wrong, that Jensen Huang is back as CEO, or that not a single national security official — from the CIA and FBI Directors to the Attorney General — has said that Alice Huang was a spy.
The story was just too good.
The Real Story 
It began with eavesdropping. The U.S. intelligence community was conducting routine foreign surveillance for technology theft by China, when it came across Alice Huang. She was a Chinese national whose Singapore company, Megaspeed, had bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips.
Jensen Huang was implicated when an NSA summary of intercepted communications involving Alice Huang referred to an unnamed “U.S. Person.” Though U.S. law requires intelligence agencies to redact Americans' names for privacy reasons, in some cases officials can ask to have them ‘unmasked,’ intel-speak for ‘revealed.’
That unnamed American turned out to be Jensen Huang.
For a year and a half, Huang had been a thorn in the side of Washington’s China hawks. And he had something cabinet officials hate to see an outsider have: a direct line to the President. Huang frequently dropped in at the White House, dined with Trump at Mar-a-Lago, flew with him to Beijing on Air Force One and was awarded the National Medal of Science by Trump.
The Proxy War 
Worst of all, in the hawks’ eyes, Huang beat them in a battle pitting free trade against national security. In December 2025, he talked Trump into letting Nvidia sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China. In exchange, the U.S. government would collect 25 percent of the chips’ value. That deal drove Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the defense hawks everywhere from K Street to Silicon Valley up the wall.
“They wanted to destroy the influence Jensen had over the president,” a former administration official told the Washington Post.
Rubio's fight with Huang was a proxy for a broader fight with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who had made himself Huang's chief protector inside the administration. Lutnick, a Wall Street dealmaker with no patience for the State Department's Cold War mindset, openly defended selling Nvidia chips to China as a way to keep Chinese developers “addicted to the American technology stack.” Huang agreed.
Rubio sided with Bessent, Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in favor of blacklisting companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China. Chief among them was Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s company. Lutnick resisted, warning it “will start a trade war with China.”
Bessent finally vented in public, saying the rest of the government had wanted Megaspeed blacklisted “for months.” Then he pointed across town: “Commerce holds the pen.”
To Rubio’s camp, Huang was the man whispering in the President’s ear, and Lutnick was the man doing what Huang wanted. Lutnick may have held the pen, but Rubio had the ink, and he was willing to spill it by circulating intelligence on the two Huangs’ “close relationship” amid Nvidia's chip deals with China.
Raw Reporting
What the CIA and FBI actually had from the NSA intercepts and their own collection was the messy, ambiguous stuff of routine counterintelligence. Called “raw reporting,” this is what intelligence analysts are trained to handle with great caution because the information lacks context and verification. Imagine what your text messages would sound like if someone read portions without context.
Politicians, though, treat raw reporting like dynamite.
The FBI had been looking at Alice Huang for more than a year, curious how a former Beijing TV journalist had turned up in Singapore with the backing to buy billions of dollars’ worth of computing power. The intercepts reportedly show that she had contact of some form with China’s Ministry of State Security, which seems plausible, but far from proof that she was a spy. Successful Chinese businesspeople in Southeast Asia are routinely leaned on by Beijing’s security services, and few feel free to turn down a meeting.
CIA officials, CNN later reported, were not convinced that the intercepts proved she was knowingly passing anything to Beijing. What’s more, if counterintelligence officials really believed that the head of America’s most important tech company was being manipulated by a Chinese honeypot, the FBI could have privately warned him with what it calls a “defensive briefing.”
But Huang never got one.
Other countries came up empty, too. Singapore, hardly soft on illegal tech brokers, ran its own investigation. Authorities there detained Alice Huang and held her passport for months, then gave it back and let her go.
“We were thorough with Alice Huang; we took her in, we investigated her, but we eventually released her because there was no basis for further prosecution,” Singapore’s Prime Minister, Lawrence Wong, said.
The Marco Memo 
None of that nuance survived the Rubio leak. Before Trump’s May trip to Beijing, Rubio authored a highly classified memo calling Alice Huang a Chinese spy, which he then circulated to the administration and, eventually, the media.
Even the Washington Post acknowledged that Rubio’s memo recast “the agency’s [CIA’s] reporting in his own more assertive terms.”
Or, without the bullshit: he cooked the books.
Asked by reporters about his role in alerting the White House, Rubio declined several times to answer.
It didn’t matter. The supposed gist of the memo leaked and the story landed on the front page of the New York Times on October 29. The rest of the press then piled on.
The problem is that no one in government who has actually seen the intelligence will back Rubio up.
Start with the Justice Department and the FBI, the agencies that actually hold the criminal case file. Attorney General Todd Blanche was asked when the Justice Department learned she might be a Chinese asset. He rejected the premise: “Nobody said that. I certainly haven’t said that.”
Blanche added that no conclusions had been reached by the department, by him or by FBI Director Kash Patel “around who she is or is not.” Patel, who usually can’t resist chiming in on anything, has been silent.
Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, was asked twice by CNN’s Dana Bash whether Alice Huang is a spy. Both times he declined to say she was.
Even Trump has undercut Rubio’s leak. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy,” he told Fox News when asked.
Vice President JD Vance says that the intelligence he has seen wasn’t enough for him or Trump to conclude Alice Huang worked for Beijing.
Even on Capitol Hill, where calling someone a Chinese spy is usually an easy applause line, members of Congress privy to the intelligence briefings have been unwilling to use the s-word.
Tom Cotton, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee and doesn’t usually hold back on China, responded to Nvidia’s reinstatement of Huang on Monday with a statement that conspicuously avoided using the word “spy.”
Democrats on the intelligence committees haven’t backed Rubio’s version either. Representative Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, walked out of a classified briefing for Congress’s top leaders and told reporters he still didn’t know whether Alice Huang had knowingly gathered secrets for Beijing or was merely a “useful idiot.”
The final word came Monday, when Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as CEO. The board said it had heard from senior levels of the U.S. government and, based on what they told it, was confident Huang's return “poses no national security risk.”
Since its October 29 scoop, the New York Times has published a behind-the-scenes piece on how its reporters “broke open” the investigation.
Something broke, anyway.
On November 6, the Times flatly reported that Alice Huang “was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security,” recruited “to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang.”
Now, in their passive-aggressive way, the Times and other outlets are backing away from that claim. Instead of admitting they got the story wrong, they’re running philosophical treatises asking, ‘What even is a spy anyway?’ — one of the funnier goalpost relocation maneuvers I’ve seen.
What even is journalism?
— Edited by William M. Arkin

articles.title: Cyberattack campaign compromising Check Point servers across 22 organizations
articles.body:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.
Campaign Summary
- GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally.
- We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims.
- The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing.
- We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin.
- The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers.
- The actor used Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.
- The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF).
- Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets.
- Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing.
- We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims.
Observed Attacker Activities
We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
HFS Scanning and Exploitation
The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.
2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.
Example POST to loginSrp1 and response
Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested
2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.
Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie
Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits.
2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.
On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.
Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop
2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.
Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.
Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.
The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.
Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant
They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.
2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.
The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.
Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration
Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.
Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.
The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.
2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.
Excerpt from exploit.py - This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers.
2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.
Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim.
2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and launched pull_<redacted_id>.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.
Excerpt from pull_<redacted_id>.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration.
2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.
2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.
- CVE-2020-1472 (Microsoft Netlogon),
- CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Netscaler),
- CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure),
- CVE-2021-26855/34473 (Microsoft Exchange) and
- CVE-2021-21972 / CVE-2023-34048 (VMware vCenter)
2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use.
Excerpt from comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_spray.py
2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure.
Note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop.
All of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners.
Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt
One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device.
After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd.
Protecting Their Access
2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.
Excerpt from cve_2026_98432.py
Example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened quickly.
Notes on Attack Timeframe and Timeline
- The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server. We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets.
- We observed GT13 attack activity between 2026-10-02 13:17:45 and 2026-11-02 03:19:46 UTC. During our observation of the actor, we did not observe any adversary hands-on-keyboard activity between ~17:00 UTC and ~00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 UTC hour. We know the risks of time zone analysis and do not put much weight into the actor’s tendency to operate in what would be a convenient UTC+7- or UTC+8 workday.
- The attack infrastructure was long established before we first saw it, as we note the attempted malware domain newpayapp[.]com was first registered on 2026-03-13 12:46:28 UTC. It may be a UTC+7-friendly coincidence that the domain was originally created with the registrant state as “Hai Phong” with country code “VN” (see Cloudflare’s RDAP service).
- We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets. We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations.

articles.title: Cyberattack campaign compromising Check Point servers across 22 organizations
articles.body:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.
Campaign Summary
- GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally.
- We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims.
- The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing.
- We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin.
- The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers.
- The actor used Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.
- The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF).
- Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets.
- Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing.
- We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims.
Observed Attacker Activities
We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
HFS Scanning and Exploitation
The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.
2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.
Example POST to loginSrp1 and response
Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested
2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.
Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie
Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits.
2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.
On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.
Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop
2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.
Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.
Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.
The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.
Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant
They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.
2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.
The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.
Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration
Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.
Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.
The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.
2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.
Excerpt from exploit.py - This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers.
2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.
Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim.
2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and launched pull_<redacted_id>.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.
Excerpt from pull_<redacted_id>.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration.
2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.
2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.
- CVE-2020-1472 (Microsoft Netlogon),
- CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Netscaler),
- CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure),
- CVE-2021-26855/34473 (Microsoft Exchange) and
- CVE-2021-21972 / CVE-2023-34048 (VMware vCenter)
2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use.
Excerpt from comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_spray.py
2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure.
Note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop.
All of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners.
Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt
One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device.
After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd.
Protecting Their Access
2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.
Excerpt from cve_2026_98432.py
Example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened quickly.
Notes on Attack Timeframe and Timeline
- The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server. We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets.
- We observed GT13 attack activity between 2026-10-02 13:17:45 and 2026-11-02 03:19:46 UTC. During our observation of the actor, we did not observe any adversary hands-on-keyboard activity between ~17:00 UTC and ~00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 UTC hour. We know the risks of time zone analysis and do not put much weight into the actor’s tendency to operate in what would be a convenient UTC+7- or UTC+8 workday.
- The attack infrastructure was long established before we first saw it, as we note the attempted malware domain newpayapp[.]com was first registered on 2026-03-13 12:46:28 UTC. It may be a UTC+7-friendly coincidence that the domain was originally created with the registrant state as “Hai Phong” with country code “VN” (see Cloudflare’s RDAP service).
- We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets. We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations.

articles.title: Microsoft Declares 'Code Red' After Historic Outage
articles.body:
Microsoft Declares 'Code Red' After Historic Outage (reuters.com) 41
			
		 	
				Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" initiative to overhaul its engineering and crisis response practices following a 24-hour outage on November 12-13 that disrupted governments, financial firms and airlines worldwide, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, said M365 Core President Jason Henderson. "Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," Henderson added. From the report:  Amanda Silver, Microsoft's corporate vice president overseeing M365 Core and Work IQ, the company's workplace intelligence platform for AI agents, said in a separate memo on Monday that engineers had to work through a "fog of war" as the outage unfolded. Despite deploying top engineering personnel, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats and struggled to maintain a cohesive picture of hypotheses and decisions because diagnostic data was scattered across fragmented internal tracking systems, Silver said.
[...] As part of the Code Red, a high-priority mobilization reserved for critical crises, Silver outlined five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft set a target of achieving worldwide resolution within an hour during future incidents and plans to deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said he would hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering group responsible for underlying Microsoft 365 services, to track actions stemming from the outage, along with weekly reviews. The company spokesperson said Microsoft is committed not only to resolving issues when they occur, but to doing everything possible to prevent future disruptions.
"Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson said, adding that he had conducted an extensive review of the broader organizational and structural issues that allowed the failures to occur. In another memo earlier this month reviewed by Reuters, Henderson said "urgent patches to our M365 Core services" took too long to deploy worldwide. "In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote.

articles.title: Working with AI
articles.body:
Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
Summary
How are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found:
- Sources of AI value. Companies are deploying AI across a dizzying range of knowledge work tasks. In particular, they are increasingly using coding agents to bring software capabilities to nontechnical roles. Interviewees report that most uses of AI add value by increasing their output, rather than by cutting costs. They attribute this both to AI accelerating existing work and to its role in introducing novel product and service improvements.
- Impact on employment. Across our interviews, we saw very few examples of domestic layoffs that were driven by AI automation. Although some companies reported hiring more due to AI, most companies reported hiring less due to AI. Many also reported reducing their use of contractors, particularly offshore ones. These reported cuts could be an early warning of job disruption in the international business services industry.
- Bottlenecks. Companies reported a range of bottlenecks, including experts resisting AI deployment and tasks that are not accelerated by AI. As coding speeds up, for example, other tasks—like code review, sales, and strategic decision-making—increasingly need to keep pace.
- Limits to top-down and bottom-up approaches. Many companies approach AI by identifying a workflow to automate and rolling out a top-down solution. This approach can lead to job insecurity, fears of workplace surveillance, and resistance from the experts needed to set up an effective and durable workflow. Companies that distribute AI tools and wait for bottom-up adoption see some valuable AI use but face bottlenecks from unequal adoption and single-task AI implementations.
- Reorganizing for AI. Interviewees described the highest-value uses as involving meaningful reorganization. Some companies are broadening their employees’ roles to ensure individuals can take ownership over whole workflows, and are redeploying employees to the “bottleneck” tasks that AI models cannot do. Some also seek to empower employees by building out infrastructure to support nondeveloper coding and by providing broad-based internal access to business data. These companies are reorganizing to take advantage of ongoing model capability improvements rather than settling on a fixed approach that assumes AI tools will remain as powerful as they are today.
Introduction
The use of LLMs has exploded across the economy. How are human organizations reshaping around these strange new collaborators? Consider an employee at a midsize law firm that we spoke to. For years, the firm’s mailroom had followed the same protocol: a scanner sent PDFs of incoming correspondence to an inbox; a mail clerk opened each PDF, skimmed it, clicked “Save As,” renamed it, and placed it in the firm’s file system. The process took five minutes per letter. One day, a senior developer visited the mailroom to watch the mail being processed. In a month, he built an AI system that eventually became two API calls, which name the document based on its first page and then assign it a place in the firm’s document system. The mail clerks “were blown away.”
An employee at another law firm we interviewed hoped AI would create “a second brain” for the firm. (“For higher-level stuff, it just opens up possibilities.”) But the firm struggled to get everyone to use AI effectively. Demand letters to potential defendants were filled with excessive em dashes and occasional errors. Attorneys building apps kept “running into the wall based on hallucinated menus or buttons that don’t exist.” Others worried about confidentiality and data security, or they just didn’t “have time to get onto this AI train.” A few power users inundated the firm with AI prose, “casually sending Claude-prompted seven-page instructions to the IT team.”
A third law firm we spoke to adopted AI early and achieved strong uptake. One of the firm’s early projects was an AI timekeeping system that saved attorneys work tracking billable hours. IT staff saw parts of their job automated, but they then focused on building secure infrastructure to host apps and manage context that served the rest of the firm. As AI tools spread, the firm realized that associates were no longer needed to write first drafts of certain legal documents. But without writing, “how does an associate know if that’s a good draft or a bad draft?” So it introduced a new workflow where junior lawyers were “required to really take that first [AI-written] draft and work with a senior attorney,” pairing off and marking up and editing the draft together.
These three firms applied the same technology in the same industry but in different ways. The first firm automated a workflow, creating efficiency gains but risking job displacement for the mail clerks. For the second, bottlenecks to adoption and effective implementation prevented job displacement but also blunted productivity gains that would benefit the firm. The third reorganized work without eliminating any jobs, because effective use of the technology required redeploying employees toward new tasks. The firm redesigned roles to maintain human expertise as a complement to increasingly capable AI models.
In this article, we explore the connections between AI-driven value and work reorganization through 66 face-to-face interviews conducted across 58 companies in the US, all of which are in the midst of adopting AI. We interviewed executives, managers, and individual contributors. We talked to employees at AI-native startups and 100-year-old businesses. We interviewed people at manufacturers and tech companies. We spoke with structural engineers, dentists, and accountants; employees at hedge funds, law firms, and private equity firms; a property manager, a trucking company, and a publisher. They’re all Anthropic customers, but many also use other AI tools. They were selected for this study because of their range across industry, size, and AI usage, though they are not a random or systematically representative sample.
As in other qualitative research, we present stories and a framework to organize them, with the expectation that follow-up quantitative research can test these ideas further. The interviews were done anonymously, both for the interviewees and their companies. Any names in the report are pseudonyms.
How are businesses adapting to AI?
In our interviews, we gained insight into how AI has become embedded in businesses across the economy. Some of the AI agents we heard about are sending faxes back and forth, as doctors’ offices refer and intake patients. Other agents are giving advice to technicians when an X-ray machine breaks, and still others are then marking up the X-rays to help patients better understand them. Agents are reading property deeds from the 1800s and working out delivery routes for gaming machines. Recently, an AI agent analyzed a company’s organizational chart and suggested departments where the company could add headcount: “Three heads here, we need to add two there, zero here.”
Mostly, agents are writing code. Interviewees described 100 pieces of software that they wrote with AI in enough detail that we could categorize them. Eighty percent of this software automated previously manual work, like spreadsheet-based financial updates or taking meeting notes. Another 20% replaced existing software, often previously purchased from outside vendors. Agents are building apps for private parking enforcement, 401(k) audits, and trademark checks for new product names. They are making dashboards to track portfolio companies, equipment repairs, and debt collectors’ phone calls.
How have human organizations harnessed these new assistants? We use our interviews to explore several aspects of these deployments. We begin by estimating how much value interviewees ascribe to AI deployments and relate that to a measure of how much organizational change they required to implement. Figure 1 plots nearly 300 AI applications that interviewees discussed in detail. We define an application as a specific AI use case in a specific company. We coded discussions of each application according to the value interviewees attributed to it and the extent to which the organization had to make significant organizational changes to accommodate it. These value assessments are primarily qualitative descriptions on the part of interviewees, not typically based on A/B tests or other quantitative assessments.1
Figure 1 shows that many light-touch AI applications can fit into an existing organizational structure, like ad hoc data analysis or slide deck design. However, many of the simplest applications were rated as relatively low value by the employees who described them. Higher-value deployments tend to require changes to processes, like AI review of every code commit, or roles, like a marketing manager who edits skill.mds containing branding guidelines instead of designing individual documents.
Several interviewees described AI adoption as essentially a challenge of organizational change: flattening organizations, shifting reporting lines, or dropping functions. At one firm, for example, executives decided that junior analysts were no longer necessary because executives could complete their own SQL queries. As one accountant put it, “It’s a combination of process re-engineering and systematic discipline.”
There are several reasons why the most valuable applications led to significant organizational change. In some cases, the AI applications required a structural change in order to be successful, such as when a policy had to be clarified so that AI agents could rigorously apply it in an assessment workflow. In other cases, initial success spurred excitement about making larger organizational changes to further harness AI. In others, the success of using AI forced downstream changes. One commercial real estate company saw its staff start sending out client-facing documents themselves. But this meant they had violated company rules that asked employees to route external materials through the marketing department. As an IT director explained, “That’s good because, hey, we got another client. That’s bad because our standard operating procedures are starting to fall apart.” These stories echo academic research that shows that organizational change is necessary to derive value from transformative technologies.
Next, we studied what, exactly, value means in the context of AI adoption. Figure 2 shows that interviewees described most AI applications as adding value by increasing a firm’s output rather than cutting costs. Around half of the applications that increased output were due to AI accelerating or expanding existing work. The other half were the result of AI improving the quality of products and services or creating new products altogether. For instance, a medical group improved service quality by using AI to give patients an up-front estimate of after-insurance costs. A commercial real estate manager mocked up vacant units for potential tenants with their own branding (“Here’s what your sandwich place would look like in this space”). A dental company introduced an after-hours AI answering service, so patients’ midnight calls no longer went to voicemail.
In one-tenth of the use cases laid out in Figure 2, value was captured directly by employees, who were either doing more enjoyable work or were doing less work altogether. One manager described how bringing AI into his construction company meant that “work can be a joy again instead of a difficult, painful thing.” Senior engineers at an engineering consultancy described being thrilled to be free of tedious standards reconciliation work.
This sentiment was particularly common in cases where AI sped up peripheral tasks that were distracting to experts, like making pitch decks for product developers or preparing CRM reports for sales representatives. An employee at one construction materials company said they appreciated a whole series of small, personal automations that were “changing my life because now I do so much less work.” An executive at a food industry company remarked on “the number of people who just have thanked me because they could take a vacation.” (This is consistent with a Danish survey that found that around 10% of employees who save time with AI chatbots say they take more breaks or have more leisure time.) But some managers were less enthused. One frustrated executive described his employees as hiding their AI-enabled successes, saying, “They don’t want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog.” A private equity manager suspected that, among workers at companies in his portfolio, “some of them are working basically half days.”
Our interviews show substantial variation in the degree and kind of value companies derive from AI. The highest-value applications involve wide-reaching organizational change. These patterns warrant attention to the specifics of AI deployments across these companies. In the following section, we assess three common adoption strategies that we observed in our interviews: top-down automation, bottom-up experimentation, and a broader reorganization around AI.
Top-down automation
Mark racked his brain: had he messed anything up recently? As a paralegal at his law firm, he was rarely called into a partner’s office and even more rarely ended up in an office with two of the firm’s equity partners. They wanted to “talk about his AI use,” a topic that filled him with dread. He had already realized that models’ continued improvement would mean “the beginning of the end for my work.” He worried, “Why would anyone want to employ someone like me?”
Mark’s fears were understandable—and far from unique. This past year, AI has loomed especially large in performance assessments across industries. Some of the most sobering moments in our interviews were when managers described making difficult decisions to terminate employees who wouldn’t adopt AI. One engineering leader described experiencing a “morale hit” after the company terminated a developer who, they said, “just kind of shut down instead of trying to embrace it.” As one person at a financial services firm said of their company’s AI push, “You either get on board or don’t. And this might not be the place for you [if you don’t].” An engineering executive described grappling with the massive performance differences he saw emerging between AI users and AI resisters. Ultimately, he said, “we had a couple people who started off extremely anti-AI, and they moved a little along the spectrum, but not enough, and so we ended up letting them go.” But even heavy AI users were not immune to fears of losing their jobs or falling behind: one operations manager said she woke at 3 a.m., fearing for her career, and asked Claude, “How do I make sure I set myself apart so that AI can’t do everything that I do?”
These cases were rare. Overall, people at five companies described pushing out employees who would not adopt AI, and only two had seen AI automation fully eliminate a position and lead to someone losing their job. (By contrast, 10 companies reported hiring more due to AI, primarily into AI implementation roles and to bolster IT support, and others had grown rapidly for a variety of business reasons.) But layoffs weren’t the only adverse employment effect. People at two-thirds of the companies we spoke to reported reduced hiring due to AI: as one person put it, “We may not be firing, but we’re not hiring.” A third of these hiring declines were due to companies actively shrinking functions through attrition without backfilling the roles. But most were the result of companies forgoing hiring that, in the absence of AI, they would have needed to scale their businesses—a finding consistent with past work suggesting that AI-native startups employ fewer workers. As an engineering leader at a health management company put it, “We’ve added a lot of capacity by buying tokens instead of hiring people.”
Beyond terminations and reduced hiring, nine companies described cutting contracted software developers, customer service representatives, legal counsel, and a range of back-office functions, many of which they had already offshored. These outsourced jobs, which are based on modular tasks (self-contained pieces of work that can be handed off separately), sometimes without high expectations for quality, have been particularly vulnerable to replacement. An executive at a company that worked with an offshore design firm said, “We’ve since fired them because now we can get better quality things faster and cheaper” with AI. A finance company downsized well over 100 offshore data and developer contractors. An operations leader at a software company explained that with AI-driven contract reviews, their “legal bill has just completely disappeared.”
These reductions were often the result of top-down workflow automation. For example, one financial technology company adopted AI customer service agents and cut its offshore customer service contracts. Instead of managing human customer service representatives and fielding escalated calls themselves, customer service managers now review transcripts of conversations with the AI agents and edit the agents’ prompts, knowledge graphs, and general operating procedures. One company built an agent as part of a document review workflow. The agent reads submissions against the company’s approval policies and passes a structured analysis to human reviewers. Deploying the agent led the company to cut the number of reviewers it expected to hire for the coming year by more than 90%.
These agentic automations—in which AI agents are given instructions and then operate largely autonomously—are more advanced than the chatbots that still define many employees’ experiences with AI. AI-native startups take these automated workflows to the extreme, both in the products they offer and in how they organize their own work. One Chief Operating Officer walked us through his one-stop agentic portal for operations, noting that 90% of his operations budget was spent on AI tokens and 10% on headcount. He said of his approach, “Look, don’t hire anybody on the back office. I’m going to automate it.”
One AI startup founder told us bluntly that their company’s pitch was to replace the back-office workers their customers currently employed: “You’re trying to fire your [data] labelers, I guess.” A founder of a marketing startup described how their “marketing factory” had flipped from humans doing 80% of the work and AI doing 20% to the opposite. Another startup founder estimated that their company spent as much on internal AI use as on labor, and that it would need three times as many employees without AI. Overall, the six startups that gave us an estimate said they would need, on average, four times as many employees without AI.
Another top-down deployment involves using AI to monitor employees more closely. Under the Anthropic Usage Policy, employee monitoring and its scope must be disclosed to employees, and the monitoring must be limited to employers’ systems for security, safety, logistics, or compliance purposes. The policy further defines employment decisions, like evaluating an employee’s performance, as high-risk, and requires a human in the loop and disclosure to employees. The workplace monitoring we heard about appeared to be compliant with these restrictions, and did not always involve Claude.
One engineering executive explained, “You want to make your work legible to your manager. But nowadays I think you want to make your work legible to the agents your manager uses.” This executive, and others we spoke to, were ambivalent about the implications of these capabilities, seeing both the benefits of more accurate performance feedback and the risks of workplace surveillance—a “panopticon effect,” as one executive put it. An operations supervisor said he started each day by reviewing an AI report on the throughput and error rate of each member of his 12-person document extraction team: “If somehow there was a lag, then I can question back to them, ‘Okay, what happened this hour?’” Another operations director set up an AI-based assessment process for the firm’s customer service representatives. An agent codes their transcripts according to dozens of performance dimensions, then routes the results to a dashboard monitored by the customer service representatives’ managers.
Top-down deployments like these shift power from employees to executives and owners. But they can also be brittle, because they can quickly become out of date or obsolete. For example, the dozens of performance dimensions that customer service representatives were rated on are scored by a two-year-old model and are not taken seriously by managers. Similarly, a law firm built a series of automations for document management but ended up with a number of low-quality “zombie” apps that were hardly used. One engineering leader described a chatbot their company had built for customer service workers—an early experiment built on an open-source chat interface—as “super basic; just chat and answer.” They said the system was difficult to update and maintain, and that “we haven’t spent any more time or money on it.”
These systems are largely built by outside vendors rather than developed directly by internal users, and are marketed as targeted solutions for a specific industry and function. In interview after interview, companies described how improvements in model capabilities rendered these products outdated. As one employee said of one such system, “It’ll be obsolete in three months.” One executive despaired of the up-front investments needed to build top-down workflows as models rapidly improved: “It’s almost like we’re trying to throw darts at a spinning dart board.”
Similar problems emerge in even the most ambitious automation attempts, those targeting knowledge work that requires deep expertise. Standing up effective workflows in these areas typically requires experts to design the agents’ prompts and evaluate their outputs. But this means experts are effectively being asked to build and maintain the very systems that could replace them. One software engineer, who we’ll call Ellen, described her first encounter with automated coding: “I don’t think that my job is secure… software engineers are going to be obsolete.” Another employee put it even more bluntly: “If I’m open to this, I’m essentially building my own coffin.”
Managers also end up facing understandable resistance from employees. Recall the company that used AI to automate an approval workflow. It intended to double the output of expert reviewers and reduce hiring by more than 90%. The human reviewers balked. As one executive put it, “Just because [a reviewer] can now do double the amount of cases, how do you incentivize them to do double the amount of cases?” The company considered offering gift cards to get reviewers to comply. At the time of our interview, the executive noted that while some reviewers were down to two minutes of review per submission, “there’s some that are hanging out in the 10-plus minutes.”
Likewise, recall the senior developer who’d automated one law firm’s mailroom. Fresh off that success, he told us, his COO put him on a more ambitious project: using AI to check for conflicts of interest among the firm’s prospective clients. Under the existing process, conflict staff would run a search, print out any hits, and pass “the buck right onto the attorney.” In under a week, he built a workflow that let attorneys request a check from an AI agent in plain language, which then routed the request through conflict-checking software. But the new workflow left it to the conflict staff to work through each potential conflict—and would often surface the types of complex and difficult conflicts that had previously been passed to the attorneys. Faced with this new work, the staff pushed back, the agent was shelved, and the firm returned to its old process.
Top-down AI deployment is already changing hiring and contracting patterns by automating whole workflows. It is also prompting resistance from experts and raising fears of workplace surveillance. That resistance can result in abandoned or fragile automations.
Bottom-up experimentation
For many companies, the problems of layoffs or the AI panopticon haven’t really arrived. Recall Mark, the paralegal who worried for his job after being called in to meet his bosses. The meeting was not the one he expected. Mark explained to us that at the meeting, the partners noted that his demand letters were better than others’ and asked him how he'd prompted AI so effectively. Mark said he’d felt hesitant about sharing his workflows. He remembered telling them, “That’s my secret sauce. I have my own workflow, my own process, and respectfully—please, do not take this the wrong way—I do not want to share with anyone.”
This pattern, of a few individual contributors thriving with AI, came up in many of our interviews, particularly for companies doing bottom-up deployments. Nontechnical knowledge workers with substantial expertise in a given domain often derived the highest value from such deployments. This is in line with prior research on Claude Code usage, which found that nontechnical experts had the highest task success rates. One accountant described “vibe-coding” an app that audits whether the 401(k) payments employers process actually end up in the investment fund they are intended for. This audit process requires matching payment records across dozens of different systems and providers and previously took accountants 80 hours. “I was able to show that to our team. They were like, ‘Wow, this is super cool,’” the accountant said. “They looked at me and they were like, ‘You built this?’ And I was like, ‘Sort of. I told Claude what I needed to do.’”
In these cases, coding tools clearly empower domain experts. A former airport operations manager told us about building a vehicle tracking app, saying, “I was wielding AI like Excalibur.” Quality assurance supervisors at a chemical plant built an app to monitor filtration rates despite having no coding experience: “They know they’re using Python because [Claude] told them.”
However, even the most dramatic success stories were often limited to changes that could be made from the bottom up. An employee at a manufacturing company explained, “We’re getting just these pockets of really cool stuff that could be great for our organization, but not necessarily a way to enable everyone to use that.” Swapping out a single software tool or building a new personal productivity app can be done by ambitious individual contributors. One investment manager at a real estate firm developed a deal tracker that replaced a third-party product that cost $10,000 per year. Another created a legacy Windows XP app that would have cost $250,000 to replace.
While many of these homegrown software replacements seem like notable upgrades at first, they still require review and ongoing maintenance—which means they can result in relatively small savings overall. How customized (and, therefore, how complex) does a deal tracker really need to be? An operations director at a large law firm considered building out dashboards to monitor their recruitment pipeline, but realized:
That’s small beans. There are plenty of SaaS [products] out there that can help you make dashboards. What is it—$30 a month, $50 a month, $100 a month, even? So, we can save that money by vibe coding. But the maintenance cost obviously goes up as well, and we have to get our talent manager to start maintaining a vibe-coded dashboard.
