The Times also notes that the Commerce Department will now be responsible for enforcing trade restrictions on Megaspeed, after facing accusations that Lutnick was too close to Huang and Nvidia, and failed to adequately police its chip sales to China.
The DOJ said last week that it has taken over the Commerce Department’s investigation, but it’s still “ongoing.” The department also recently added a rule aimed at blocking a loophole that could allow Chinese firms to access banned AI chips remotely. According to the DOJ, Nvidia added Megaspeed to its no-sell list last year after the Commerce Department requested Nvidia’s records on its “direct or indirect” sales to the company.

articles.title: The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
articles.body:
Weeks before the end of the legislative session, some members of Congress are scrambling to reauthorize a controversial warrantless wiretapping authority, possibly by attaching it to a must-pass military spending bill. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politicothat Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) could be attached to the National Defense Authorization Act. It’s the latest in a grueling fight over a major spying rule that hasn’t technically lapsed.
The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
Warrantless wiretapping proponents are rushing to beat the looming blue wave.
“We don’t have two weeks to work just on FISA,” said Rounds, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “But if it’s amended onto the NDAA then you can move it forward and get that done in time.”
FISA allows for the warrantless surveillance of certain foreigners’ communications, ostensibly on national security grounds. In part because of FISA’s broad scope, Congress revisits it every few years, both to reauthorize the authority and to reform it. The last effort to do both failed. Despite pressure from President Donald Trump, Congress failed to reauthorize FISA over the summer, in part because leadership wouldn’t allow any amendments — particularly attempts to limit its sweeping scope — to be debated or introduced. (Trump didn’t help matters when he made Bill Pulte the acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, who reportedly bragged about purging one-third of the DNI staff, is now the director of federal housing.) But the surveillance authority didn’t actually lapse because the FISA court rectified surveillance under Section 702 back in March, meaning the surveillance state can keep chugging along as is for another four months.
So why the urgency? If you haven’t heard, there’s about to be a new Congress in town — one that is even less likely to give Trump seemingly unlimited spying powers without some semblance of reform.
Support for — and opposition to — FISA isn’t a clear-cut partisan issue. Last time around, a bipartisan coalition led by House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT), the ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, led the campaign for a “clean” reauthorization of FISA. Their efforts were defeated largely because of holdouts from the Freedom Caucus, whose privacy concerns echoed those of liberal lawmakers. FISA’s critics wanted reform, not abolition. Their goal was to make it harder for intelligence agencies to use the statute, which is intended for foreign targets, to access Americans’ communications.
“It was remarkable watching two dozen House Republicans stand up to the establishment, stand up to Mike Johnson, and fight to reform FISA,” said Michael Baick, an organizer with the OpenAI boycott campaign QuitGPT, which has been advocating for FISA reform to stop AI surveillance. “This has always been a bipartisan issue where Americans of all stripes can agree, and trying to make deals with the establishment to maintain the status quo, while the ground is shifting, is just short-sighted and missing what this moment really is.”
“I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time.”
Johnson and Himes were adamantly opposed to any reining in of Section 702, stressing the need for a so-called “clean reauthorization.” Both claimed there had already been reforms. “It ain’t the same FISA,” Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) declared in April.
But the changes reformers most wanted were missing. Among them were a warrant requirement and an end to what critics say are major loopholes. Under Section 702, intelligence agencies can pull the communications of non-US persons not in the United States — that is, foreign nationals outside the country. But federal agencies like the FBI and NSA can buy Americans’ data from private brokers, a practice FBI director Kash Patel admits is ongoing. And intelligence agencies can use Section 702 to obtain the communications of non-US persons who are communicating with Americans — a workaround known as the “backdoor search loophole.”
“I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time,” Don Bell, senior policy counsel at the Constitution Project of the Project on Government Oversight, told The Verge. “This is something everyone knew was coming down the pike. There have been months to do this, and I don’t think anyone is saying don’t reauthorize at all. The argument is this is an incredibly powerful surveillance tool, and there needs to be guardrails in place to protect people’s constitutional rights.”
Himes, arguably the Democratic Party’s biggest champion of FISA, seems willing to give Trump one more win before the blue wave crashes down in Washington. “I made it clear to some very senior administration officials that they should get this thing done in the lame-duck,” he told The Hill, “because it’s, you know, going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.”
But Himes didn’t have the votes this summer, and it’s even less likely that he’ll have the votes for a clean reauthorization now.

articles.title: “Pervert glasses" named word of the year by Macquarie Dictionary
articles.body:
Each year, the Macquarie Dictionary calls together a select Committee to discuss the new words and definitions that have entered the Macquarie Dictionary over the past year. The aim of this is to select one of these to be awarded the Committee’s Choice Word of the Year.
As part of this process, our editors create a longlist of words across 13 categories which, over the course of a few hours, are whittled down into a shortlist. And from this, the Word of the Year is chosen.
The Committee this year was comprised of:
- Editorial Team at Macquarie Dictionary
- David Astle – crossword maker, radio host, and writer
- Tiger Webb – language research specialist, ABC
The shortlist is then opened to the public to register what you think the Word of the Year should be. The word with the most votes is awarded the People’s Choice Word of the Year.
You can review the final shortlist here (and for those interested, the longlist here). Thank you for helping us decide on the defining new word of 2026!
Macquarie Dictionary Word of the Year 2026
2026 has undeniably been another year of rapid technological development, especially in the world of AI, as it finds its way into more and more parts of our lives. This year’s Word of the Year winner and runners up reflect this continued development, but also recognise that life does continue in and around our changing world.
Committee Winner
PERVERT GLASSES
plural noun Colloquial camera glasses; smart glasses.
[from the use by some of filming or taking photos of others without their knowledge or consent]
‘The coinage pervert glasses is a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026 in so many ways. On the one hand, we’ve seen a massive acceleration in the capabilities of AI and products that integrate it. At the same time, the undeniably critical nickname pervert glasses mirrors the widespread calls to hit the brakes on this seemingly unchecked development. The name represents the year we’ve all endured, with AI, the manosphere, increasing surveillance in supermarkets, and more. Sure these new gadgets might be marketed as smart glasses or camera glasses, but it seems to us that pervert glasses paints a more apt reflection of the year.’
–THE COMMITTEE
Committee Honourable Mentions
PMOS
noun (polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome) a disorder, possibly genetic, leading to irregularities in ovulation and menstruation in women; associated with acne, excess hair growth, insulin resistance, and obesity. Formerly known as PCOS (polycystic ovarian syndrome).
‘As awareness of medical misogyny (a WOTY 2025 honourable mention) spreads, we hope to see more terms like PMOS entering the dictionary. It shows the power that language can hold, both negatively in the problems caused by the commonly misleading term PCOS, and positively in how this decade-long Australian-led campaign to rename this condition was recently adopted worldwide.’
–THE COMMITTEE
AGENTIC
adjective (especially of artificial intelligence) able to act or make decisions independently.
‘While it might not be the most flashy, funny, or socially impactful word on the surface, agentic has seen an exponential increase in usage over the last 12 months. Where 2024 and 2025 saw the development and massive spread of large language models, the release of agentic AI tools such as OpenClaw and the mischief they recently wrought has brought this otherwise very technical term firmly into the mainstream.’
–THE COMMITTEE
MARRICKVILLE PAUSE
noun Colloquial a temporary halt in conversation by people in the inner-west suburbs of Sydney, to await the passing of a loud, low-flying aircraft, after which the conversation continues.
[so called because the suburb Marrickville lies directly beneath a flight path, in very close proximity to the international airport]
‘It is undeniable that we are facing major cultural shifts in the digital world, and as a result, seeing huge language innovation at an international scale. Marrickville pause represents a departure from this trend – a highly localised term for a purely physical phenomenon, but one that is so universally experienced by people who spend time in the area.’
–THE COMMITTEE
People’s Choice Winner
And we have a threepeat! For the third year running, the public have aligned with the Committee’s choice by selecting pervert glasses to be crowned People’s Choice Word of the Year 2026!
PERVERT GLASSES
plural noun Colloquial camera glasses; smart glasses.
[from the use by some of filming or taking photos of others without their knowledge or consent]
People’s Choice Honourable Mentions
DIGITAL DEMENTIA
noun a supposed condition characterised by short-term memory loss, attention deficit, impaired decision-making, etc., thought to result from an excessive reliance on digital devices and artificial intelligence.
‘Digital dementia is, of course, not a real medical diagnosis but that hasn’t stopped the fear of an increasing reliance on digital devices from resonating deeply. People are finding that they’re struggling to navigate without Google Maps and to make and remember plans without iCal. It will be interesting to see if all of this outsourcing does in fact lead to impaired cognition in the long term.’
–THE COMMITTEE
AI;DR
interjection Colloquial a term used by a reader to indicate to others that an online item has been created by AI and is not worth reading.
[AI + d(on’t) or d(idn’t) r(ead); modelled on TL;DR]
‘A nice play on TL;DR (a code for too long; didn’t read), AI;DR gives fellow readers an instant heads-up that the text to follow is what they consider to be AI slop. As the sheer volume of AI generated text is ever-increasing, this succinct code will become a much-welcomed time saver.’
–THE COMMITTEE

articles.title: US To Blacklist Asian AI Firm Megaspeed After Nvidia Scandal
articles.body:
US To Blacklist Asian AI Firm Megaspeed After Nvidia Scandal (bbc.com) 68
			
		 	
				The U.S. Commerce Department plans to blacklist Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed and its subsidiary Speedmatrix over suspicions that they helped Chinese companies obtain restricted Nvidia AI chips. The move follows allegations that a former Megaspeed executive had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while working as a Chinese intelligence asset, although Commerce officials say their investigation into the company began nearly two years ago. The BBC reports:  The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US. The company is mainly a developer of data centers, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang. [...] When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang. Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US. China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

articles.title: Hackers Compromise Check Point Servers In 22 Organizations
articles.body:
Hackers Compromise Check Point Servers In 22 Organizations (bleepingcomputer.com) 2
			
		 	
				Hackers have compromised 24 Check Point Security management servers across 22 organizations in 17 countries in a suspected cyberespionage campaign, according to threat intelligence firm GreyNoise. BleepingComputer reports:  The researchers track the activity as GT13 and confirmed it was ongoing between October 17 and November 2, when their visibility ended. However, given the threat actor's persistent access to Check Point devices, they believe the campaign remains active. GreyNoise says the 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries, and show no clear evidence of specific targeting. They include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors. The attacks were launched from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes.
A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments. While GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached, it observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232 during the post-compromise stages. The vulnerability is an authentication bypass in Check Point SmartConsole that allows attackers to obtain an application login token and authenticate with administrator privileges. Check Point warned about the flaw in July, marking it as an actively exploited zero-day. articles.title: Dozens of oil and shipping tankers hacked in recent weeks, per report
articles.body:
U.S. officials suspect Iranian hackers may be behind as many as 50 cyberattacks targeting shipping vessels in recent weeks, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.
The ships carrying oil, liquefied gas, and other explosive chemicals were hacked as they traveled across Asia and Europe. Several oil tankers headed toward the U.S. coast in August also had their navigation systems breached, prompting cybersecurity teams within the FBI and Coast Guard to board the vessels.
The report said officials are investigating if Iran is expanding its recent wave of hacks against the U.S. by targeting large vessels to sow fear among shippers, disrupt routes, or to cause an explosion at a port. (Ships have backup controls in the event that automated systems are hacked or fail.)
Hackers may have been abusing a bug dubbed FortiBleed, which allows hackers to break into networks by compromising vulnerable Fortinet-made routers. A joint FBI-Coast Guard security alert from September warned that Fortinet routers are used on shipping vessels.
Iran has been firing back on all sides since the start of the U.S./Israel-led war earlier this year, which killed the country’s supreme leader. Many of Iran’s retaliations have been in the form of cyberattacks, with U.S. officials blaming Iran for hacks targeting hundreds of American water providers and U.S. medical tech companies.
A spokesperson for the FBI did not respond to a request for comment about the shipping hacks or whether it had a more accurate figure.

articles.title: How to Make a Lovable City
articles.body:
Everyone loves the streets of old cities like Verona, Bruges, and Prague. The reason might seem obvious: they are lined by beautiful historic buildings. But people also love the streets of Osaka, Taipei, and Hong Kong. While the buildings of the latter cities are mostly modern and nondescript, their streets are still full of character and enchantment.
The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte (pronounced ‘zitter’) sought to explain what makes some public spaces more successful than others in a lively, opinionated masterpiece called The Art of Building Cities, published in 1889. Sitte argued that the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small, creating a sense of shelter and intimacy, defining picturesque views and perspectives, and making public buildings appear larger and more dignified by comparison. He denied the importance of symmetry and claimed, counterintuitively, that monuments should be pushed to the edge of squares, and that great public buildings should generally be entangled in a mass of everyday housing.
Sitte’s book was explosively successful, seizing the imagination of late nineteenth-century Europe. For a few decades, Sitte was a decisive figure in international urban planning, and planners across the world strove to implement his ideas. But after modernism came to dominate Western planning in the mid-twentieth century, Sitte was mostly forgotten.
Sitte’s attacks were directed against the repetitive grids, sweeping boulevards, and impersonal regularity of most nineteenth-century urban planning. To many people today, however, nineteenth-century urbanism is relatively appealing; certainly, it is a lot more attractive than the motorways, slab blocks, and concrete plazas that came after. This can make Sitte strange to read, but it also makes him even more important now than he was in his own time.
Anyone who wants to build beautiful cities today needs to understand what it is that makes the most beloved cities of the past so successful. Focusing only on the appearance of buildings can only get you so far. As Sitte showed, some of the world’s most impressive buildings are badly let down by their surroundings, and form part of inhospitable and uninviting public spaces. Equally, neighborhoods consistent with Sittean principles can be wonderfully charming even if their constituent buildings are nothing special. Understanding these principles may be the key to building new neighbourhoods and cities that people truly love being in.
Create enclosed spaces
The first principle of The Art of Building Cities is the importance of creating physically enclosed public spaces. People feel calmer and more protected in such spaces, which they experience as ‘outdoor rooms’. An enclosed outdoor area can also develop its own character, just as kitchens, bedrooms, and bathrooms have their respective characters. Sitte would have seen a city without enclosed public spaces as analogous to an extremist open-plan house, where the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom are open onto each other and bleed constantly into one another’s character.
While the rooms of a house are created with partition walls, the enclosed spaces of a city are created with buildings. A conundrum for urban designers is that the building wall of a square generally has to be repeatedly broken to provide access. A square is thus like a room with five or ten large doors, permanently left wide open, undermining its sense of enclosure. Sitte was keenly interested in how to handle the entrances to squares so as to mitigate this.
The picture above shows the Grand-Place of Brussels. Most of the entrances are at the corners, and at each corner, only one street enters. These streets continue the plane of the square rather than entering at a diagonal. This means that, from almost any point in the square, the two building walls appear to overlap each other, effectively concealing the entrance to the street and preserving the sense of enclosure. The resulting ‘turbine square’ is so common in old towns that, as Sitte said, ‘it can be considered as one of the conscious or subconscious principles of ancient city building’.
Even better than a turbine square, in Sitte’s view, was one whose entrances had been bridged over, creating a fully continuous building line around the square. This is particularly common in Spain. The Plaça Reial in Barcelona has seven entrances, but six have been bridged over, so that the square feels like a courtyard or cloister. Colonnades, which Sitte thought to be a greatly underrated device in urban design, provide a simple way to achieve this.
London’s Trafalgar Square is an example of the opposite, a ‘square’ that is only weakly enclosed. Wherever one stands, one can generally see two or more of the wide and busy roads that join it. Like many nineteenth-century squares, Trafalgar Square was never intended to be an enclosed space, but rather was designed to improve the flow of carriages between the Strand and the West End.
An even more extreme example of an unenclosed ‘square’ is the Place de la Concorde in Paris, which has no fewer than nine roads entering and exiting it, and buildings on only one side. The space is bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians, who must work their way across successive roads without buildings to shape their route and shelter them on their way.
Sitte applied this logic to streets as well as squares, arguing that curves and T-junctions should be used to visually terminate streets and give them a sense of enclosure. The picture above shows Broad Street, one of America’s rare curving streets. The combination of the curve of the street and partial T-junction at the end means that Broad Street is visually closed by the Federal Hall National Memorial, creating a famously beautiful and charismatic space. The second photograph shows a more typical Manhattan street, experienced as an endless canyon separating continents of buildings, what Sitte called ‘parallels vanishing at infinity’.
Squares should not be too large
If a square is too large, it loses its sense of enclosure, and its buildings look strangely diminished by their surroundings. Sitte provided a rule of thumb in sizing squares: the dimensions of a square should not be greater than twice the height of the principal building in it. The pictures above show two examples of over-large squares: the Plaza de la Armería in Madrid and Heroes’ Square in Budapest. Both feel demoralizingly vast, with the monumental buildings they are meant to showcase (Madrid Cathedral, and Budapest’s Hall of Art) dwindling to visual insignificance on the horizon, so that they resemble doll’s houses. In both squares, the buildings are so miniaturized that they no longer seem like enclosing walls, leaving the visitor exposed in a huge open space. This problem could be solved by making the buildings much taller, but although the square would then feel enclosed, the buildings would have become terrifyingly huge, as if meant for giants rather than human beings (the courtyard of Les Espaces d’Abraxas near Paris is an example of this pitfall in the wild).
Some of the world’s most famous squares are, in fact, far too large. St Peter’s Square in the Vatican, seen above, was designed by the famous artist Bernini, and it does indeed look impressive in drone footage. For human visitors, however, it is an exhausting place, overwhelming without being impressive. The Basilica looks small and stubby, exactly the opposite of the desired effect. On a summer’s day, the vast, unshaded space becomes relentlessly inhospitable, and visitors huddle under the colonnades for shelter.
By contrast, the small square in front of the Pantheon in Rome exemplifies the features Sitte prized. It is impossible to fully capture its feeling of enclosure in a two-dimensional photograph, but some sense of the intimacy of the space is apparent in the pictures above, which show how this magnifies the Pantheon. The Pantheon is a smaller building than Madrid Cathedral or Saint Peter’s Basilica, but it is much bigger relative to the square. This allows it to retain its dignity, despite the fact that the level of the street has risen by 1.3 meters since Antiquity, swallowing the steps that originally led up to the entrance.
Symmetry is overrated
At the time Sitte was writing, many planners believed that harmonious spaces should have regular, symmetrical plans, an idea which remains influential today. In English we even use the confusing word ‘square’ for any enclosed public spaces, whatever their shape.
Sitte rejected this, believing that symmetrical spaces do not necessarily feel harmonious at ground level, and that asymmetry is not generally disharmonious at all. The pictures above show the perfectly symmetrical Place Vendôme in Paris. Seen from a satellite, it is visually striking and certainly neater than an irregular space. Its chamfered plan supposedly inspired the design of Chanel’s No 5 perfume bottle. Pedestrians, however, generally do not stand at the exact point at which the objective balance of the buildings is reflected in their field of vision: the various points and angles from which they do experience it may even make it feel quite awkward.
Above is the Piazza delle Erbe, a market square in Verona. This ‘square’ has an odd shape, an elongated and slightly wonky pentagon. Nobody is likely to model perfume bottles on it. But at human level, this does not matter as pedestrians can never take in all five sides at once, and so its irregular form is barely even visible. For the most part, the irregularities are ‘seen only on paper’, and to the extent they are visible, they are not experienced as imperfections. Sitte argued that they in fact serve to subtly arouse visual interest, and also create happy recesses that can host resting places, statues, or other public art.
Move monuments to the edges
If you were putting an ornament in your living room, you would be very unlikely to stand it in the middle of the carpet. It would get in the way, break up the space, and might well look lost and isolated. Nor would you place it in front of one of the room’s main features, like the fireplace. It would block the view of the fireplace, and the fireplace would be a disagreeably busy backdrop. Almost certainly, you would put it against the wall, preferably a relatively neutral wall to create a calm background.
Sitte thought the same considerations applied to the placing of sculptures, fountains, and other monuments in outdoor spaces. Statues should not be placed in the middle of squares, where they would block natural routes, break up the space, and look isolated and diminished. Nor should they be placed on axes with key buildings, where they block the view of the architecture. Instead they should line the sides, where they can stand out against relatively neutral backgrounds.
This was implicitly understood in Antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance, and Sitte illustrates his book with examples from all three periods. Above, for example, is the Piazza della Signoria in Florence. The numerous statues line the sides of the square, leaving the center free for people to pass through or mill about. This is advantageous for the statues too: Michelangelo’s David (today a replica, since the original was moved indoors) stands out splendidly against the plain masonry walls of the Palazzo Vecchio.
Later planners became fascinated by the apparent neatness of centering statues. Above is the Victoria Memorial in London. The Memorial stands on the main axis of the Mall, blocking the view of Buckingham Palace behind it. This is not advantageous for the Memorial either, whose outline clashes confusedly with the complex detailing of the building. If you search through pictures of the Memorial, you will notice that most photographers picture it from an awkward oblique angle, the least bad way to capture both the monument and the central pavilion of the palace.
Isolating statues against the sky is not much better. A bronze cast of David was later placed on the Piazzale Michelangelo, at the center of a wide square with stunning views over Florence. The statue is enormous, over five meters tall, but it looks strangely miniaturized in its location. Sitte remarked that contemporary tourists often came away with the drastically false impression that it was life-sized. We judge size partly by comparison, and when an object is isolated from comparators, its size becomes harder to assess. This is why the backdrop of a wall can make sculpture look bigger and grander by providing a constant visual key.
In Sitte’s view, the plain edge of a small square was not only an acceptable site for a statue, but the best one. Sitte disliked museums, which he called ‘art prisons’, and thought that only people with a ‘special mental preparation’ could enjoy art under their ‘morbid influences’. The Sittesque city would be one that teemed with art, but woven into the urban fabric as an adornment of ordinary civic life.
Buildings need context
Sitte’s view on buildings was similar. Nineteenth-century architects tended to place major public buildings in the middle of squares, judging that this gave them greater dignity. Sitte thought this ‘pedantic, futile modern practice’ destroyed the square and squandered the opportunity to frame the public building with vernacular architecture. He pointed out that many historic cities were in fact designed along the lines he proposed. Of the 255 churches of Rome, 41 adjoined other buildings on one side, 96 on two, 110 on three, and two on all four. Only six were freestanding, two of them modern churches of expatriate Protestant communities.
The most striking examples of this arose when nineteenth-century governments actually demolished the vernacular buildings that surrounded historic monuments. This practice, often known by its French name dégagement, was surprisingly common: nineteenth-century planners thought that it displayed the monuments better. It provides a useful experiment on the effect of freestanding versus adjoined monumental architecture.
For example, Notre Dame Cathedral was formerly approached through a narrow street called the Rue Neuve Notre Dame. The street was demolished by the government planner Haussmann in the nineteenth century to create the Parvis Notre-Dame, a large square that the cathedral still faces today. Haussmann intended to improve the view of the cathedral, but the effect is the opposite. The vernacular fabric formed a visual frame, defining and concentrating views onto the facade. It provided scale, making the cathedral look larger by contrast to the ordinary buildings around it. It also prevented visitors from seeing the whole facade until they were very close, close enough that it towered up terrifically before them. Exposed and isolated, Notre Dame looks smaller and lonelier.
Sitte thought that cities should move in the opposite direction. The Votive Church in Vienna was built in the 1870s on what Sitte described as a ‘desolate monster plaza’ that was ‘intolerably exposed to high wind, inclement weather, heat and dust, as well as to the din of the streets, and the incessant clanging of trams.’ The church does indeed have an awkward and lonely feeling. Sitte thought that the architecture of the building was actually very good, and that the defects in its effect were entirely the fault of its location. He proposed building up regular urban fabric on most of the ‘monster plaza’, defining three small squares with well-framed views onto the church. Sitte’s motives were aesthetic, but we should also note the density and spatial efficiency of his scheme.
Another way to understand this contrast is to look at whole cities planned on Sittesque and anti-Sittesque principles. The pictures below show Padua and Washington DC. It is as though a figure-ground switch has taken place: in Padua, the buildings are molded around spaces; in Washington, space is molded around buildings. Monumental buildings in Washington sit alone on their city blocks, untouched by vernacular fabric. Monumental buildings in Padua constantly link up with vernacular fabric to shape small, sheltered spaces from which they can be properly enjoyed.
The rise, fall, and rise of Camillo Sitte
The Art of Building Cities was an immediate success, landing, in the words of Sitte’s English translator Charles T Stewart, ‘like a demolition bomb on the city planning practices of Europe’. Within a year of publication it had prompted the redrawing of urban expansion plans in Germany and Austria, and Sitte was being approached by town officials seeking his advice on their own plans. By Sitte’s death in 1903, advocates of his ideas were to be found in prestigious positions in cities including Munich, Berlin, and Vienna, either teaching or as official city architects.
Two Helsinki neighborhoods demonstrate the effect of Sittesque ideas on urban planning. In the nineteenth century, Helsinki followed a neoclassical grid plan, with straight streets meeting at right angles. In the early twentieth century, it switched dramatically to a Sittesque approach, introducing curving streets, turbine squares, T-junctions, and asymmetrical spaces. The resulting neighborhood is full of pleasing, characterful spaces and unexpected ‘old town’ effects, even though it is made up of the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets as its predecessor.
But Sitte’s influence was curiously short-lived. In the decades following Sitte’s death in 1903, European urban design came to be dominated by the modernist movement. Everything that Sitte hated about nineteenth-century planning was vastly amplified in modernism. With honorable exception, the modernists treated public space as merely whatever was left over after the buildings had been placed, and had no sympathy with Sitte’s approach of treating spaces as primary and shaping the buildings around them. Instead of lining the edge of a city block with buildings (a ‘perimeter block’) they preferred to orient all blocks in the same direction (‘parallel blocks’), often with a seemingly arbitrary angle to the street. Sitte had decried the gridiron blocks of the nineteenth century for the weakly defined spaces they created. But by twentieth-century standards, the straight ‘corridor streets’ of the nineteenth century look comparatively Sittesque.
Modernists also wanted to reduce the built footprint, leaving more space for greenery, parking, and roads. Sitte’s preference for small squares and enclosed spaces was in tension with this. Many modernists saw him as an impractical romantic. The critic Sigfried Giedion described Sitte as ‘a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry’.
Ironically, modernism proved to be Sitte’s great vindication, as modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide. Architects of all stylistic persuasions have once again become interested in streets and squares, in creating public spaces with intimacy and character. Designers associated with the ‘New Urbanist’ movement are often openly followers of Sitte, and famous New Urbanist towns like Seaside in Florida, I’On in South Carolina, and Poundbury in Dorset were explicitly designed under Sitte’s influence. But the Sittesque revival goes far beyond this. Prominent contemporary practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber produce highly Sittesque urban designs, creating intimate infill schemes that recall the old towns and bazaar districts of the Middle Ages.
Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently. Many recent attempts to make traditional streets and squares look awkward or stilted. This should not surprise us: building cities is an art perfected over hundreds of years. City-builders today are lucky that Sitte distilled and recorded its key principles, just before the art itself was lost. Studying Sitte can help us to relearn it.
Phoebe Arslanagic-Little is a writer and policy researcher.
Samuel Hughes is an editor at Works in Progress.

It also prevented visitors from seeing the whole facade until they were very close, close enough that it towered up terrifically before them. Exposed and isolated, Notre Dame looks smaller and lonelier.
Sitte thought that cities should move in the opposite direction. The Votive Church in Vienna was built in the 1870s on what Sitte described as a ‘desolate monster plaza’ that was ‘intolerably exposed to high wind, inclement weather, heat and dust, as well as to the din of the streets, and the incessant clanging of trams.’ The church does indeed have an awkward and lonely feeling. Sitte thought that the architecture of the building was actually very good, and that the defects in its effect were entirely the fault of its location. He proposed building up regular urban fabric on most of the ‘monster plaza’, defining three small squares with well-framed views onto the church. Sitte’s motives were aesthetic, but we should also note the density and spatial efficiency of his scheme.
Another way to understand this contrast is to look at whole cities planned on Sittesque and anti-Sittesque principles. The pictures below show Padua and Washington DC. It is as though a figure-ground switch has taken place: in Padua, the buildings are molded around spaces; in Washington, space is molded around buildings. Monumental buildings in Washington sit alone on their city blocks, untouched by vernacular fabric. Monumental buildings in Padua constantly link up with vernacular fabric to shape small, sheltered spaces from which they can be properly enjoyed.
The rise, fall, and rise of Camillo Sitte
The Art of Building Cities was an immediate success, landing, in the words of Sitte’s English translator Charles T Stewart, ‘like a demolition bomb on the city planning practices of Europe’. Within a year of publication it had prompted the redrawing of urban expansion plans in Germany and Austria, and Sitte was being approached by town officials seeking his advice on their own plans. By Sitte’s death in 1903, advocates of his ideas were to be found in prestigious positions in cities including Munich, Berlin, and Vienna, either teaching or as official city architects.
Two Helsinki neighborhoods demonstrate the effect of Sittesque ideas on urban planning. In the nineteenth century, Helsinki followed a neoclassical grid plan, with straight streets meeting at right angles. In the early twentieth century, it switched dramatically to a Sittesque approach, introducing curving streets, turbine squares, T-junctions, and asymmetrical spaces. The resulting neighborhood is full of pleasing, characterful spaces and unexpected ‘old town’ effects, even though it is made up of the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets as its predecessor.
But Sitte’s influence was curiously short-lived. In the decades following Sitte’s death in 1903, European urban design came to be dominated by the modernist movement. Everything that Sitte hated about nineteenth-century planning was vastly amplified in modernism. With honorable exception, the modernists treated public space as merely whatever was left over after the buildings had been placed, and had no sympathy with Sitte’s approach of treating spaces as primary and shaping the buildings around them. Instead of lining the edge of a city block with buildings (a ‘perimeter block’) they preferred to orient all blocks in the same direction (‘parallel blocks’), often with a seemingly arbitrary angle to the street. Sitte had decried the gridiron blocks of the nineteenth century for the weakly defined spaces they created. But by twentieth-century standards, the straight ‘corridor streets’ of the nineteenth century look comparatively Sittesque.
Modernists also wanted to reduce the built footprint, leaving more space for greenery, parking, and roads. Sitte’s preference for small squares and enclosed spaces was in tension with this. Many modernists saw him as an impractical romantic. The critic Sigfried Giedion described Sitte as ‘a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry’.
Ironically, modernism proved to be Sitte’s great vindication, as modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide. Architects of all stylistic persuasions have once again become interested in streets and squares, in creating public spaces with intimacy and character. Designers associated with the ‘New Urbanist’ movement are often openly followers of Sitte, and famous New Urbanist towns like Seaside in Florida, I’On in South Carolina, and Poundbury in Dorset were explicitly designed under Sitte’s influence. But the Sittesque revival goes far beyond this. Prominent contemporary practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber produce highly Sittesque urban designs, creating intimate infill schemes that recall the old towns and bazaar districts of the Middle Ages.
Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently. Many recent attempts to make traditional streets and squares look awkward or stilted. This should not surprise us: building cities is an art perfected over hundreds of years. City-builders today are lucky that Sitte distilled and recorded its key principles, just before the art itself was lost. Studying Sitte can help us to relearn it.
Phoebe Arslanagic-Little is a writer and policy researcher.
Samuel Hughes is an editor at Works in Progress.

articles.title: Jevons Paradox in AI: Cheaper Tokens Won't Pay for Capex
articles.body:
Cheaper AI Tokens Won't Pay for $560 Billion of Capex
Updated 24 November 2026
Contents
Key takeaways
- Token volume and token prices are moving at roughly the same speed, so cheaper inference on its own does not grow AI revenue.
- The price of a fixed level of capability collapses each year, while the cost of running frontier models rises; the revenue sits at the frontier.
- Closing the gap between capex and revenue needs money that today pays for labor, and outcome pricing is how vendors are reaching for it.
- The capex and cash flow figures from March have grown worse: five hyperscalers spent $560 billion in the first three quarters of 2026.
In March I wrote that the hyperscalers’ answer to collapsing inference prices is Jevons: cheaper tokens create so much demand that total spending grows anyway.
On volume, they look right. Google processed 9.7 trillion tokens a month in May 2024. In May 2026 it was 3.2 quadrillion, 330 times as many. Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle spent $230 billion on capex in the third quarter of 2026 alone, almost four times what they spent two years earlier.
But tokens aren’t dollars. Revenue is price times volume, and the price is falling too. So my question is: does demand for tokens grow faster than the price of a token collapses?
The arithmetic
If the price of a token falls 10x and volume grows 10x, revenue is flat. Revenue only grows when volume grows faster than the price falls.
Google’s first-party model APIs went from 7 billion tokens a minute in Q3 2025 to nearly 32 billion in Q3 2026, up 4.6x. Google’s tokens across all products grew 6.7x between the I/O keynotes of 2025 and 2026. OpenRouter went from 0.5 trillion to 128 trillion tokens a week in 20 months, about 27x a year. On the price side, MIT researchers find that the price of reaching a fixed benchmark score falls 5 to 10x a year, and Epoch AI finds that cost per task at fixed performance falls about 13x a year.
Volume and price move at about the same speed. That proves nothing by itself, because Google’s tokens aren’t sold at fixed-capability prices (like the ones Epoch measures). But it lines up with what Mert Demirer, Andrey Fradkin, Nadav Tadelis and Sida Peng found when they used OpenRouter and Azure data to estimate short-run price elasticities “just above one” and concluded that this leaves “limited scope for Jevons-Paradox effects.” At an elasticity of one, a 10x price cut buys 10x the tokens for the same money.
That matches how a lot of buyers behave. Say a bank’s head of operations has $2 million approved for AI contract review, and then the vendor cuts its token prices tenfold. The bank can now review ten times as many contracts, which is great. The budget still says $2 million. To spend more, the head of operations would have to walk into the CFO’s office and argue that the product got cheaper and so deserves a bigger budget, and I wouldn’t want to make that case. So the bank spends the same $2 million. The vendor can say, truthfully, that token volume grew tenfold.
But I guess there’s also a counterargument. Cheaper tokens change what people build. When inference is nearly free, developers design agents that call a model hundreds of times per task, and a recent theory paper argues this can make demand rise faster than prices fall. That may happen.
Two price curves
“The price of a token” hides two curves that move in opposite directions. (1) The price of a fixed level of capability is falling. GPT-4-level answers cost a small fraction of what they did in 2023, and the decline continues. (2) The cost of using the best model available is rising. The same MIT paper finds that the cost of running frontier models on benchmarks rises 3 to 18x a year, because each generation is larger and reasons for longer.
A concrete case: to run the Artificial Analysis benchmark suite, Claude Opus 5.5 at maximum effort used 218 million output tokens, almost three times the median model, at about $10 per task. At low effort the same model used about a tenth of the tokens.
Spending probably follows the frontier curve (at least up until now). In enterprises, open-weight models now handle 19% of tokens but get 4% of spend, while frontier labs take 69% of deployment dollars. Cheap tokens and expensive tokens are close to two separate markets (the cheap one grows fast in volume and barely registers in revenue).
The volume is real
I don’t want to wave the demand away. Google’s token count is the clearest public series we have, and it’s steep.
Agents account for much of it. A paper by Bai, Brynjolfsson, Pentland and co-authors finds that agentic coding tasks use about 1,000 times more tokens than chat about the same code. Anthropic reported in 2025 that multi-agent systems use about 15 times more tokens than chat. OpenRouter dates February 6, 2026 as the last day humans used more tokens on its platform than agents did.
Where the money has to come from
If cheaper tokens alone don’t grow revenue, the money has to come from somewhere else. Bain estimates AI needs $2 trillion of annual revenue by 2030 to fund the compute being built, and that it will still be $800 billion short even if companies reinvest every dollar AI saves them in sales, marketing, support and R&D.
You can already see vendors reaching for that money in their pricing. Intercom charges $0.99 for each customer case its Fin agent resolves, a price set against the cost of a support agent’s time, whatever the tokens cost. Salesforce has changed its Agentforce pricing three times since 2024. The direction is clear. Vendors want to be paid per outcome, and an outcome is priced against a (human) wage.
Workers aged 22 to 25 in the jobs most exposed to AI saw a 13% relative drop in employment compared with less exposed peers. US employers cited AI in about 121,000 announced job cuts in the first ten months of 2026, about a fifth of all announced cuts.
Receipts
Spending grew faster than I expected when I wrote in March. Back then the five companies guided to $660 to $690 billion for 2026. Their SEC filings show $560 billion of cash capex in the first three quarters, with $230 billion in Q3 alone. That excludes finance leases, so the full figure is higher.
The cash flow squeeze I described has arrived. Oracle spent 174% of its operating cash flow on capex in its fiscal 2026 and Amazon 94% in 2025. Microsoft is at 63%, Meta at 60% and Alphabet at 56%, all well above where they were a few years ago.
Who keeps the money
So far the clearest winner is the company selling the equipment. Nvidia reported $116 billion of revenue at a 75% gross margin in its latest quarter, and its revenue has grown in step with hyperscaler capex for three years.
The model labs sit lower. Press reports put OpenAI’s gross margin at 33 to 39%, depending on the quarter. Anthropic’s S-1 shows about an 85% gross margin, but it books training compute under R&D, so the figure only measures the cost of serving existing models. Even so, it suggests the cost of serving tokens may be falling faster than their price.
Markets have priced the split. Since ChatGPT launched, the semiconductor index has roughly tripled while software stocks and the S&P 500 are both up about 70%. Chips have also fallen 41% from their June peak, so the market is less sure than it was in the summer.

articles.title: Top MIT Physicist: Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About 'Taking over the World'
articles.body:
Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist
Apparently they discuss overthrowing the US government after a few drinks.
by Clare Hymer
24 November 2026
Employees at US artificial intelligence company Anthropic openly talk about “overthrowing the US government” and “taking over the world”, a world-renowned physicist has claimed.
In an interview with Novara Media, Max Tegmark, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said: “When I talk to people who work for Anthropic, after they’ve had a couple of drinks, the conversation often gets into overthrowing the US government and taking over the world.”
“They tend to not use words like ‘coup’ and ‘overthrow the US government’. They instead use the code phrase ‘alignment without control’,” he said.
‘Alignment without control’ is the idea that AI should be kept in check by being instilled with certain values – likely those shared by Anthropic, Tegmark said – rather than being directly controlled by humans.
“We get the sort of future that Alan Turing predicted, where it’s going to be Anthropic’s machine-god running Earth, and then the rest of us just have to hope that somehow it’s gonna be nice.”
Turing, widely regarded as the founder of computer science, famously warned in 1951 that once machines started thinking, we should expect them to take control.
Tegmark said the comments from Anthropic staff should alarm anyone who cares about democracy. “These companies really don’t seem to like it [democracy]. They have lobbied really hard to even prevent any meaningful government oversight of them,” he said.
He added: “Here in the US, OpenAI and Anthropic are less regulated than a sandwich shop.”
Novara Media has approached Anthropic for comment.
Tegmark’s disclosure comes as protests against AI are ramping up across the world.
As Anthropic started trading on the stock market at a staggering $2tn valuation on Thursday, protesters gathered at both the Nasdaq exchange in New York and the firm’s San Francisco headquarters demanding an AI development slowdown.
On Saturday, over 1,000 people marched against “AI extinction” in London in what campaigners said was “the biggest AI safety march in history”.
Clare Hymer is head of articles at Novara Media.

articles.title: Why the US Army is about to blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa
articles.body:
The US Army is moving ahead with plans to detonate the nation’s stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, at approximately 9:00AM CST on Wednesday. The Verge reached out to experts on what to expect, and will keep this post updated.
Why the US Army is about to blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa
The US Army is scrambling to contain any potential lead pollution that could spread if an old stockpile of explosives blows up.
What material is the Army planning to detonate?
There are 68 drums holding about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, an unstable chemical compound created to detonate munitions like grenades. The US started using lead azide as a primary explosive almost a century ago before “moving away” from it about 15 years ago because of how difficult the material is to store and transport, Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), said in a Tuesday press briefing. At that point, the US transferred its remaining stockpile of lead azide to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Lead azide will explode at 350 degrees Celsius (662F). But it is also sensitive to flame, friction, or sudden shock, including fluctuations in temperature.
Some of the material on site in Iowa is more than 60 years old. The material can crystallize as it degrades over time, becoming unstable enough to explode even at ambient temperatures. The Army noted some deterioration of the material in 2009 — but not any “dangerous crystallization” at the time, according to Cekada.
“It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”
The chemical was stored in liquid form, embedded in sawdust and burlap bags inside the drums. Water and ethanol were also added to the containers to keep the lead azide from freezing in the winter. But during a March inspection, Cekada said ATF noticed “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels.” That made the material too unstable for them to open the barrels to add more water and ethanol, Cekada said. Removing a lid might cause the barrels to detonate.
Why is the Army detonating it now?
Officials have been trying to figure out what to do with the crystallized lead azide since that alarming March inspection. The Army initially hired a contractor to safely dissolve the chemicals but canceled the contract earlier this year, according to reporting by The New York Times. Using a chemical neutralization agent “proved to be an unsafe method,” Army Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the 71st Explosive Ordinance Disposal Group, said at the Tuesday briefing, because crystallization on the outside of the barrels made it too risky to open the lids.
“Everyone that we’ve spoken to through their experience has determined that this is the only safe path forward,“ Cekada said at the briefing. If they leave the chemicals as is, he said, they’re still at risk of exploding. “It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”
What are the risks?
Compared to an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion, a controlled detonation is supposed to limit the amount of lead dust unleashed on surrounding communities and the environment. Still, the dust plume could reach as far as 100 miles away from the site. The Army has released maps showing where lead dust is expected to travel based on its modeling.
The last time the Army disposed of lead azide this way at a comparable scale was in 1977, according to Teller. At the time, they detonated 7,000 pounds of the material in Colorado in open air “with zero mitigation.” Even then, 75 percent of the lead particulate stayed on site, Teller said at the briefing. The Army now believes it can “significantly reduce” the spread of that last 25 percent of lead using walls made up of four 16,000-gallon water tanks to capture lead particulate and hopefully prevent it from escaping into the atmosphere.
The 80-year-old earth-covered magazines holding the lead azide are cracked and deteriorating, Teller noted, and they are likely to break open after the detonation. To prepare, they’ve covered it with tarp and a special containment screen for lead. They also plan to flood it with 2 feet of foam to capture particulate pollution. Adam Telle, Acting Secretary of the Army, also said the Army has set out “state of the art gel blocks in huge quantities all around to ensure that we absorb as much of this blast as we possibly can.”
There is no “safe” level of exposure to lead
Last week, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club sought a court order to stop the explosion from taking place, pending an Environmental and Health Impact Statement and an investigation into alternatives to detonating the material. President Donald Trump chimed in on social media, calling for a pause until a federal appeals court gave the Army the green light after previously granting a temporary stay. The court on Monday denied the emergency motion to stop the explosion, clearing the way for the Army to move forward.
What precautions can people nearby take?
The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (Iowa HHS) recommends that anyone in potentially affected areas stay indoors and keep windows shut for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation. Iowa HHS also suggests switching off HVAC systems that might bring outdoor air inside or set them to modes that recirculate air, and using an air purifier with a HEPA filter.
FEMA is helping relocate Middletown residents and others within a voluntary 5-mile evacuation zone. People who are pregnant, children, and individuals with chronic diseases should evacuate the affected areas, Sean Kaufman, principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, said at the briefing. “Outside of that area, if you’re close to that proximity and you’re uncomfortable, I think you need to do what you need to do to take care of your family,” Kaufman said.
There is no “safe” level of exposure to lead, a neurotoxin that poses health risks when inhaled or ingested. Kids are at increased risk because their brains are still developing and are also more likely to touch contaminated surfaces and then stick their fingers in their mouths. But most adverse health effects — which can include fatigue and gastrointestinal upset alongside impacts on brain development — are connected to chronic lead exposure rather than as a result of a one-off event.
“It is likely this exposure will not result in any observable acute clinical signs,” Will Sander, associate professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, says in an email to The Verge. “Overall, the risk is minimal, and there should be no long-term concerns.”
What happens after the explosion?
“The Army has done this before a long time ago and took lead measurements afterward that were low but hazardous (in my opinion),” Chris Kohler, an adjunct instructor at Indiana University who is an expert on hazardous waste, environmental remediation, and chemical hygiene, says in an email to The Verge. “The detonation will spread lead in the atmosphere. Not a desirable outcome.” Kohler and other experts say it’ll be important to continue monitoring the explosion site and surrounding areas to see if there needs to be any more remediation.

articles.title: Just a Few Bugs
articles.body:
I'm an independent security researcher. Over the years I've reported vulnerabilities to a number of vendors and manufacturers, and several of those reports have become CVEs.
For most of the past year I've been working on Google's current Pixel phones. I reverse engineered the Samsung radio stack (under embargo), the IMS and RTP media code, the Trusty trusted apps, the MediaTek M90 modem RIL and the Android telephony framework, amongst other things. In that time I filed 95 reports through the Android and Google Devices Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP), and around 95% of them came with a working proof of concept.
In total, the VRP has paid me $250, in a single payment.
I should say at the outset that I have nothing against Google. My project Box began as a fork of their AI Edge Gallery; I've worked on it most days for a year, and Google have taken features from my fork back into their own. I also maintain Iris, a hardened fork of Chromium. Much of what I do is built on Google's work. This page is solely about what happened to the security bugs I reported through their programme over twelve months.
Three things kept happening.
Bugs were fixed after being closed. For every closed report, I extracted the relevant binary from Google's current factory image and compared the exact function the report referred to. Eight had been fixed in shipped code, with a bounds check, a permission or a validation step added precisely where I'd said one was missing. All eight had originally been closed as a "duplicate" or as "not a vulnerability". None was paid and none was credited. Two more have since been fixed in the QPR3 beta.
Bugs were closed for reasons the code doesn't bear out. More than a dozen others were closed as duplicate, infeasible or "can't reproduce", yet the defect is still there, unchanged, in the current build. I'm not suggesting anyone owes a reward for a bug that hasn't been fixed, and I'm not claiming one. My point is simply that the stated reasons for closing them don't hold up once you look at the binary.
A reward promised in writing has never been paid. In January Google confirmed a valid bug and raised both its severity and its reward, in writing. Three months later they reversed all of it, with no new evidence. They then said they would "stand by our word" and pay $250 anyway as a "discretionary payment exception". That was in January. Ten months of "processing", "soon" and "no date" later, it still hasn't been paid. The report itself was submitted before December 2025.
One line in that thread still puzzles me. Google told me in writing that they were paying the Safety Center reward "even though our final technical assessment rated it as a duplicate of a report with no security impact." If the bug had no security impact, there is nothing to pay for. If it's worth paying for, then it did have an impact. Both statements are in the same ticket.
Where things stand
- $250 Safety Center reward (Moderate). Approved in writing in January and confirmed in writing several times since. Ten months on it remains unpaid, and the ticket has been closed.
- Two High severity reports, still "Assigned". Google formally rated both as High. Neither has a reward decision or a CVE yet. One of them has already been fixed in shipped code three times: in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) in October, in the public November stable release (CP4A.261105.040.D1, rolled out to all Pixels on 10 November 2026), and again in the latest QPR3 beta (DP11.261030.003, released on 12 November 2026). The ticket is still "Assigned" and the reward field is still empty.
- One Moderate report, still "Assigned". Rated Moderate on 28 October. No reward decision.
- Ten findings fixed after being closed. Each was closed as a duplicate, infeasible or not a vulnerability, and later fixed in shipped code. No reward and no credit for any of them.
- Total received: $250.
Everything in the tables below is a closed report, and Google's wording is quoted directly from the issue tracker. I've deliberately left out the technical details of the three reports that are still "Assigned", along with anything under active coordinated disclosure.
Every report on this page is a closed ticket. Google's own position, stated on these tickets, is that they do not grant or deny permission for disclosure and that researchers are free to publish at their discretion. Nothing still under assessment or active coordinated disclosure is included here.
How I checked
I followed the same process for every closed report in the tables:
- Extract the exact binary, library or jar named in the report from Google's current factory image (rango and yogi Pixel builds, September and October 2026).
- Unpack it with the appropriate tool for the container: debugfs for ext4, fsck.erofs for EROFS, and a second pass through apex_payload.img for APEX modules.
- Locate the function the report cited, using symbols where they survive and, where they don't, matching byte patterns from the disassembly quoted in the report.
- Compare the shipped code against what the report described as vulnerable, using the NDK's llvm-objdump. The system binutils has no AArch64 backend and returns nothing without raising an error, which is worth knowing before you trust an empty diff.
Each report was given one of four verdicts: PATCHED (a check has been added that wasn't there when I reported it), STILL PRESENT (the code is unchanged), N/A (reported against this exact build, or Google described it as intended design) and CANT-DETERMINE (the binary is missing or the build doesn't match).
I didn't rely on Google's security bulletins or the supplementary patch lists. A silent fix with no bulletin entry and no credit won't appear there by definition, so the only way to find one is to compare the shipped code yourself.
The reward promised in writing that was never paid
This concerns ticket 467575499 / 470814942. On 23 January 2026 Google wrote that they had "confirmed this is a valid bug", were "increasing severity" and "increasing reward", and would "issue a payment for the new amount once it has been processed". On 24 April, without any further analysis, they reversed all three. In what they called a "Final Assessment", the same bug now "does not qualify for a reward or severity increase".
In June they wrote that they wished to "stand by our word regarding the reward". On 10 July they set out the figures: "$250 for Safety Center, $250 for the mic bug, $500USD total". They described this as "honoring our initial promise", whilst still referring to the Safety Center half as a duplicate with no security impact. The microphone half was paid. The Safety Center half was moved into a "discretionary payment exception" with, in their words, no "exact credit date". The most recent reply, in October, says much the same: still approved, still no date.
Rated High by Google, fixed in shipped code, reward still blank
Not every report ended as a duplicate or "not a vulnerability". In this case Google's own panel rated the report High severity, High quality and assigned it for remediation. The fix has since shipped three times: in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) in October, in the public November stable build (CP4A.261105.040.D1), and in the latest QPR3 beta (DP11.261030.003). The ticket is still marked "Assigned", and the reward and CVE fields are still blank, so I've kept the vulnerability itself out of this write-up. The screenshots below show only the process: a report Google rated High and confirmed in writing as eligible for a reward, then left sitting at "Assigned" after the very condition they had set had been met.
It isn't the only one. A second, unrelated report was also rated High severity, High quality by the same panel. A month later it is still "Assigned", the reward is still "with the panel" and the ASR fields are still blank. I haven't named the report or included any technical detail; the screenshots show only the rating and the state of the reward.
The duplicate ID Google admitted was wrong
When Google closes a report as a duplicate, it's closed against an internal "canonical" bug ID. I asked for the IDs behind several of mine. For two entirely unrelated bugs they gave me the same internal ID, 479203197: one was a Rust keystore panic in a trusted app, the other a C++ out-of-bounds read in the RTP media parser. They're written in different languages, sit in different subsystems and belong to different teams. A single internal report cannot be the original for both.
Google acknowledged this in writing on both tickets: "Giving you this ID for your other report was a mistake on our end," and, separately, "we made a mistake when linking the duplicate tickets." So at least one supposedly verified duplicate was marked as such without anyone checking it against the report it named.
Duplicates that appear months later, against reports I can't see
Many of my reports followed the same course. Filed, assigned, worked on by an engineer, and then, months later and with no new technical comment in between, quietly changed to Duplicate. The original is always an internal ticket I can't view, usually accompanied by a note that it was "previously reported by an internal Google engineer". I have no means of seeing that report, confirming that it exists, or confirming that it predates mine.
There are a great many of these. Of the 95 reports I've filed, 34 were closed as duplicates. A few of those are my own resubmissions and appeals folded back together, so it comes to roughly 26 distinct findings that Google accepted as real and then attributed to a report I'm not allowed to see. A duplicate isn't a rejection: it's Google confirming that the bug exists and saying someone else found it first. In 26 of my cases, that someone was an internal engineer who, by Google's account, found the identical bug in the same month I did, in firmware that had only just been released.
It's the timing I keep coming back to. I always work from the current month's factory image, so every report I file concerns firmware released that month, often only a few days earlier. When a bug I found in an image that shipped last week comes back weeks later as something Google has apparently had open internally for months, I'm in no position to check it, and it happens again and again.
On the one occasion I pressed hard enough to find out which build the original was filed against, the explanation was at least plausible. Report 549662989 was marked as a duplicate of one filed against a Pixel 10 (blazer:16/CP1A.260505.005), and PixelModemService ships the same code on both generations, so I accepted it. That was the exception. The ID mix-up described above shows what the process looks like when I can actually check it: the same internal ID given as the "original" for two completely unrelated bugs, and admitted in writing to be a mistake. If one supposedly verified duplicate was marked without anyone comparing it to the report it named, I've no reason to assume the two dozen I can't check were handled any more carefully.
The DCMO DcmoReceiver bug is a case in point. Google say my re-filed report (585012607) duplicates 545652324, which they describe as having been filed on 12 August 2026 by another external researcher, with the same root cause. I can't confirm any of that. Opening 545652324 returns "Access denied", as has every other original I've been referred to, so the date, the author and the root cause are Google's word alone. What I can check is the code, and the defect is still present and unpatched in CP4A.261105.040.D1, months after the date they give for the original report.
The "not a security vulnerability" template
Early on, Google closed one of my findings with their standard message: "not a security vulnerability, logged for potential remediation in a future version, considered closed". They later withdrew it in writing: "You are completely correct. This finding is indeed a legitimate security vulnerability. It was incorrectly closed as 'not a security vulnerability' due to an oversight during triage of this specific ticket."
The same template has since been used to close several more of my reports. On my own tickets alone it has been shown to be wrong more than once, by Google's own admission, and the issue was subsequently patched using the code I had submitted.
Closed as "Intended Behavior" by a "rate-limit bot"
From now on, whenever Google closes one of my reports, I'll publish it here. The two reports below were closed in the same way, so it's worth being precise about what happened. Both had already been assigned and triaged. A Google triager then manually moved each one back to "New", and a minute later, from the same personal account, posted a message describing itself as "an automatically generated message" from the "Google Security Bot". The message closed the report as Won't Fix (Intended Behavior) on the grounds of a rate limit, and stated "we will not be able to see any of your responses".
The genuinely automated messages on my tickets come from a separate system account. These came from the person who had handled the ticket manually a minute before, which is difficult to reconcile with an automated rate limiter. The second report was closed in this way even after I'd supplied a full reproduction on a locked, release-keys phone. Both defects can be verified directly from the shipping image.
A zero-click SMS remote code execution chain in the radio daemon, closed as "not a security vulnerability"
This is ticket 559521028. The MediaTek RIL on the Pixel 11 (libmtkmipc-ril.so, loaded by mtkfusionrild) reimplements the AOSP SMS, WAP push and 3GPP2 parsers in native C++, but keeps AOSP's habit of indexing buf[i] without checking bounds. In Java, reading past the end of a buffer throws an exception that gets caught. In native code nothing is thrown, so an over-read leaks memory and an over-write corrupts it.
There are two defects. Both can be reached with a single incoming SMS, with no user interaction and no app installed:
- Defect A, a heap over-read that leaks data to the sender. PduParser::getAddress and constructUserData take their copy length straight from a length byte in the PDU, which the attacker controls (the TP-OA length, or TP-UDL set to 0xFF). Neither checks it against the real buffer size, so both can read up to about 255 bytes beyond the end of the PDU buffer. Those bytes are copied into the parsed message and passed up the stack, which means a remote sender can read rild's heap memory back out of the delivered message, the notification or the delivery report. That leaks heap and library pointers and defeats rild's ASLR. On this build mtkfusionrild isn't instrumented with MTE (only BTI and PAC), so memory tagging doesn't catch the read.
- Defect B, an out-of-bounds write the attacker controls. BearerData::specialProcessForCtWapPush masks its output cursor with & 0xffff but never checks it against the 255-byte destination, and one branch uses a raw byte from the message as the memcpy length. A crafted 3GPP2 bearer data message drives the write past the end of the buffer with content of the attacker's choosing.
Use the leak to defeat ASLR, then use the write to corrupt a chosen object. That's the standard route to remote code execution in rild, the radio daemon, which runs as the radio user and has a direct channel to the baseband.
I was particularly specific about how the code is reached. The RIL does have one sanity check on PDUs, smsDeliverPduCheck, but it only sits on the branch that forwards the raw PDU to the framework. The native parser is reached by a separate path, from dispatchSms to onHandleSmsMessage to dispatchSuplMsg to SmsMessage::createFromPdu, with no check on it at all. That path depends on a SUPL gate, doesSuplExist(), which returns true for as long as rild is running on any normal device: its global is initialised to 2 in .data (confirmed in the shipped binary) and changes to 1 as soon as MediaTek's location daemon starts. The unchecked parser therefore runs on every incoming SMS, and the trigger can be a silent Type 0 SMS that the user never sees.
I re-checked both defects in three shipped builds: the October stable release (CD1A.261005.003), the November stable release (CP4A.261105.040.D1, SPL 2026-11-05) and the DP11 QPR3 beta. No bounds check had been added to any of these paths.
This is static analysis of the shipped binary. I don't have a modem test rig, as the report makes clear, so there's no runtime exploit attached. On 12 November the team asked for a live software proof of concept. Two days later, on 14 November, the report was closed as Won't Fix (Infeasible) with the template "we have investigated this issue and determined that this is not a security vulnerability... logged for potential remediation in a future version", and the ASR Severity field was set to NSBC. That is the same template Google have already withdrawn on another of my reports, here applied to an unchecked, attacker-controlled memcpy length in the radio daemon that can be reached with zero clicks and is still present in the shipping build.
Some of the other closed bugs, in plain terms
A few more of the closed reports, kept short. Each is the bug, roughly how it works, and how it is reached.
An OTA update the device will install, signed by the wrong key (ticket 541986810, closed Duplicate). RecoverySystem.verifyPackage is the check that decides whether an update package is really signed by Google. It looks at two certificates and never confirms they are the same one. The trust check looks at the certificate sitting first in the package. The signature is then verified against a different certificate, chosen by an issuer and serial number that are also read from the package. So an attacker puts Google's genuine, public signing certificate first to pass the trust check, puts their own certificate further in, points the signature at that one, and signs the package with their own key. The check passes for a package they signed. It is reached through the sideload or update path, where the signature gate that is supposed to stop an unofficial package does not.
DNS still leaves the phone when you turn on "Block connections without VPN" (ticket 552188030, closed Duplicate). VPN lockdown is meant to stop any traffic that is not inside the tunnel. DNS queries are left exempt from that block, for every app, not just the device's own traffic. So even with lockdown on, an app's DNS lookups leave the device outside the VPN, which leaks which sites are being resolved and gives a channel the lockdown is supposed to close.
Any app can switch off your Lock-on-Disconnect (ticket 552305734, closed Infeasible, still present). The Cross-Device stack exports a broadcast receiver, PermissionBroadcastReceiver, with no permission on it, and it acts on the broadcast without checking who sent it. Any installed app, holding no permissions, can send that broadcast and force an immediate un-enrollment of the user's Lock-on-Disconnect security feature, turning off a protection the user had switched on.
The share sheet fetching a picture it should not (ticket 538314136, closed Infeasible, still present). The intent resolver renders a caller-supplied icon URI without checking the caller is allowed to read it. An app hands it a URI that points at content belonging to another user or profile, and a privileged process fetches it on the attacker's behalf and hands it back.
Any app cancelling another app's on-device AI model load (ticket 558472707, closed Infeasible, still present). cancelModelLoad in the NPU manager service does not check who is calling, so any app can cancel a different app's model load and deny it the hardware AI path.
A radio service you can crash with one value (ticket 555984702, closed Can't Reproduce, still present). The grilservice radio-config path reads an array size straight from an incoming parcel with no cap and allocates it. A crafted size forces a huge allocation and takes the service down, dropping telephony.
Any app can bind the Play Store's setup service (ticket 564059393, closed Working As Intended).
