articles.title: From CUDA and Jax to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver
articles.body:
From CUDA and JAX to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver
Some time ago, I shared a blog post about working with Cayley graphs, where I solved combinatorial puzzles using AI coding agents, PyTorch on GPUs, and JAX on TPUs. Recently, Google released TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for TPUs, and I wanted to see how well it works on the same task: whether a PyTorch-native TPU stack could match my A100 training pipeline and my JAX beam search in speed and solution quality, or maybe even beat them.
The short version: getting TorchTPU to work was easy; getting it to work efficiently was considerably harder. My initial training port was 1.65x slower than the A100 implementation, while the first TPU beam search was 5.7x slower than its JAX counterpart.
After optimizing eager execution, rewriting attention, eliminating dynamic tensor shapes, fixing a subtle deduplication bug, and investigating an attention-routing regression, the results changed substantially. Training reached comparable wall-clock performance to the A100, and the optimized TorchTPU beam search became 25% faster per level than JAX on the same eight-chip v6e machine, producing the same total solution length across six test puzzles.
Along the way, the investigation improved the solver itself and resulted in an upstream TorchTPU GitHub issue that led to attention-routing fixes.
The code is available on Kaggle notebooks running on a free TPU v5e-8:
As in the previous post, the code and the experiments were done by coding agents (Claude Code and Codex): I decided what to port, what to measure, and how to judge the results, and they did the implementation and the profiling.
The problem
The CayleyPy Professor Tetraminx competition requires finding the shortest sequence of moves that solves 1000 scrambled puzzles. Formally, it is a shortest-path problem in a Cayley graph (each puzzle state is a node, and each of the 24 possible moves is an edge) with an 88-sticker state.
My solver uses beam search guided by a learned neural heuristic — a 3.4M-parameter PieceTransformer. Instead of treating the 88 stickers individually, it groups them into 50 physical pieces, turns each piece into a token, adds a class token (51 tokens in total), and runs four small transformer layers with eight heads of size 32. At the end, an all-neighbours Q head (a head that predicts, for each of the 24 moves, the distance to solved after that move) outputs 24 numbers. So the beam scores all 24 children of a state with one forward pass on the parent.
For training, the signal is a mix of cheap random walks and exact ground truth:
- Random walks of 2–40 moves from the solved state. A state p moves into a walk has two known labels: undoing the last move gives distance p - 1, and continuing the walk gives p + 1.
- Exact 24-way labels from a breadth-first search (BFS) table at depth 5 or less.
- The puzzle’s 24 spatial symmetries, used as data augmentation.
On the A100, one epoch takes 142.7 seconds. My best checkpoint is epoch 1500 of a 2000-epoch run, about 80 hours in total.
What is TorchTPU
TorchTPU is not PyTorch/XLA: there is no LazyTensor tracing, no xm.mark_step(), and no xla_device(). Instead, TorchTPU lowers ATen ops directly to StableHLO and runs through PJRT and libtpu (PyTorch’s core ops are translated straight into XLA’s input format and executed by the TPU runtime). Once you import torch, "tpu" works as a device string just like "cuda".
It has three execution modes:
- Eager (the default): runs one op at a time asynchronously.
- Fused eager (TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1): defers ops and fuses them across op boundaries without needing torch.compile.
- Compiled (torch.compile(fn, dynamic=False)): graph compilation targeting the TPU backend.
Three rules matter in practice:
- Static shapes were the reliable path: with the TorchTPU builds and operators I used, fixed tensor shapes and torch.compile(..., dynamic=False) worked best, and every new shape meant a full recompile.
- Data-dependent output sizes were the most expensive: ops like nonzero, masked_select, unique, bincount, and even x[bool_mask] still run in eager mode, but they force a .cpu().item() host round-trip to learn their output size, and a compiled graph gets specialized to that one size, so each new size means another compile.
- Nothing falls back silently to the CPU: an op that TorchTPU doesn’t implement raises an error instead of quietly running slowly.
Part 1: training, from 1.65x slower to 1.08x faster
I ran the first port on a Cloud TPU machine with four v6e chips, using DDP with one process per chip and a global batch of 512, so each epoch saw exactly the same number of samples as on the A100. Before the code could run on the TPU at all, I had to remove four GPU idioms (masked_select in the loss, boolean-mask indexing when expanding labels, 12 .item() metric reads per step, and sampling training anchors on the CPU instead of keeping the 0.19 GB anchor table in TPU memory). This first working version took 234.8 seconds per epoch, 1.65x slower than the A100. I was able to bring it down to 132 seconds with two changes.
Fused eager
The first win was practically free: turning on fused eager (TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1). Only the model’s forward and backward pass ran under torch.compile; the rest of the trainer (the random-walk sampler with its 40-iteration loop, label expansion, the loss, and the metrics) ran in eager mode, one op at a time. In default eager mode, that data pipeline took 61.3 ms per step. Wrapping it in torch.compile brought it down to 29.7 ms, while fused eager, which fuses the ops at run time without any code changes, got it to 13.1 ms. The pipeline is many tiny ops, and on this workload they fused better than they compiled; I didn’t profile why, since the cheaper option was also the faster one. Setting that single environment variable dropped the epoch time from 234.8 s to 176.5 s.
The attention rewrite that was almost thrown away
Still, 176.5 s was slower than the A100, and the GPU profile didn’t help. On the A100, the input stage and embedding gradient took 67% of the step; on the TPU, the same stage took only 0.96 ms (0.8%), and the model was spending ~90% of its time in attention.
A roofline at the model’s own shapes explained why. A square 8192³ GEMM hits 361 TFLOP/s on one v6e chip, and the model’s QKV and FFN GEMMs hit 212–259 TFLOP/s, while attention ran at 3.0 TFLOP/s. With T = 51 and head_dim = 32, every attention matmul is 51x32x51 on a 128x128 matrix unit (MXU) — roughly 2.5% tile occupancy. Padding head_dim to 128 or T to 64 actually made things slower (0.83x and 0.81x). As a result, attention is about 3% of the model’s FLOPs but about 90% of its time on the TPU.
If you want to keep the same model (for a fair comparison), you need to keep the same shapes and find other improvements. Standard scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA) expects (B, H, T, Dh), so the QKV tensor has to be permuted to move the heads to the second dimension. Rewriting attention with torch.einsum keeps the heads in their original dimension and avoids the permutes:
q, k, v = qkv.view(B, T, 3, H, Dh).unbind(2)        # heads never leave dim 2
s = torch.einsum("bthd,bshd->bhts", q, k) * scale
p = s.float().softmax(-1).to(v.dtype)               # fp32 softmax, on purpose
a = torch.einsum("bhts,bshd->bthd", p, v)
The fp32 softmax is there for numerics. On the TPU, the einsum and SDPA versions disagreed by a relative 3.3e-3, so I checked both against a float64 reference on the CPU: both were about 4.6e-3 away from it, because the TPU’s matrix unit uses a single-pass bf16 multiply even for “fp32” matmuls unless you raise torch.tpu.precision. In bf16, keeping only the softmax in fp32 closed the remaining gap between the two versions.
This change was almost rejected. The agent first measured it on the forward pass only, where it looked slower (einsum 5.51 ms vs SDPA 4.56 ms), and discarded it on that basis. Thankfully, I decided to check the full forward+backward pass: the profiler attributed much of the backward-pass overhead to layout conversions around SDPA’s saved tensors, which cost far more than the forward pass saved. Across forward+backward, one layer dropped from 25.14 ms to 14.85 ms (1.69x faster). That pushed the whole epoch down to 132.0 s — 1.08x faster than the A100.
A checkpoint with deadlocks
The most confusing bug was in checkpointing. Saving a checkpoint only from rank 0 is a standard pattern:
if is_main:
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), path)      # deadlocks under fused eager + DDP
Under fused eager, the tensors in state_dict are still deferred. When rank 0 reads them, it executes a graph that includes this step’s DDP collectives, while the other ranks are already waiting at the next barrier. The checkpoint file would grow to 1.1 MB, then 2.2 MB, and freeze forever while every rank sat busy. The fix is to move the tensors to the CPU on every rank and write the file on one:
cpu_state = {k: v.detach().to("cpu") for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}   # all ranks
if is_main:
    torch.save(cpu_state, path)
The trap only fires in the mode that gives the speedup, which made it harder to find.
Summary of training changes
Training results
On Kaggle’s free v5e-8 (eight chips, 64 samples per chip), the training notebook run 186 epochs in 7.41 hours, with a median of 142.4 seconds per epoch against the A100’s 144.2 over the same epochs.
Over epochs 177-186, the training loss averaged 15.131 on the v5e-8 and 15.132 on the A100, and top-1 accuracy was 0.488 against 0.483. On exact labels, the TPU checkpoint at epoch 186 is on par with the A100 checkpoint at epoch 200: its best predicted move is truly optimal for 99.0% of states, against 98.9%. The best checkpoint trained eight times longer and is still better.
Part 2: beam search, first attempt
With training done, the second half was porting my beam search solver (KhoruzhiiSolver, the CUDA beam searcher from the previous post) to TorchTPU. Training needed targeted fixes; the solver needed a rewrite. It relied on torch.unique for deduplication, boolean-mask indexing, and dynamic tensor shapes (cand.index_select(0, unique_pos[:B])), none of which works well on a TPU.
So I wrote beam_tpu.py from scratch in pure PyTorch with fixed shapes across every step. Instead of dropping duplicates, I sort candidates by hash, flag adjacent matches, and assign duplicate scores +inf so topk simply never picks them:
sort_h, sort_idx = h.sort()
dup_sorted = torch.cat([no, sort_h[1:] == sort_h[:-1]])
dup = dup_sorted[sort_idx.argsort()]
score = torch.where(dup | ~valid, BIG, score)
To share a 1M-wide beam across chips, each chip holds an equal share of the beam slots, and a child’s owner chip is determined by its hash. Every step runs the Q-head forward on local parents, routes children to their owners via all_to_all_single, deduplicates globally on each owner, and runs topk for the next level. States are stored as int8, and the tree bookkeeping stays outside the compiled step so the level counter doesn’t trigger a recompilation.
The search doesn’t go all the way to the solved state: it stops as soon as a beam state appears in the exact depth-6 BFS table (27.8M states), and the table supplies the optimal last six moves. In the first TorchTPU version, this endgame tail (a Zobrist hash and a searchsorted over the table for each level, each ending in .item()) ran as eager ops on the TPU and took ~176 s after a 73 s solve. The JAX driver had always done it in NumPy on the host, so I did the same: identical moves on 3000 checked states, at under a millisecond per state. Running the model over fixed-size chunks inside a single scan didn’t change the step speed, but it kept one copy of the model in the compiled graph instead of one per chunk, shrinking the cached compiled code from 363 to 162 MiB.
I first tested an August pre-release of TorchTPU on six hard scrambles (1M beam, 4x v6e). It matched my JAX kernel on path length (186 vs 185 moves, every path replay-verified) but was 5.7x slower (1973 s vs 345 s). The profile showed that cross-chip all_to_all cost only 0.6 ms per step, while model inference took ~83% of the time. Then I moved to the public torch_tpu==0.2.0 on Kaggle, and the results were surprising: the gap narrowed to 2.8x per beam level, but quality dropped, with TorchTPU finding 194 moves where JAX reproduced its 185.
When a backend change exposed an algorithmic bug
Because Kaggle has a long TPU queue, I moved to Cloud TPU v6e to debug the 8 moves lost between the pre-release (186) and 0.2.0 (194). Two things had changed in 0.2.0: torch.topk had reverted from a stable tie-breaking order back to an unstable default, and bf16 attention on sequence lengths that are not a multiple of 128 no longer ran the whole module in fp32 (more on attention below).
On eight v6e chips, forcing the old low-index tie-breaking in topk took 0.2.0 from 193 moves back to 187, the pre-release’s number there. But why should tie-breaking change path length at all? On four chips, every fixed tie order I tried (lowest index first, highest first, a random shuffle) gave 185 moves; only 0.2.0’s native order gave 188. Something in the beam was turning tie order into path length, and that something was my deduplication.
Because the Q head scores children from the parent, a state reached from two parents arrives as two copies with different scores. My dedup sorted candidates by hash and kept the first copy in each run, and since torch.sort is unstable on both builds, “first” was whichever copy the backend left in front. When 0.2.0 changed the tie order, good states started to disappear because their worse duplicate survived. JAX’s dedup uses a stable argsort on score-sorted buckets, so it keeps the better copy.
Replacing “keep first” with a segment-min over (score, index) (so duplicates always keep their best score) added 0.5% overhead and fixed the issue:
On ten more puzzles, this fix cut total moves from 319 down to 302, improving seven of them and worsening none.
Flash attention and the GitHub issue
One regression really was TorchTPU’s: on the same chips, 0.2.0 ran a beam level 1.7x slower than the pre-release. Timing each piece of a level separately showed that everything except attention was as fast or faster in 0.2.0. The cause was routing: 0.2.0 sends short attention shapes to its Flash attention kernel, which pads the 51-token sequence to a 128-token tile, so 84% of each score tile is padding. Turning Flash off with torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp(False) puts attention back on the plain XLA path (yes, .cuda. — TorchTPU respects PyTorch’s standard SDPA backend switches, which live under torch.backends.cuda):
With Flash off, a full beam level is 4x faster than with 0.2.0’s default and 2.4x faster than the pre-release. The 2026-11-04 nightly, which already routes short sequences away from Flash, is as fast as the workaround.
Two things hid this at first. The --fp32-attn arm that I added to test attention precision still went through Flash, so it only made things slower. And PyTorch’s AOTAutograd cache is keyed on the graph, not on the attention backend flag, so a second process quietly reused the Flash-compiled graph and reported identical times until each run got its own cache directory.
My agent wrote up the measurements and reported the issue to the TorchTPU repository with a Colab reproduction and a table of attention timings across head sizes and sequence lengths. It turned out that the short-sequence fix had already landed on main three days after 0.2.0 was tagged, but it hadn’t been released. The report also noted that a newer routing rule on main would make some 128–256-token shapes slower. The TorchTPU team picked it up, merged a series of attention-routing fixes, and closed the issue on November 21.
Summary of beam search changes
Beam search results
With the dedup fixed and Flash turned off, I reran the comparison on one eight-chip v6e machine with the public torch_tpu==0.2.0 and JAX 0.11.0 (the version in Kaggle’s TPU image).
TorchTPU now runs a beam level 1.25x faster than JAX with the same quality.
On Kaggle’s v5e-8, the picture is closer. TorchTPU with Flash off is still about 10% faster per beam level, but the median scramble takes slightly longer (49.9 vs 48.7 s), because it checks the hit flag only every four levels and runs extra levels, and it found one move more (186 vs 185):
JAX remains my main beam search solution for now as I have yet to run TorchTPU on a wider beam. And the investigations helped push the JAX kernel further: bounding temporary buffers reduced the compile-time memory for a 128M beam from 39.5 to 12 GiB per chip, and a 256M-state beam works on eight v6e chips.
A100 vs TPU: the differences that mattered
Conclusions
I started this experiment to see whether TorchTPU could replace my A100 + JAX setup, and on this task it can: the same model trains at the A100’s speed or slightly faster, and the beam search matches JAX on quality and is a bit faster per level.
However, a native PyTorch API does not eliminate the need for hardware-aware engineering. Static shapes, deferred execution, tensor layouts, compilation caching, and kernel selection all mattered considerably. Optimizations that helped training did not necessarily help inference, and seemingly minor changes in backend behaviour exposed a latent bug in my search algorithm.
The migration also improved both implementations: fixing deduplication reduced solution lengths, the attention investigation contributed to upstream TorchTPU improvements, and revisiting memory management enabled larger beams in JAX.
More broadly, this project demonstrated how AI coding agents can participate in experimental engineering rather than simply code generation. Claude Code and Codex implemented alternative approaches, profiled execution, constructed controlled experiments, investigated regressions, and prepared reproducible bug reports. My role was to formulate hypotheses, choose meaningful metrics, question misleading measurements, and decide which trade-offs were acceptable.

articles.title: Zero data retention with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in beta
articles.body:
Zero data retention with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in beta
Over the past few months, we've been developing Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) for our business customers. EFS provides state-of-the-art detection of sophisticated misuse, while remaining compatible with zero data retention (ZDR): neither Anthropic nor any cloud providers retain enterprises' data.
Since we announced EFS in September, we've been developing it further with over 100 of our customers—including a quarter of the Fortune 100 and many companies in industries with strict rules on data visibility (like healthcare, financial services, and law). Leading enterprises like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe have been evaluating EFS in private beta.
“Enterprise Frontier Safeguards gives us exactly what we asked for: our logs stay in a Wells-managed environment under Wells-managed keys. We keep custody of our data while Anthropic operates the detection. That split is what lets our teams put frontier models to work safely and meet our obligations to customers, employees, and regulators. We helped shape these safeguards because our industry needs them.”
“Where we have regulated or highly sensitive data, having Enterprise Frontier Safeguards with zero data retention will allow us to confidently accelerate our AI deployment across those highly regulated and sensitive client engagements.”
“As a company that runs critical infrastructure, safety matters as much to us as model capability. We need a solution that gives us strong safeguards while allowing us to keep our data in our own account. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards delivers just that.”
“At Stripe, protecting customer data is foundational to how we operate. Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards will enable us to use frontier models with added protection against misuse. It will also let us retain conversation logs in Stripe’s AWS environment, with access and review governed by Stripe’s security controls.”
“With EFS, customers can keep sensitive data in their own environments, protected with their own encryption keys, while still preserving the specialized safety mechanisms frontier capabilities require. That balance, keeping enterprises in control of their data without abandoning frontier-model safety, is critical to broader adoption of advanced AI in security-sensitive organizations like Cisco.”
Now, we're opening up EFS in public beta. In this post, we explain how EFS works in more detail, how it stays compatible with ZDR, and how businesses can join the beta program.
How EFS provides automated safety monitoring with ZDR
Customers who rely on legacy ZDR are protected by Claude's classifiers: our real-time safeguards that screen individual requests to assess whether they might cause harm. But sophisticated attacks generally occur across multiple queries—and any single request might, in isolation, look harmless.
For example, our September threat intelligence report describes an operation against roughly fifty organizations in which an AI agent divided the work of an attack among many other agents running in parallel. It saved the credentials it had harvested between sessions, so that the attackers could easily resume their campaign. Viewed one request at a time, this attack would have appeared as separate, more benign tasks.
To catch attacks like these, we use a second defensive layer, known as automated safety monitoring. This layer looks for patterns of misuse across many requests. Through EFS, Anthropic can provide automated safety monitoring without storing any customer data. Instead, our automated safety monitoring system analyzes data stored entirely on infrastructure controlled by our customers.
When automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for you to review. These cases can be read from your cloud storage or through an API, and can be integrated with security information and event management systems. They do not include inputs and outputs.
Once it's set up, automated safety monitoring can help your team detect intentional misuse that could lead to serious harm (like offensive cyber operations). It can also help detect agents that take actions beyond a user's intentions, such as—in extreme cases—using a software exploit to access an internal database or external system.
Zero data retention and EFS
With EFS, you bring your own storage for storing inputs and outputs. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider keeps a copy of your data once it is delivered to storage you control. This provides you the following guarantees:
- Zero data retention. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider retains your data. You bring your own storage and store your own data. Inputs and outputs are deleted promptly after they're written to your own storage. You configure your own access policies and audit logging, and encrypt safety data with your own keys.
- No operator human review. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider personnel access your inputs and outputs. Only automated safety monitoring can access this data.
- We never train on your data. Inputs and outputs are used only for automated safety monitoring, never for model or classifier training.
You can use EFS through the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, or Claude on Google Cloud. When you use EFS through Amazon Bedrock or Claude on Google Cloud (Google Managed), it's operated by your cloud provider, and the end-to-end data flow stays within that cloud's boundary.
You can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage in your own account for your storage, depending on where you use Claude. Your cloud provider bills you for that storage as usual, including reads, writes, and key operations (plus any applicable network transfer).
Get started
EFS is available on the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, and Claude on Google Cloud. Support for EFS in Microsoft Foundry is coming soon.
Eligible customers will be notified with instructions on how to get started. Read our developer docs to learn how to set it up, and our security whitepaper (opens in new tab) for how the architecture works, or deploy it through consulting partners like Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC.

articles.title: Amazon’s Decart acquisition is a bet on using software to narrow the gap with Nvidia in the AI chip race
articles.body:
Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.
The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.
Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.
By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.
In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.
One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.
Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.
In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”
Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”

articles.title: Investigation of Polymarket Insider Trading on the Reinstatement of Jensen Huang
articles.body:
Polymarket : Autopsie d'un délit d'initié sur la réintégration de Jensen Huang chez NVIDIA [!NOTE] Pourquoi cet article et cette analyse ? Depuis quelque temps, je constate que Polymarket devient un véritable terrain de jeu pour les délits d’initiés, et le climat politique autour de la nouvelle administration Trump rend ce type d’asymétrie d’information encore plus propice. J’ai donc développé un algorithme qui surveille en permanence les marchés les plus sensibles : chaque transaction y est analysée par des modèles statistiques et des outils de traçage de flux on-chain. J’ai finalisé l’algo il y a deux jours à peine. Dans la nuit même, en voyant l’alerte se déclencher, j’ai mené une première analyse à chaud sur les transactions… avant de voir tomber quelques heures plus tard le tweet de Donald Trump confirmant l’asymétrie. Et vous allez voir que le communiqué officiel de NVIDIA n’était que la cerise sur le gâteau. Cette enquête documente, à la minute et au hash près, un cas assez probant de délit d’initié sur Polymarket détecté en temps réel. En résumé : Pourquoi ce cas est particulièrement suspect Sur un marché de prédiction, rien ne permet d’affirmer avec une certitude absolue ce qui motive un parieur. En revanche, l’analyse des données on-chain met en lumière un faisceau d’indices particulièrement troublant autour du compte ljhggk : - Le timing : Les achats s’arrêtent en pleine nuit, 89 minutes avant que Donald Trump ne publie son soutien sur Truth Social. - L’asymétrie du pari : 4 648 $ misés sur une issue cotée à seulement 6,5 %, transformés en 71 518 $ après l’annonce officielle de NVIDIA. - Le profil du wallet : Un compte Gnosis Safe Proxy créé 81 heures plus tôt, 100 % monothématique sur ce seul événement. Simple coup de chance ou réelle information privilégiée ? En décortiquant les transactions bloc par bloc, le scénario d’un simple pari au hasard devient difficile à croire. 1 · L’Anatomie du trade : 71 518 parts accumulées en pleine nuit Entre 02:19:11 et 03:28:20 CET (01:19 - 02:28 UTC) dans la nuit du dimanche au lundi 23 novembre 2026, le carnet d’ordres du marché Will Jensen Huang rejoin NVIDIA by December 31, 2026? était totalement assoupi. La probabilité implicite stagnait à 6,5 %, reflétant un consensus quasi-unanime : suite à sa démission du 12 novembre, un retour de Huang avant la fin de l’année paraissait exclu. C’est à cet instant précis qu’un acteur unique déploie une stratégie d’absorption agressive, découpée en 4 ordres limités successifs : Le relevé des 4 transactions sur Polygon Chaque transaction a été retracée. Les 4 transactions ont été incluses dans les blocs sans rejet Registre complet : [!NOTE] Verdict technique de l’exécution : L’opérateur n’a pas étalé ses achats sur 24 heures pour moyenner son coût. Il a exécuté un achat massif et concentré en pleine nuit européenne/américaine, absorbant 34 % de toute la liquidité vendeuse disponible sur le contrat, ce qui pourrait montrer qu’il a eu l’info quelques heures avant et qu’il n’a pas spécialement eu le temps de l’étaler davantage. Dès son dernier ordre complété à 03:28:20 CET, il s’est totalement arrêté de négocier. À noter : le compte s’était déjà positionné sur de petits montants sur ce pari dès sa création, mais sans jamais approcher de volumes comparables à ce qui a levé l’alerte cette nuit-là. Cette montée soudaine en conviction renforce encore la suspicion. 2 · La Reconstitution temporelle : 89 minutes d’avance sur le monde réel Le cœur du dossier réside dans la corrélation temporelle entre la clôture de l’accumulation on-chain et la chaîne des déclarations publiques. 02:19 CET ─── 03:28 CET ──────── 04:57 CET ────────────────────── 14:30 CET ─── 15:40 CET [Achats] [Fin Accum.] [Post Trump] [PR NVIDIA] [Résolution] 4 648 $ Verrouillé « I hope the Board... » Officiel 1.00 $ 71 518 parts Truth Social Wall Street 71 518 $ ▲ │ │ └──── +89 min ─────┘ │ └────────────────────── +11h 02min ────────────────┘ 1. Le premier déclencheur : La publication de Donald Trump (+89 min) À 04:57:00 CET (22:57:00 EST le 22 novembre), Donald Trump publie sur son réseau Truth Social : « I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A. » Il ne s’agit pas d’une consigne officielle, mais le poids politique est massif : la mise à l’écart de Huang reposait sur des craintes de sécurité nationale. Le soutien explicite de Trump débloque immédiatement la situation. Le contrat bondit instantanément de 0,065 $ à 0,14 $ dans les échanges de la nuit. 2. L’officialisation : Le Conseil d’Administration de NVIDIA (+11h) À 14:30:00 CET (08:30:00 EST), exactement une heure avant l’ouverture de Wall Street, NVIDIA diffuse son Communiqué officiel de réintégration. Le Conseil d’Administration confirme avoir voté à l’unanimité la réintégration immédiate de Jensen Huang au poste de CEO et Board Member, précisant avoir reçu l’assurance des plus hauts échelons du gouvernement américain quant à l’absence de risque sécuritaire. Le contrat binaire grimpe vers 0,985 $, avant d’être résolu et encaissé à 1,00 $. 3 · L’Empreinte on-chain : Ce que révèle le profil du wallet Pour évaluer si une transaction relève d’un simple pari ou d’un comportement suspect, l’analyse on-chain apporte des indices précieux. Le compte ljhggk présente plusieurs caractéristiques typiques d’un portefeuille temporaire (burner proxy) : flowchart LR EOA["Portefeuille personnel (EOA)
0x3e0f9ada318fa8...
Adresse signataire directe"] -->|Déploiement Safe| Proxy["Gnosis Safe Proxy
0xdf8616e18da2ad...
Âge : 81h · Pseudo : ljhggk"] Proxy -->|100% Capital| Trade["Marché Unique : NVIDIA
4 648 USDC sur YES @ 6,5 ¢
Zéro diversification"] Trade -->|Dénouement| Cashout["Position Résolue
71 518 USDC (+1 438%)"] 4 · D’où viennent les fonds ? En inspectant l’adresse à l’origine de la création du compte Polymarket (0x3e0f9ada318fa8...) sur Polygonscan, on fait un constat surprenant : son historique affiche 0 transaction. Le wallet est totalement vierge et n’a jamais interagi directement avec le réseau Polygon. Ce n’est donc pas ce wallet qui a directement fourni ou transféré les fonds on-chain. Le rôle du pUSD et du bridge Polymarket Sur Polymarket, le fonctionnement des soldes et des ordres repose sur une certaine mécanique : - Aucun besoin de gaz sur le wallet personnel : L’utilisateur signe ses ordres d’achat hors-chaîne depuis son navigateur. C’est le relais officiel de Polymarket (Relayer) qui diffuse les transactions sur la blockchain et règle les frais de réseau à sa place. - Le concept de pUSD (Polymarket USD) : Pour négocier sur le carnet d’ordres, la plateforme utilise son propre jeton interne indexé sur le dollar : le pUSD. Ce jeton n’est pas envoyé par un particulier, mais émis automatiquement par le protocole lors d’un dépôt. - Le contrat de bridge / séquestre : Quand un utilisateur approvisionne son compte, les USDC réels sont déposés dans le coffre de séquestre de Polymarket (Collateral Vault). En contrepartie, le bridge de Polymarket crée (mint) les pUSD équivalents directement sur le contrat proxy unique de l’utilisateur (0xdf8616e1...). - L’origine des capitaux : Les fonds engagés proviennent très probablement d’un retrait direct depuis une plateforme d’échange centralisée (comme Binance, Kraken ou Coinbase) vers l’adresse de dépôt assignée par Polymarket, d’un autre portefeuille externe via une passerelle cross-chain, ou d’un paiement bancaire direct via le partenaire d’intégration fiat (MoonPay). Ce montage montre que l’acheteur a utilisé une adresse totalement vierge pour signer les ordres sans laisser d’antécédents directs, en faisant transiter sa liquidité directement par les infrastructures de dépôt de Polymarket. Conclusion Sur les marchés boursiers traditionnels, prouver un délit d’initié demande souvent des mois d’enquêtes et de réquisitions. Sur un carnet décentralisé comme Polymarket, la dynamique est différente : les flux financiers et les horodatages sont publics et consultables par tous en temps réel. On ne saura sans doute jamais avec certitude qui se cache derrière ce wallet, ni si l’opérateur a simplement eu une intuition exceptionnelle. Mais entre l’absorption brutale de liquidité en pleine nuit, l’arrêt net des achats 89 minutes avant la prise de parole politique, le profil monothématique du compte et l’asymétrie totale du trade, le faisceau d’indices reste particulièrement lourd. Ce cas illustre à quel point les marchés de prédiction constituent aujourd’hui un observatoire inédit de la circulation de l’information. Depuis quelque temps, je constate que Polymarket devient un véritable terrain de jeu pour les délits d’initiés, et le climat politique autour de la nouvelle administration Trump rend ce type d’asymétrie d’information encore plus propice. Simple coup de chance ou réelle information privilégiée ? En décortiquant les transactions bloc par bloc, le scénario d’un simple pari au hasard devient difficile à croire. 1 · L’Anatomie du trade : 71 518 parts accumulées en pleine nuit Entre 02:19:11 et 03:28:20 CET (01:19 - 02:28 UTC) dans la nuit du dimanche au lundi 23 novembre 2026, le carnet d’ordres du marché Will Jensen Huang rejoin NVIDIA by December 31, 2026? était totalement assoupi. Dès son dernier ordre complété à 03:28:20 CET, il s’est totalement arrêté de négocier. À noter : le compte s’était déjà positionné sur de petits montants sur ce pari dès sa création, mais sans jamais approcher de volumes comparables à ce qui a levé l’alerte cette nuit-là. Cette montée soudaine en conviction renforce encore la suspicion. 2 · La Reconstitution temporelle : 89 minutes d’avance sur le monde réel Le cœur du dossier réside dans la corrélation temporelle entre la clôture de l’accumulation on-chain et la chaîne des déclarations publiques. 02:19 CET ─── 03:28 CET ──────── 04:57 CET ────────────────────── 14:30 CET ─── 15:40 CET [Achats] [Fin Accum.] [Post Trump] [PR NVIDIA] [Résolution] 4 648 $ Verrouillé « I hope the Board... » Officiel 1.00 $ 71 518 parts Truth Social Wall Street 71 518 $ ▲ │ │ └──── +89 min ─────┘ │ └────────────────────── +11h 02min ────────────────┘ 1. articles.title: India's opposition storms Meta's offices to get its Instagram accounts back
articles.body:
India's opposition storms Meta's offices to get its Instagram accounts back
Last Friday, activists from the Indian Youth Congress, the youth wing of India's main opposition party, forced their way into the building housing Meta's offices in Hyderabad, where they ended up clashing with police among overturned potted plants.
The scene repeated itself the same day in Mumbai, with anti-Meta slogans spray-painted on the building's walls and placards burned in front of the entrance, while in Gurugram, near New Delhi, banners demanded the return of the movement's accounts.
Mumbai police registered a complaint against four of the organization's leaders and detained several protesters.
This anger stems from the November 19 blocking of the Instagram accounts of the youth wing's president and of the party official who oversees it. The Congress accuses Meta of obeying orders from the BJP, Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist party, and of restricting, along the way, thousands of accounts belonging to journalists, creators and influencers critical of those in power.
The movement had warned on X that it would storm the company's offices across the country if the accounts weren't reinstated. Promise kept, then. And the method pays off, since two accounts were restored the day after the protests, according to the group's social media chief, who is now giving Meta seven days to lift all restrictions targeting opposition voices.
Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, compared with around 70,000 over the whole of 2025. The government, for its part, issued almost 200,000 blocking orders between March and July, and since February has required platforms to remove flagged content within three hours, compared with 36 previously.
India is also Meta's biggest market by number of users, and this newfound docility looks an awful lot like an effort to protect its bread and butter.
On the BJP side, a spokesperson accuses the protesters of trashing the Hyderabad office and bragging about it on social media. Meta, meanwhile, still hasn't said anything, caught between a government that gives orders and an opposition that kicks down its doors.
Source: The Verge

articles.title: Hacking radiators for fun and no profit
articles.body:
Hacking radiators for fun and no profit
My flat has a bunch of electrical radiators, branded Acova. They have a remote. Each. Fixed to the wall right next to it. This means I have to get up from my seat to turn a radiator on. Worse, I might have to get to an entirely different room.
Unlike the TV remote, my radiator remotes are not IR (although an IR variant does exist, and was already hacked), but RF. With no other information, I whipped out my trusty RTL-SDR Blog V3.
As is now usual, Claude helped me quickly detect the signals of the remotes, establishing that they use 868.2 MHz. So I got myself a Heltec V3 for that frequency. Unlike my SDR, it would let me send data, in addition to receiving it.
After more poking with the Heltec, I realized that the remotes seemed to use proper cryptography during pairing, and all communications thereafter were encrypted. That meant that trying to crack the exchanges from sniffed data would most likely not work.
So I took one apart.
Promising! Next to the big black square is a connector with 6 pin holes labelled X1. Most likely a debug port for engineers and technicians working on the product.
After identifying the GND pin with a conductivity tester, and failing to conclusively identify the 3.3V pin, I tried the first guess of Claude for the mapping, with SWDIO on the 4th pin from the top and SWCLK on the 2nd pin from the top. It worked first try!
Fortunately, the MCU did not have any protection enabled, so I was able to dump the whole firmware, and to read memory freely. After I installed Ghidra, Claude was able to analyze the firmware to determine the whole protocol, including the cryptography, as well as dump the session key (determined at pairing).
Interestingly, the firmware is labelled “ComfoRF” and bears marks of the Zehnder Group, of which Acova is a subsidiary. It embeds mbed TLS with various cryptographic primitives, but only ends up using AES-ECB, and implements its own finite-field Diffie-Hellman. Also, it has some logic to use a hardware implementation of AES available on a different variant of the MCU.
With this, I could determine exactly what the MCU was sending to the radio chip. However, I could not read and send commands just yet. The SPIRIT1 radio chip does its own transforms to make the transmission more reliable (FEC, interleaving, whitening), before 2-GFSK modulation. These steps are only partially documented and specific to the SPIRIT1. To use my Heltec module, I would need to know exactly what these steps do.
What I did have were the exact contents of messages going into the radio (read from the MCU using SWD) and of messages going out of the radio (captured using the Heltec). After collecting a few samples, I turned it into a math problem for Opus 5.5, which eventually managed to determine the exact transform used in the SPIRIT1. The real (also generated) prompt was longer, but in essence:
The task. A black-box deterministic function F maps an input byte-string X to an output. I observe pairs (X, Y) where Y is a fixed 64-byte window onto F(X) — the full output may be longer; only the first 64 bytes are seen. Recover F well enough to invert it: given Y, recover X. Approach it however you like; form your own model before reading "What I ruled out."
Data.
- pairs.txt — 5 labelled examples (<input_hex> <output_hex>): input is the full 57-byte record, output the 64-byte window.
- outputs.txt — 1831 unlabelled output windows from the same system.
Observations (verified on the data).
1. Fixed additive mask: Y = M XOR T(X), with M a fixed position-indexed sequence. XORing two outputs cancels M, and the zero runs line up with where the two inputs are equal.
2. Partially linear over GF(2): in some regions Y_i XOR Y_j depends only on X_i XOR X_j; in others it doesn't — so T isn't globally linear.
3. Input-independent invariant block: output bytes 12..27 are identical across every example, even though the inputs differ there. The central anomaly.
4. Leading correspondence: output 0..7 tracks input 0..7, degrading further in.
What I ruled out (read after forming your own view). Modelling T as a GF(2)-linear expansion plus the additive stream M and searching exhaustively: best ~73% of bits, never exact. Observation 3 can't come from a linear expansion, so a non-linear or block-structured component is involved — don't re-tread the linear-only family.
The Claude-generated description of the whole protocol is available in a separate article.
And now the fun begins. I added a separate tab to my TV control panel, dumped the session key of all remotes, and can now control all radiators from my computer, or even my phone. I can even do it remotely, to come back to a warm home!
It took more effort than taking control of the TV, both from me and from Claude, but it worked out in the end. Without Claude, such a project would have likely taken me dozens, if not hundreds, of hours, but it only took about 9 hours of my time, all included.
Now I just need to find a way to control the weather…

articles.title: David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
articles.body:
Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network.
David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
Early screenings of David Fincher’s latest film are raising questions about whether the director used generative AI.
Following a number of Cliff Booth critics screenings that took place last week ahead of the film’s premiere on November 25th, moviegoers rushed to social media to lament what they saw. One of the most vocal reactions came from YouTuber / director Patrick Tomasso, who said on X that he walked out of his screening feeling “completely gutted” and that the film featured “some of the most blatant and egregious AI use” he has ever seen from a major studio. Tomasso also insisted you can see AI-generated footage in Cliff Booth’s trailers that have been posted online, and he was confident that Fincher’s latest film is filled with “slop as you know and loathe it. The shit you can pump out of Higgsfield.”
Others echoed Tomasso’s sentiments, writing that “the amount of AI in the CLIFF BOOTH movie is astounding to an absurd degree” and vowing to “never watch another Fincher, Pitt or Tarintino [sic] movie again.” Yet some critics enjoyed the film and suggested that the bad AI people thought they were seeing might have actually just been bad CGI. Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used in any capacity to make the film, but Netflix’s heavy involvement in the film’s production and the company’s recent investments in generative AI technology left many suspicious.
It did not help that David Fincher, in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times, responded to questions about his thoughts on AI with “I’m not a Luddite, so I don’t fear the unknown.” Fincher also reasoned that the anti-AI crowd is advocating for artists to stop iterating on their creative processes: “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid? How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?” The spiel made it sound like he might be jumping on the AI bandwagon.
Set about a decade after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff Booth picks up in 1977 at a time when Booth (Pitt) has left his life as a stuntman behind to become a fixer who quietly deals with scandalous problems for Hollywood elites. Cliff still works a number of side gigs as a projectionist and bartender. But the movie is primarily focused on his budding romance with critic-turned-talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) and his working relationship with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a TV actor who needs Booth’s services to keep his wife (Carla Gugino) from being murdered.
At least one trailer for the film features some baffling shots of what looks like people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage that make it seem like there might be some generative AI in the mix. It’s hard to tell from the trailers whether that’s actually the case, but in a moment when many creators have been trying to pass off AI generations as human-made art, it’s not surprising that people are suspicious.
Netflix has been incorporating AI into its movies and series for some time now, and it seemed like the company was doubling down earlier this year when it acquired Ben Affleck’s startup, InterPositive, for around $600 million. Rather than turning text into visual outputs like many commercially available AI tools, InterPositive’s AI models are designed to generate assets based on footage captured during a film’s production. According to Netflix, InterPositive’s AI was developed with the intention of making it easier to tweak details like lighting or to remove unwanted background elements. The company also made a big deal of emphasizing that InterPositive’s models were highly customizable and well suited to replicating a human director’s signature style.
Netflix buying InterPositive and absorbing the company’s development team is part of why there has been so much speculation about AI being used in Cliff Booth. If Cliff Booth actually uses AI and the visuals really are as bad as some have said, it would be a major knock against both Netflix and Fincher — a director known for his meticulous (obsessive, some might argue) attention to detail.

articles.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
articles.body:
GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
- Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
- An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.
- In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.
- The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.
In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.
Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.
Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.
Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.
Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.
We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.
The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.
With our research partner, Onava(opens in a new window), we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.
Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. It is important to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.
Our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. The laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.
This work is an early step toward programmable molecular design at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.

- Design for what happens after binding. We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.

As we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for new medicines could also be misused. Our Preparedness Framework guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.
While lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines.

It is important to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.
Our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models.
Some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins.
The laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.
This work is an early step toward programmable molecular design at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.
- Find minibinders for harder targets. We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short.
- Design for what happens after binding. We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.
- Design a wider range of molecules. Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein.
As we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for new medicines could also be misused. Our Preparedness Framework guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.
While lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines.
- 2026

articles.title: I'm not excited about tech anymore
articles.body:
I'm not excited about tech any more. For the longest time I was excited about new devices, new apps, new platforms—all of it. I've gradually lost interest. I don't think I've grown more cynical—I've always been a cynic. Tech is only interesting when it provides value and it only provides value by being useful. Most new tech isn't useful.
If you're a developer, you are—whether you want to or not—staring down incorporating AI into your workflow. Is it useful? It can be. It can also wreak havoc in your codebase and move your team's bottleneck from authorship to code review. Am I excited about AI? No, no, not at all. I'm not excited about an industry that's consumed the entirety of the internet to enrich a handful of people. I'm not excited about an industry that's building data centers wherever it can, sucking up water and power as it goes. I'm not excited about an industry dedicated to deskilling entire professional fields, to devaluing art and creativity, to flooding the internet with worthless slop, sludge, and spam.
I don't care about self-driving cars. I'd rather have folks in a position to make a living driving taxis. I'd rather we invested in public transit and infrastructure.
I don't care about a folding phone. I have an unremarkable phone with a display that works.
I don't want to be recorded in public by your goofy-looking glasses. I don't need VR—the real world is fascinating without a company mediating the experience.
I don't need crypto.1 Money is a store of value that you can exchange for goods and services. Crypto is a bad investment vehicle with a value totally untethered from reality.2
I don't care about your social platform or short-form video. I'd rather read a book or watch a movie. Your social platform is an echo chamber. Your video is unending and uninteresting.
I don't care about your AI search. Your AI search is worse than what it's replacing: it's less accurate, it takes more energy to run, and it provides no benefit to the publishers it draws upon to provide answers. I want to enter a query, get accurate results, and go to the page providing the answer.
Streaming platforms are now effectively cable, just delivered over a different medium. Streaming music means renting your library in perpetuity.
Appliances don't need an internet connection. Appliances don't need a subscription. They just need to work and work reliably. No refrigerator should require a firmware update.
Cars shouldn't require subscriptions.
I don't need to be tracked. I don't need personalized recommendations. I don't need to establish a relationship with a brand. If I need something, I'll do some research and buy it. Every ad, every tracker, every beacon is something new to block.
So, what am I excited about? Well, mostly, things that are boring and things that are stable. Open protocols, standards, and other things that have stood the test of time. I like email.3 I love RSS. I like APIs and integrations. I like decentralized social platforms. I love tools that do one thing and do it well. Examples? I've got those.
- Fastmail: they do standards-compliant email. It's performant and reliable, and they charge a reasonable price.
- Kagi: I search and I get relevant results. The price is fair.
- Navidrome: I can stream my own music and enrich it with plugins and complementary tools like AudioMuse-AI.
- linkding: I save a lot of links. I share some of those links. They all go through linkding. I archive what I save and store the archive in an S3 bucket.
- Obsidian: all of my notes and writing exist as files on my local disk. It's absurdly configurable and even supports alternative syncing methods. I have a theme that aligns with my site's design and a few custom plugins. It does exactly what it sets out to do, and more if you need it.
What else? ActivityPub, ATProto, CoreDNS, Headscale, NextDNS, bunny.net, DNSimple, and on and on.
Do one thing. Do it well. Be useful. Don't exploit people.

articles.title: 2035 Came Early
articles.body:
tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire, GL gears, xeyes, a voice, the weather over curl, or Firefox.
I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.
Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.
  Atwood’s LawAny application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009
I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.
In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev.
One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev.
It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package, over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.
I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev
It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix.
  Aside What is unkernel? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.
In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.
The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm,11With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload.22The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.
JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.
Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.
Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland, and they float over the terminal you started them from.
GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.
Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.
Network. curl, git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay.33Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list. 
The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈
Here is Firefox in trynix, and it loading trynix.dev, and then loading Firefox again inside itself.44Don’t get too excited: this took over 4 hours. The inner Firefox needed JIT disabled, the middle one ran without GL, and the outer page used a Wisp relay on my laptop since wisp.unkernel.dev cannot reach itself.
Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯
2035 came early.

articles.title: Declare is a UI language for you and your AI
articles.body:
Just as SQL is a domain-specific language for database queries, Declare is a DSL for user interfaces — for taking the custom, fluid experience you have in mind beyond a prototype, into a real app: structured, verifiable, and with the design written plainly in its code.
Declare in 10 minutes →
Run the calendar →
The language, in one file →
01
A calendar that zooms through time, a desktop with real windows: complete programs, each readable end to end and checked by the compiler. Open one, or edit it live in the browser you’re using.
1
Day, week, month and year views are one surface, zooming continuously; a view doesn’t switch so much as become the next one, and every motion can be interrupted. It runs on real data: drag an event to another day, and it’s moved.
568
lines of code, plus 228 of comments — four views, zoom, drag and edit
177 KB
over the wire, gzipped — app (structure, logic, styling) and runtime
0
lines typed by hand — human-designed and directed, built with AI
Run Declare Calendar →
View & edit source →
2
→
The acid test for a UI language: multiple applications, windows that drag, resize, layer and minimize into live thumbnails, a magnifying dock, menus that follow focus, and separately loaded apps running inside its windows. Elsewhere that is a project assembled from several libraries; here it is one program.
3529 lines — 2011 code, 939 comment · 264 KB over the wire · every pixel drawn from shapes, no image assets
3
1,000,000 issues · search as you type · edit in place, with undo · not one line of virtualization code
1508 lines — 983 code, 251 comment · 194 KB over the wire, before its data · no dependencies
And more:
Weather →
Market Map →
Birds →
To-do →
Asteroids →
02
Declare was designed first for the people who make interfaces. Layout, motion, states, theming and drawing are the language itself, not libraries bolted on — so the experience you have in mind is something you can write down directly, and read back later as it was meant.
Rules
Data
Motion
Three things follow one value: the number, the bar’s length and its color. Click to change v — all three update together, because each is a relationship that stays true, not a step someone remembered to run.
LIVE · EDITABLE
Revert
40
click anywhere to change v
In Declare, yes. A small language gets it started; these four tools let it catch its mistakes, fix them, and finish.
One installable skill: the language, the library, the conventions, the working loop — nothing to reconstruct from a repository. And declare-help answers any name or error code on demand.
Every diagnostic names the broken rule and the valid rewrite. Try it: change textColor to color in the panel above and read what comes back.
The Inspector can tell you or an agent why a live value is what it is, what it depends on, and what happens if you change it — live, in the running program, not guessed from source.
A formal six-rung ladder, from parse to pixels, is how an app is shown to be correct. Your AI climbs it one rung at a time, and every rung reports what it proved — and what it cannot see.
Measured: given the same brief, the same agent built a ticket-buying app twice. The Declare app was 1,279 lines to React’s 2,666, and its first build that ran passed all eleven hidden checks; React’s passed six. Single runs, not yet a benchmark — every run is in the repository.
The calendar above was built this way: human-designed and directed, built with AI, and kept honest by the compiler.

WHY DECLARE
Start with the obvious objection. AI writes most code now, and it is best at the languages it has seen the most — so the sensible move is to use whatever has the biggest corpus and let the model figure it out. By that logic the era of new programming languages is over.
That argument gets its facts right and its conclusion backwards. Writing code is now nearly free; trusting it costs what it always did. An AI writing React verifies its work by resemblance — this looks like the billion lines it trained on — and resemblance is not correctness. Meanwhile less and less code passes under human eyes, which leaves the language and its compiler as the one reviewer that is always present. Handing the writing to a machine doesn’t make the language irrelevant. It makes it load-bearing.
Declare set out to be two things at once.
Expressive. A language that can say what a real interface is — not just data entry screens, but fast, polished, custom software designed to be used, even enjoyed: views that become the next view, motion that carries meaning, layouts that answer to content and to the screen they are on.
Verifiable. A language that can be learned, written, debugged and tested by an AI, and whose programs a compiler can check rather than guess at.
Most attempts to make code safe for machines make it duller for people. Declare refuses that tradeoff. Every feature that makes a program checkable — one tree for structure, style and behavior; every dependency visible to the compiler; one decider for each value — is also what makes it short, and readable to the person who has to judge it.
A well-designed experience is a set of decisions — how it should look, how it should move, what should feel inevitable — and those decisions are yours. An AI can produce a standard-looking app easily, and in Declare it can produce one verifiably. What it cannot supply is a custom-crafted design.
That is why layout, motion, states, theming and drawing are part of the language itself rather than libraries: a Spring on an attribute, a layout as a value a view holds, a mode as a state you are in or not. The continuous version of an interface is often less code than the discrete one. And because a Declare program is one complete description — no separate stylesheet, no framework lifecycle, no build of a dozen files — the design you meant is written plainly in the code, where you, a colleague or an AI can read it back and see that it is still what you meant.
What an AI gets from a mainstream stack is corpus leverage: fluency by imitation — broad, shallow, self-contradictory, unverifiable. The other kind is comprehension leverage: a language small enough to hand to a model whole, regular enough that its programs can be analyzed rather than pattern-matched, and backed by a compiler that turns each mistake into a precise correction. Corpus leverage arrives free with popularity. Comprehension leverage has to be designed in, and it is the only kind a new language can compete on.
It is a measured bet: a small language handed to a model in context has beaten the same model writing Python (study →), and a compiler that explains its errors measurably improves a model’s repairs (study →).
Declare was built the same way it is meant to be used: eval by eval. An agent that had never seen the language was given a written application spec and the Declare download, and built the app while I watched — how long it took, what it tripped on, what it found missing, how well its code read, how well the app worked. Another agent built the same spec in React. Over a hundred runs, what improved was not the model but the language: the same ticket-buying app went from 48 minutes to 24, compiler errors per build from 32 to 6. In the latest pair the Declare app was 1,279 lines to React’s 2,666, and its first build that ran passed all eleven hidden checks; React’s passed six. Single runs, not yet a benchmark. The runs, in full →
The most prized quality of a great interface — the continuity you feel in the best native apps — has always been bespoke: specialist craft, one interaction at a time, locked to a platform, and wrong in ways nothing catches. Declare makes that continuity the grain of the language, and puts it where a compiler can check it. The calendar is the proof: four views as one zooming surface, about 600 lines, human-designed and directed, and built with AI.
There is another generation of experiences beyond today’s hand-crafted best — built on a foundation with continuity at its core, deployed as widely as a URL, and shaped by people with an idea of how software should feel, working with an AI at their side. Declare is built to find out what they make.
Further: the FAQ · how it works · the whole language, in one file
WHERE THIS CAME FROM
I co-founded Laszlo Systems and led the team behind OpenLaszlo — a declarative UI language, first shipped in 2002, that pushed right to the edge of what that era’s web browsers could handle.
What brought me back to UI development was Mesa, a zoomable canvas app I built without using a browser framework, toolkit, or higher-level language. Mesa renders a thousand live objects at a 60fps floor, even on a phone. It’s been positively amazing to see how fast today’s browsers have become — and how powerful and flexible today’s web platform is.
And yet the web as it actually stands is still, mostly, slow and clunky. Even brand-new sites. How can that be?
It turns out the browser isn’t what makes the web feel worse than a good native app. It’s what we’ve built on top of it. A lot of accumulated code — and a lot of accumulated habits — take their toll, and the interfaces that do escape them are hand-crafted, one at a time, by specialists.
In June I handed the original OpenLaszlo compiler to an LLM and got back a modern port that compiles any OpenLaszlo program perfectly, byte-for-byte.
Seeing those programs again through fresh eyes — and seeing how small and how fast the sites built with them are — I decided the language deserved to be modernized. Declare is what came out of that: a direct descendant of OpenLaszlo, with the core ideas intact, built on an entirely new foundation, and shaped to be written with an LLM.
Enjoy!
— David Temkin
THE LANGUAGE
Declare is a language for building application interfaces. This file is the language: every form the grammar accepts and every rule the compiler enforces. The compiler completes it — every error carries a code, a position, and the rewrite that resolves it (§12), so nothing here needs to enumerate edge cases.
Declare is new, and no LLM has been trained on it. It resembles React, CSS, and HTML in places, and this file is where those resemblances stop. Every complete program below is compiled by the test suite, so the examples are current by construction; where this file and the compiler disagree, the compiler is right.
