articles.body:
Six Artworks Under $1,000 We’d Love to Give (and Receive!) This Holiday
There’s an unparalleled joy in watching a loved one unwrap something they both never anticipated and immediately know they’ve needed all along. These types of gifts are often the most unexpected, surprisingly personal, and typically, one of a kind.
Our partners at Joy Machine have generously curated a selection of artworks that fit this category. Priced under $1,000, the collection includes pieces by an international group of artists that longtime Colossal readers will surely recognize. From playful drawings in walnut ink to uncanny kitsch sculptures, these works are perfecting for gifting this holiday season, even (especially?) if that gift is to yourself.
Seattle-based artist Debra Broz applies her training in ceramic conservation to a practice that involves scouring flea markets and thrift shops for ceramic figurines, breaking their forms, and reassembling the figures as surreal hybrids.
Dutch artist Collin van der Sluijs is a master of several styles, with a background in graffiti and street art and a parallel interest in the delicate, impeccably detailed features of the natural world.
Collect “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” ($550)
With a deep love for the flora and fauna near her home in the Pacific Northwest, Stevie Shao creates folk art-inspired works through bold color palettes and arresting patterns.
Japanese artist Misato Sano is best known for her cheeky wooden carvings of poodles and pugs, which she translates to two-dimensions in this playful rendition that might just make us want to get up and get moving.
Collect “Let’s work out” ($150)
Through large-scale paintings and small woodcuts, Danym Kwon meditates on the mundane activities like folding laundry or strolling around the park that allow memories to emerge and be understood anew.
Collect “A Quiet Afternoon” ($350)
Layering acrylic paint with crisp edges that evoke paper collage, Rachel Hayden blends the patterns of a summertime picnic with the eerie colors and atmosphere of fall, perfect for the perpetually witchy pal.

articles.title: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
articles.body:
After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man.
Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.”
The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff.
“The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added.
The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct, which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.”
Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company.
The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The president reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role
Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” The Wall Street Journal writes.
Huang will likely need the administration’s support as he weathers an upcoming wave of congressional scrutiny from a newly Democrat-led government. The CEO is scheduled to appear for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week and, in the coming weeks, he will be called to appear for a number of different closed House hearings, including for the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee.

articles.title: Threads comes to iPad and takes a page from X’s playbook with cashtags
articles.body:
It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Instagram’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet. In an overnight update, the company rolled out a big-screen version of the X competitor. It’s also added another new feature, borrowed from X: the stock-tracking feature known as cashtags.
While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect. Instead of offering a multi-column interface as on Threads’ web app, the iPad app focuses on the user’s main feed in a single-column layout. There are also options to swipe right and left from the main screen to access the search screen and the feeds menu, respectively.
The iPad app isn’t the company’s only update in the latest release. According to a post from Threads engineer Guy Dickinson, Threads will now support cashtags — a feature popularized by Twitter years ago for tracking live stock information. These specialized tags start with the dollar sign (“$”) followed by a ticker symbol. When you click on a cashtag, you can follow the discussions around the stock.
In addition, Threads is adding live stock quotes, charts, and other context at the top of each cashtag’s page. As you search for a particular cashtag, the autocomplete search results will display the stock’s current price and the percentage it’s up or down. Dickinson says the feature will currently support NYSE and Nasdaq stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Cashtags will be supported on the web, iOS, and Android. However, they’re just now rolling out, so you may not immediately see them.
The update points to Threads’ broader ambition to compete with X, not only as a destination for discussions about various topics, but also as a place where people can track real-time news and information. Cashtags in particular could attract traders and investors to Threads who typically rely on X.
Despite facing stiff competition from X, Meta announced earlier this year that Threads topped 500 million monthly users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company believes the app is on track to reach a billion users over time.

articles.title: Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see
articles.body:
Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.
The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.
But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.
This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18.
Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.
Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.
The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

articles.title: The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch
articles.body:
Computer Science > Machine Learning
  [Submitted on 23 Nov 2026]
Title:The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence is never negative, yet PyTorch users have reported negative values for years, and the standard advice is to clamp them at zero. The sign is only the visible part of a silent failure. Many machine-learning applications compare nearby distributions, where conventional KL formulas lose accuracy. On 8.5 million inputs with certified references across 18 closed-form KL families and F.kl_div, we find widespread errors in values and gradients on CPU and GPU. Among scalar families in ordinary parameter ranges, over 85% of FP32 values have at least 1% relative error near KL 10^(-7) (FP16: 10^(-3)), and about 30% become negative at smaller divergences. More precision is not the cure: evaluated one precision higher, the same formulas still leave 7--51% of FP32 values significantly wrong for 22 of 23 configurations. Stable closed-form decompositions, compensated arithmetic, and analytic gradients remove over 97% of significant errors in the working format. Strict repairs eliminate significant errors on 7.2 million scored closed-form samples and correctly round all 567 million scored F.kl_div components. The errors affect parameter fitting, Bayesian decisions, identical-start distillation (up to 97% top-1 disagreement), KL-based layer rankings in a quantized LLM, and 19--59% of GPT-2 circuit edge scores. With the repaired code they all but vanish. Code and data: this https URL

articles.title: Have You Been Attacked by an Owl?
articles.body:
Personally, I have not been attacked by an owl, but more than a few folks in nearby Brookline have. Possibly, per the associate director of field conservation at Zoo New England, by one of the weird owls.
Please also enjoy a chuckle at the article’s ambiguous headline:
Owls have attacked at least a dozen people in the Brookline area. I’m one of them.
Perhaps author Milena Fernsler is a victim of an owl attack. Alternately, perhaps Fernsler is an actual owl. Naturally, I prefer the latter explanation.
Previously in unprovoked avian assaults: I Was a Victim of Bird Strike

articles.title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
articles.body:
LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
5 min read
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?
Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.
So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.
It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks
Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.
So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone???
This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!
Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.
Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.
And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now.
This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for me and have my best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example.
On the existential threat or tool question, I'm firmly in the tool camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.
- And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this. ↩︎

articles.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
articles.body:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”
The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’
Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.
It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”
In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.
It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.
Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.

articles.title: The Big Idea: Dan Moren
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Dan Moren
Posted on November 24, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi Leave a Comment
Legality does not equal morality, and author Dan Moren’s band of heisters have got just the charm and questionable ethics to prove it! Hop in your spaceship and follow along in the Big Idea for his newest sci-fi novel, Eternity’s Tomb.
DAN MOREN:
Who among us has not been tempted by the idea of a victimless crime?
On one of our earliest dates, my now wife asked me what felony I’d commit if I could get away with it, and while it may have been attempt to ensure a long and healthy(?) relationship through extortion, my answer was quick enough: an elaborate heist—the kind of elegant, perfectly executed plan where you get away clean and nobody gets hurt.
Alas, I never have pulled off the perfect heist, but the good news is that the next best thing to perpetrating crime is writing about it.
For Z, the protagonist of my new book Eternity’s Tomb, things haven’t really gone to plan. Not so much a career criminal as a career opportunist, Z is just finishing a stint in jail when a floating brain in a jar named Ayex dangles an enticing proposition: recovering a spaceborne tomb that’s been lost for millennia, along with—naturally—all of its riches. Along for the ride are the rest of Z’s former crew: ursine mechanic Graham, genetically engineered murderbird Whistler, and hotshot pilot Trix—who also just happens to be Z’s ex. (It didn’t end well.)
Now, let’s just hang a fedora on it: does the main thread of this plot stem at least in part from my childhood love of classic tomb raids like Indiana Jones? Absolutely. Like any good dungeon crawl, adventures like these pit our band of heroes against devilish traps, labyrinthine tunnels and passages, and more than a few surprises. It’s good old-fashioned pulpy fun.
Right?
See, here’s the thing: the older I’ve gotten, the more I’ve been forced to confront the complexities of those stories. Did those “recovered” pieces really belong in a museum? Was this so-called “archaeology” just out-and-out grave-robbing? What is a tenured professor even doing dodging boulders; shouldn’t he be grading? Is this all being supported by student tuitions?!
So, in the hopes of forging an ethically sustainable adventure plot, I started to concoct a scenario wherein guilt wasn’t a foregone conclusion. What if, I theorized, the tomb in question had been launched from its planet of origin into the stars, on a long and winding path destined for a black hole where it would ultimately be destroyed? What if the civilization that had dispatched it had long since ceased to exist? Who would this really hurt? Moreover, what if said civilization hadn’t just died out, but had instead been wiped out by a planet-level catastrophe? Wouldn’t there be some virtue to recovering its remaining artifacts? (And, you know, liquidating just a meager portion of it as a finder’s fee.)
Suffice it to say, there are no easy answers. I’d set out to write a straightforward adventure story, but ultimately tying myself in narrative knots to avoid the ethical complexities felt like cheating. So rather than duck and dodge the problem like it was a barrage of poison darts triggered by a pressure-sensitive floor, I made the only logical choice: having my characters themselves grapple with the implications.
Granted, this is a crew of thieves and criminals we’re talking about—their moral compass may be a tad off-axis to begin with.
Still, even criminals live by a code. They—unlike globetrotting academics, apparently—have lines they won’t cross. My crew doesn’t see themselves as the bad guys so much as people who just want lives outside of the confines of what society has prescribed for them. Sometimes, for them to survive on those margins, that means bending the rules—but what it doesn’t is mean picking on people who can’t afford it. They’re criminals: they may have lied, stolen, and cheated, but come on—they’re not jerks.
Eternity’s Tomb: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Powell’s|Porter Square Books

articles.title: You can lock in Hulu and Disney Plus for as low as $5 per month for a year
articles.body:
The Black Friday offers on streaming services are rolling in, and the latest deal includes Disney Plus and Hulu for a steeply discounted monthly rate. There are sales happening for both the ad-supported and ad-free tiers that offer full access to both services, and either will save you quite a bit of money.
You can lock in Hulu and Disney Plus for as low as $5 per month for a year
Or, opt for the ad-free plan for $14.99 per month instead of $21.99 for 12 months.
For those who despise ads, you can opt for the ad-free version for $14.99 per month (was $21.99) for a year, costing you $180 instead of $264 over the duration. This deal is located in a small banner near the bottom of the sale page via Hulu or Disney Plus. The ad-supported tier drops from $12.99 to just $4.99, so you’ll pay $60 over the course of the year instead of $156. You have through Cyber Monday, November 30th, at 11:59PM PST to take advantage of the lower prices.
The Hulu and Disney Plus bundle is one of the best values in streaming, especially if you have kids who can’t get enough Disney movies and other cartoons. On the other hand, Hulu is home to plenty of shows made for adults, including Furious (a crime drama that gripped this household like no other show this year), The Bear, Shōgun, Alien: Earth, The Lowdown, and many more. It’s worth the subscription just for those alone.
The bundle includes Star Wars and Marvel content plus fun, uplifting shows to dig into over the holidays, like Bob’s Burgers, Futurama, The Simpsons, and It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia, to name some mainstays that tend to attract subscribers.
If you’re considering other subscription services, we covered discounts on Paramount Plus (I might snag this to watch Cupertino), HBO Max, and Peacock. (The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins is fun!)

articles.title: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
articles.body:
Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like:
- Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app)
- Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once
- Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins)
- Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this)
Here’s a demo: https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0
We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer.
Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as
1. More people turn into power users of agents, and 2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP.
Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval.
Interestingly, we were almost forced into this solution because we had around 4 weeks to build this product (after a pivot), and traditional fiat with a partner bank would have caused far too many regulatory and compliance slowdowns.
Because of that, the only fast option that remained was using stablecoin wallets. It also ensures we aren't a Money Services Business (MSB) since we don’t hold control or access to the user’s funds.
Each call to the wallet creates what we call one-time or recurring standing permissions. For a one-time payment, your agent makes an MCP call, and you receive a notification in our mobile app. Once you swipe up in the app and approve with a passkey (or your device’s biometric method), we create a one-time permission that instructs your wallet to send $X to your recipient’s address.
Trusted contacts let your agent send money to people that you’ve previously authorized without explicit passkey approval. Generally, these are people that you’d trust to send your money back even if your agent made a mistake.
We’re also able to support sending money to someone off Versine using claim forwarding, where the user authorizes us to forward a specific amount to a future address (which we create once we verify a recipient's OTP).
Param worked on scaling vector search at Databricks and harness evals at Glean. Harshith worked on core Stripe Connect fee-processing infrastructure and built an AWS Fargate autoscaler at Amazon. Vishnu worked on intent-based agent testing infrastructure at Amazon. None of us were experienced in stablecoin or crypto infra before working on Versine but our distributed systems experience has helped us a lot.
We'd love for you guys to try it! It's available on iOS and Android and as an MCP on ChatGPT and Claude. We also support a public MCP and REST API for other agents.
Please let us know how you find it and if it works as you'd hoped!

articles.title: Millions of bitcoin are probably lost for good. Almost none can be proved gone
articles.body:
Millions of bitcoin are probably lost for good. Almost none can be proved gone
Estimates put the lost coins at 2.8 to 3.8 million. Only a sliver can be shown to be gone; the rest is a landfill, a password and a guess.
About 20.1 million bitcoin have been mined so far. A good share of them will probably never move again.
In 2017 the analytics firm Chainalysis estimated that between 2.78 million and 3.79 million BTC were already lost, Fortune reported. That was 17% to 23% of the coins mined at the time.
It is still the figure most reports quote, and it rests on assumptions. A coin that hasn't moved in ten years might be lost, or its owner might just be patient. The blockchain can't tell the difference.
The coins nobody has touched since 2010
The biggest pile of unmoved bitcoin is also the oldest. In 2013 the researcher Sergio Demian Lerner spotted a pattern in the earliest blocks that points to a single miner, since nicknamed "Patoshi".
He estimates that miner earned about 1.1 million BTC, and almost none of it has ever been spent, Cointelegraph reports. Many people assume the miner was Bitcoin's creator, Satoshi Nakamoto. Lerner himself says that can't be proved. Whether those coins count as lost depends on who is counting. That one choice moves the estimate by about a million.
A hard drive in Newport
In 2013 James Howells threw out a hard drive holding the keys to 8,000 BTC. It ended up in a landfill run by Newport City Council in Wales, according to Wikipedia's account of the case.
For more than a decade he asked to dig for it. The council refused, the High Court dismissed his claim in January 2025, and the Court of Appeal refused to let it go further that March. The drive is still in the ground.
Eight wrong guesses
Stefan Thomas, a programmer, was paid 7,002 BTC in 2011 for making an explainer video about bitcoin. He kept the keys on an encrypted IronKey drive and lost the paper with its password.
The drive allows ten tries before it encrypts its contents for good. He had used eight, Cointelegraph reported in 2021, and later reports still describe him as having two left.
The vault that wasn't
Some "lost keys" stories turn out to be something else. When Gerald Cotten, the founder of the Canadian exchange QuadrigaCX, died in December 2018, the exchange said its customers' crypto sat in cold wallets only he could open.
A 2020 staff review by the Ontario Securities Commission found otherwise. It said most of the shortfall came from fraud by Cotten, rejected the idea that the money was locked in cold wallets nobody could open, and put clients' losses at at least C$169 million.
Read more: Was FTX a Ponzi scheme from the beginning?
Burned on purpose
Some bitcoin is lost on purpose. Coins sent to an address like 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE can never be spent, because nobody holds a key for it. People use addresses like this to "burn" coins in public.
Even the first block has some. The 50 BTC reward in the genesis block can't be spent because of a quirk in Bitcoin's original code, according to the Bitcoin Wiki. Coins like these are the only ones anyone can prove are gone, and they are a tiny share of the total.
A supply nobody can count exactly
Bitcoin's 21 million cap is fixed in its code. Supply passed 20 million in March 2026, The Block reported, and the last coins will be issued over the next century or so. Lost coins don't change those numbers. They still count as supply, in wallets that will never sign another transaction.
Mt. Gox shows how blurry the line can be. About 850,000 BTC went missing there in 2014, and about 200,000 turned up in an old wallet a month later. Its creditors are still being paid, twelve years on.
So "lost bitcoin" is mostly an estimate, with a few cases that are certain. Everything else sits somewhere between a landfill and a wallet whose owner is just very patient.
Read more: Is CeFi less secure than DeFi?
Frequently asked questions
How many bitcoins are lost?
Nobody knows exactly. The most quoted figure is a 2017 Chainalysis estimate of 2.78 million to 3.79 million BTC, which was 17% to 23% of the coins mined at the time. It treats long-unmoved coins as probably lost, so it is an estimate, not a count.
Can lost bitcoin be recovered?
Only by someone who has, or finds, the private key. There is no central party that can reissue or reverse coins. Coins sent to a burn address, or the genesis block reward, can't be spent by anyone.
Are Satoshi Nakamoto's coins lost?
Nobody knows. About 1.1 million BTC mined in 2009 and 2010 is attributed to one early miner, often assumed to be Satoshi, and almost none of it has moved. The attribution can't be proved, and unmoved coins are not necessarily lost.
Do lost coins reduce bitcoin's 21 million cap?
No. The cap and the issuance schedule are fixed in the code, and lost coins still count in supply figures. They simply can't move, so fewer coins are usable than the supply number suggests.
What is a bitcoin burn address?
An address that nobody holds a private key for, often a readable "vanity" string such as 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE. Coins sent there are visible on the blockchain but can never be spent again.

articles.title: Huang reportedly admitted to more than two affairs to Nvidia’s board
articles.body:
In a complete U-turn, Nvidia’s board on Monday reinstated Jensen Huang as the CEO and president of the chipmaker, just a fortnight after he resigned.
During a meeting before his reinstatement, however, Huang admitted to more affairs beyond the two that have been reported in the news, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Early in November, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair in a letter to employees. At the time, he was ostensibly talking about his relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (not related to Jensen). Later, it was reported that he’d also had a relationship with Nvidia’s VP of health, Kimberly Powell.
Afterwards, Reuters reported that he also had an affair with another employee.
It’s not clear which affairs Huang admitted to during this recent conversation with Nvidia’s board of directors.
Huang’s return was spurred by a personal intervention from the U.S. government, Nvidia’s board said in a statement on Monday, and President Donald Trump apparently called the board to bat for Huang’s reinstatement.
The Wall Street Journal reports that over the weekend, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told Trump and Vice President JD Vance that the Justice Department wasn’t investigating Huang and there was no evidence that he was a national security risk, after which both contacted the company’s board.
Huang received a “hero’s welcome” at Nvidia’s HQ, with several employees applauding his return.

articles.title: Bambu’s five-nozzle P3C isn’t quite the 3D printer I expected
articles.body:
Three weeks ago, Bambu Lab introduced the state of the art in home printing tech at $2,499 — now, you can get many of its fancy new features for less than half the price.
Bambu’s five-nozzle P3C isn’t quite the 3D printer I expected
Bambu cut a few corners — and motors — to reach that price.
Like that bigger H3C, the new $1,149 Bambu P3C can also swap between materials on the fly, mix different colors to produce much of the rainbow, mix soft and hard materials, even mix different sizes of nozzle and different diameters of filament so you can switch between high speed and fine detail in a single print.
But Bambu cut more corners than I expected to hit the lower $1,149 / £999 / €1,149 launch price today, and I think they made more of a tinkerer’s 3D printer than one suited for either beginners or pros.
Some of the changes were completely expected, like its smaller 256 x 256 x 260mm print area (much like Bambu’s other P-series printers), and that it supports seven automatically swapping tools instead of nine. (Seven is still quite a lot when affordable toolchangers like the $849 Snapmaker U1 typically offer just four.)
But unlike the H3C, the P3C doesn’t come fully loaded, and it doesn’t load itself. While it has slots for seven rolls of filament and up to seven independent tools (including thicker-than-usual 2.85mm filament, or pens, cutting blades, and debossing and foil transfer tools if you want it to double as a Cricut), it only comes with five 0.4mm print nozzles by default.
And while five is still one more color than you’d get with an $800 Bambu P2S Combo, the 3D printer I’d buy for myself, the Bambu P3C’s automated material system (AMS) is the first Bambu has shipped without any motors to automatically load your filament.
Don’t get me wrong: You can still keep five colors of filament ready to go at a moment’s notice, one more than the P2S, by keeping them loaded into the P3C’s five independent nozzles. You can also buy and fairly easily install two more printheads as well, though they cost up to $100 each.
But loading those nozzles is a slow and surprisingly manual process where you have to shove a string of filament down a tube, quite a long distance by hand, after waiting for the machine to preheat each one, and it feels like a step backwards after years using the earlier motorized versions of Bambu’s AMS. Then again, the P3C doesn’t have to spend time and filament purging between colors like the P2S does.
I expect many 3D printing enthusiasts will see $1,149 for the Bambu P3C as a pretty good deal, assuming they haven’t written off the company’s gadgets after Bambu’s open source snafus. Even five nozzles is enough to load all five rolls of Bambu’s “PLA Palette” cyan, magenta, yellow, black, and white (CMYKW) filaments for color mixing to produce beautiful creations like the company’s new hummingbird test print, which came out almost flawlessly on my first try.
But you should know that color mixing isn’t necessarily a foolproof way to produce some colors, like the brown tree branch that’s supposed to be the hummingbird’s perch, and I’m not looking forward to manually pulling and pushing a roll of brown filament to change that. Bambu says I should probably try a feature called “mixed color sublayer” for better results, and I also suppose I could daisy-chain a normal motorized AMS to one of the P3C’s printheads, as that is a supported workflow. But that’s why I’m suggesting we’re in tinkerer territory.
I asked Bambu about the decision to not include filament-loading motors in the P3C’s AMS system, and here’s part of the statement I got back from spokesperson Karlie Hou: “The AMS 3P’s design deliberately omits the auto‑loading feature as part of the effort to offer premium multi‑head performance at roughly half the price of the flagship H3C system, allowing a far broader audience — hobbyists, small studios, and educational institutions — to enjoy premium multi‑head, multi‑color printing experience.”
The company says it should take around five minutes to manually reload five nozzles. “In the next [software] update, we aim to shrink the total hands‑on time for loading five spools to under one minute,” the company writes, though that seems like a tall order.
Maybe I’ll put the P3C to a year-long test like I did with the P2S, and see how often I actually need something CMYKW can’t do for me, and whether the filament stays dry when left in the printheads for a long time. The question is: What printers should I test against? Are there any upcoming ones I should wait for?

articles.title: What Cloudflare Doesn't Tell You
articles.body:
What Cloudflare Doesn't Tell You
Cloudflare has arguably done more to push modern internet technologies than any other company. The work they have done to enable TLS, IPv6, post quantum encryption, and other modern standards for millions of websites deserves a tremendous amount of credit.
While this is great, Cloudflare also hides many of the shortcomings of the underlying infrastructure from both users and website owners. Yes, you can connect to a Cloudflare website and it'll allow for IPv6, post quantum encryption, and TLS. But Cloudflare's connection to the origin server might be entirely unencrypted and rely exclusively on IPv4. This creates a huge mismatch between what is being presented to users and the reality of the connection.
One of my biggest problems with this is the fact that Cloudflare doesn't do enough to notify website administrators about these issues. While Cloudflare provides tools to inspect these, comprehensive visibility is lacking. The Cloudflare dashboard should notify you about each of these issues where Cloudflare is following better practices than your origin server, without website administrators having to dig through and specifically look for this information. Clear warnings and proactive alerts to administrators would help greatly.
Not only that, but according to Cloudflare's own documentation, they actively prefer IPv4 over IPv6 when making origin server requests, which is particularly disappointing for a company that has done so much to advance IPv6 adoption:
For proxied DNS records that have both an IPv6 and IPv4 origin address, Cloudflare will prefer the IPv4 address when connecting to your origin server.
Even when website administrators invest in deploying IPv6 on their origin servers, Cloudflare still prioritizes IPv4.
I also believe the industry should consider adding functionality so CDNs and other intermediate networks can expose origin TLS connection information alongside their own. This would allow users and network researchers to better understand the encryption state of the entire path and hold website owners accountable for bad security practices. A similar mechanism could expose which IP version is being used to communicate with the origin server.
Cloudflare has an opportunity to not only make modern internet technologies accessible to users, but also encourage adoption of those technologies throughout the underlying infrastructure. Cloudflare should be a catalyst for modernizing the internet, not a mechanism that allows website owners to avoid modernization indefinitely. Improving transparency would be a meaningful step toward achieving that goal.

articles.title: Jetty Pro
articles.body:
Hypercritical
Jetty Pro
My first two Mac apps, Front and Center and SwitchGlass, were both created back in 2020 to restore features from DragThing, the venerable Mac app that was retired in 2019. The one tiny feature that Front and Center provided was literally a single checkbox within DragThing’s preferences. SwitchGlass went a bit farther, recreating one specific kind of floating palette from DragThing (and classic Mac OS).
After 24 years of development, DragThing had a ton of features. People often joked that I was destined to slowly reimplement all of DragThing’s functionality in a series of small apps. Put another way, they were saying I was doomed to make strange little Mac apps with extremely limited appeal (and sales).
Perhaps to prove them wrong, the next app I created was Hyperspace, which provided a way to reclaim disk space without removing any files. Hyperspace was still a nerdy app, but at least it had somewhat broader appeal than my earlier efforts. Who doesn’t want to save disk space? But more importantly, it was totally unrelated to DragThing. I had broken the curse!
Alas, there was one more (small) thing from DragThing that I missed. I used to have a DragThing palette in the corner of my screen containing some commonly used folders. In earlier versions of macOS, it was possible to pin the Dock to a screen corner, but that wasn’t really what I wanted either. I just wanted a small, separate palette of folders in the corner.
This is not a hard problem to solve. Plenty of Mac apps can provide something close to what I want…but not exactly what I want, in the specific way that I want it. For many years, I got by with some folders in the corner of my desktop. But the problem nagged at me.
A few years ago, I went so far as to implement my desired feature in SwitchGlass, adding the ability to create a small, extra palette full of folders in addition to the app switcher. But it felt incongruous with the rest of the app, so I never shipped it. And I didn’t want to maintain my own private fork of SwitchGlass, so I abandoned that branch of the code.
How It Started
Today, AI coding agents are helping to produce a bounty of new, niche Mac apps, many made by people who have little or no coding experience. Even for experienced software developers, vibe coding has made it possible to create apps that were previously “not worth building” due to an unfavorable ratio of effort to payoff.
It’s in this context that I revisited my “little palette of folders” idea. Surely I could vibe-code a simple app just for me in a day or two, right?
That was three and a half months ago.
How It’s Going
So what happened? The well-known programmer’s credo comes to mind: “We do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy.” Indeed.
I began the project by feeding a coding agent the source code to my app, SwitchGlass, as a starting point. I wrote SwitchGlass six years ago using a substantially more primitive version of SwiftUI. (For the developers out there, it predates @Observable and @State, and it supports Macs all the way back to macOS 12 Monterey from 2021.) I asked a coding agent to modernize the code and generalize it to support an arbitrary number of palettes instead of just one app switcher palette per display.
It worked, and quickly! But it was pretty shoddy. Many optimizations and niceties from SwitchGlass had been lost. So I dove in to fix them…and maybe add one or two more features, I guess…
Now, after months of work, I’ve created a bit of a monster. But in the process, I’ve fulfilled a long-held dream of mine—a dream I had set aside years ago because I thought it was impossible. I’ve replaced the Dock.
Only Apple…
If you’ve read any of my Mac OS X reviews, you know that I’ve always been dissatisfied with the Dock. Over the past couple of decades, I’ve gotten used to it, but I still bump up against its limitations and undesirable behaviors every day. (Undesirable to me, anyway.)
To pick just one example, I’ve always wanted clicking on a folder in the Dock to open that folder in the Finder. The Dock did work this way for several years, but in 2009’s Mac OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard (…I think?), Apple switched to requiring a Command-Option-click to open a folder in the Finder. Since then, I’ve been Command-Option-clicking folders in the Dock many, many times per day. It’s a small thing, but it adds up: seventeen years of Command-Option clicking!
But what could I do? I was forced to continue to use the Dock because there are so many things that “only the Dock can do” in macOS. I was reminded of this harsh reality when I created SwitchGlass. Why doesn’t SwitchGlass show notification badges? Why does the Calendar icon show today’s date in the Dock but not in SwitchGlass? Why don’t app icons in SwitchGlass bounce when the app needs attention? Why can’t I quit an app from SwitchGlass?
Though I did find a workaround for that last one, the answer to most of these questions is that third-party apps simply can’t do all the things the Dock can do. The Dock is part of the operating system, and it enjoys special privileges and deep integration that no third-party app can match.
This remains true today, especially for sandboxed apps sold through the Mac App Store like SwitchGlass (and all my other Mac apps). But what about apps that aren’t in the Mac App Store? What about unsandboxed apps? How close can they come to doing all the things the Dock does, especially if they use private APIs that are forbidden in the Mac App Store?
I aimed to find out. I hatched a plan, which I announced on episode 706 of Accidental Tech Podcast on August 26, 2026. I would create two apps: one called Jetty that would be sold through the Mac App Store, and a more powerful, unsandboxed app called Jetty Pro that would be distributed directly to customers, outside the Mac App Store.
But as I worked on the two apps, it became clear that “plain Jetty” was not that great. It had all the same limitations as SwitchGlass when it came to duplicating the features of the Dock. After less than two weeks of work, I abandoned plain Jetty and concentrated entirely on Jetty Pro.
After three and a half months of work, there are still things that only the Dock can do, but the list is not very long. I don’t expect most users to fully replace the Dock with Jetty Pro, but I’m happily doing so. If only my 2001 self could see me now!
Jetty Pro
Now, finally, I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to. Here are some of the highlights:
- Jetty Pro palettes are extensively customizable. Nearly every palette layout metric can be adjusted. Jetty Pro can simulate the Dock backgrounds from macOS 15, 26, and 27, and it provides several of its own background appearances as well. The image at the top of this post shows just some of the possibilities.
- Jetty Pro lets you customize the icon of any item in a palette—even the Finder. And if you’ve ever wanted to break an app out of Squircle Jail, now you can do it.
- Unlike the macOS Dock, Jetty Pro will show folder label colors (without also setting a folder symbol). You can even apply color labels to folders independent of their labels in the Finder.
- Don’t want to see “Running in Background” apps in macOS 27? Jetty Pro can hide them.
- Want to hide notification badges for specific apps, but only in specific palettes? Jetty Pro can do that. And unlike the Dock, Jetty Pro can even hide notification badges on the System Settings app.
- Jetty Pro can exclude or include running apps of your choice on a per-palette basis.
- Jetty Pro lets you choose what happens when you click (or modifier-click) an app or folder in a palette.
- A Jetty Pro palette can be configured to appear on a single display, selected displays, or on every display, while also choosing which attributes, like size and position, are allowed to vary per display.
- Use Jetty Pro to augment the macOS Dock with additional palettes, or use it to replace the Dock entirely. It’s up to you.
Jetty Pro is available for a special introductory price of $9.99 per year (plus applicable taxes) until the end of 2026, with a 14-day free trial.
To learn more, including why a subscription is the only way to pay for Jetty Pro, please read the extensive documentation.
As you might have already guessed, Jetty Pro uses every private API it can get its hands on, and it requires a ton of special permissions, all of which are explained in the documentation. For sensible security reasons, macOS makes it (increasingly) cumbersome for users to grant these permissions. But Jetty Pro needs them to do what it does. Check Settings > General in Jetty Pro and make sure it says “All permissions have been granted” at the bottom. If not, click the “Details…” button for further instructions.

Hypercritical
Jetty Pro
My first two Mac apps, Front and Center and SwitchGlass, were both created back in 2020 to restore features from DragThing, the venerable Mac app that was retired in 2019. The one tiny feature that Front and Center provided was literally a single checkbox within DragThing’s preferences. SwitchGlass went a bit farther, recreating one specific kind of floating palette from DragThing (and classic Mac OS).
After 24 years of development, DragThing had a ton of features. People often joked that I was destined to slowly reimplement all of DragThing’s functionality in a series of small apps. Put another way, they were saying I was doomed to make strange little Mac apps with extremely limited appeal (and sales).
Perhaps to prove them wrong, the next app I created was Hyperspace, which provided a way to reclaim disk space without removing any files. Hyperspace was still a nerdy app, but at least it had somewhat broader appeal than my earlier efforts. Who doesn’t want to save disk space? But more importantly, it was totally unrelated to DragThing. I had broken the curse!
Alas, there was one more (small) thing from DragThing that I missed. I used to have a DragThing palette in the corner of my screen containing some commonly used folders. In earlier versions of macOS, it was possible to pin the Dock to a screen corner, but that wasn’t really what I wanted either. I just wanted a small, separate palette of folders in the corner.

Today, AI coding agents are helping to produce a bounty of new, niche Mac apps, many made by people who have little or no coding experience. It’s in this context that I revisited my “little palette of folders” idea. Surely I could vibe-code a simple app just for me in a day or two, right?
That was three and a half months ago.
How It’s Going
So what happened? The well-known programmer’s credo comes to mind: “We do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy.” Indeed.

I asked a coding agent to modernize the code and generalize it to support an arbitrary number of palettes instead of just one app switcher palette per display.
It worked, and quickly! But it was pretty shoddy. Many optimizations and niceties from SwitchGlass had been lost. So I dove in to fix them…and maybe add one or two more features, I guess…
Now, after months of work, I’ve created a bit of a monster. But in the process, I’ve fulfilled a long-held dream of mine—a dream I had set aside years ago because I thought it was impossible. I’ve replaced the Dock.
Only Apple…
If you’ve read any of my Mac OS X reviews, you know that I’ve always been dissatisfied with the Dock. Over the past couple of decades, I’ve gotten used to it, but I still bump up against its limitations and undesirable behaviors every day. (Undesirable to me, anyway.)
To pick just one example, I’ve always wanted clicking on a folder in the Dock to open that folder in the Finder. The Dock did work this way for several years, but in 2009’s Mac OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard (…I think?), Apple switched to requiring a Command-Option-click to open a folder in the Finder. Since then, I’ve been Command-Option-clicking folders in the Dock many, many times per day. It’s a small thing, but it adds up: seventeen years of Command-Option clicking!
But what could I do? I was forced to continue to use the Dock because there are so many things that “only the Dock can do” in macOS. I was reminded of this harsh reality when I created SwitchGlass. Why doesn’t SwitchGlass show notification badges? Why does the Calendar icon show today’s date in the Dock but not in SwitchGlass? Why don’t app icons in SwitchGlass bounce when the app needs attention? Why can’t I quit an app from SwitchGlass?
Though I did find a workaround for that last one, the answer to most of these questions is that third-party apps simply can’t do all the things the Dock can do. The Dock is part of the operating system, and it enjoys special privileges and deep integration that no third-party app can match.
This remains true today, especially for sandboxed apps sold through the Mac App Store like SwitchGlass (and all my other Mac apps). But what about apps that aren’t in the Mac App Store? I aimed to find out. I hatched a plan, which I announced on episode 706 of Accidental Tech Podcast on August 26, 2026. The image at the top of this post shows just some of the possibilities.

articles.title: Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on One Port
articles.body:
Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on One Port
November 23, 2026
I started building restorekit.org dongles a few months ago at the Recurse Center. They are small inline USB-C boards that sit between a host computer and a target mac. They set the target mac into DFUDevice Firmware Update: Apple's lowest-level recovery mode built into the boot ROM, so even a bricked Mac can be reflashed. mode over USB-PDUSB Power Delivery: the communication protocol over the CC wire used to negotiate power, roles, and vendor-defined commands. without having to touch the target at all, and work with an open-source toolkit for restoring macs without the need for another mac.
The original board, the Dongle-Lite, is USB 2 only. A single USB 2 hub (CH334F) connects both the dongle’s MCU and the target mac through a single cable, while a PD PHYPhysical-layer transceiver chip that encodes and decodes USB Power Delivery packets on the CC wire. (FUSB302B) sends Apple’s DFU commands on the CC line.
I recently learned from timo at Twocanoes that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery. I obviously immediately wanted to support this on the hub for faster recovery, but the problem was cost. At first I designed a “proper” USB 3 board using a GL3510 USB 3 hub and a pair of TI SuperSpeed muxes (HD3SS3220 and HD3SS3212). It basically doubled the parts count, and BOMBill of Materials: the full list of components and quantities required to assemble one board. cost, required me to increase the size of PCB to ~100 mm, and topped out at 5 Gbps transfers between host and target (USB 3.1 Gen 1).
I really didn’t want to make a board that cost more than twice the Dongle-Lite just to get USB 3 speeds.
So with the 2nd version Dongle-Pro, I tried a kinda crazy USB-C experiment: drop the USB 3 hub completely, keep a cheap USB 2 hub on D+/D-, and route the USB 3 SuperSpeedUSB 3.x's dedicated high-speed TX/RX differential pairs, physically separate from USB 2's D+/D- wires. lanes as a straight passthrough from host to target on the same USB-C port.  The idea being that in theory the USB 3 and 2 controllers on a USB-C are completely independent, and should work simultaneously.
Since high-speed USB 3 is super prone to interference I didn’t really have a choice other than to purchase a view boards and test it out.
Well… I just got the boards in from JLC and… THEY WORK! They establish a full 10 Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection while connecting the dongle’s USB 2 hub and MCU over the exact same port. After some aggressive cost optimization, the 10 Gbps board also ended up cheaper and smaller than the USB 2 Dongle-Lite.
How USB 3 and USB 2 Share a Port
Like I mentioned earlier, USB-C is not a single data bus. Inside a standard USB-C port, USB 2 and USB 3 sit on completely different sets of pins:
Every USB-C port has two mirrored 12-pin rows: A1 through A12 on top, and B12 through B1 on the bottom, so a cable works rotated either way.
- USB 2 (D+ / D-): a single 480 Mbps pair in the center (pins A6/A7 and B6/B7 are shorted together).
- USB 3 (TX/RX): 2 separate high-speed lanes on the outer edge. Only 1 set is active depending on orientation.
- Control & sideband (CC, SBU): CC1/CC2 detect cable orientation and negotiate USB-PD; SBU1/SBU2 (A8/B8) are used by Apple’s 1.2 V debug UART.
This continues to the computer’s xHCIExtensible Host Controller Interface: the USB controller inside your computer that manages both USB 2 and USB 3.x root ports. controller: a single physical USB-C port is actually wired to two independent root ports: a USB 2 port and a USB 3 port.
A standard USB 3 hub chip like the GL3510 is actually just two hubs in 1 package (a USB 2 hub and a USB 3 hub). On my first iteration of the Dongle-Pro, everything ran through that chip even though the dongle’s own MCU only speaks USB 2 Full Speed (12 Mbps) and has no need for the USB 3 speed.
On the Dongle-Pro v2, the two buses are split apart:
- USB 2 (D+/D-) runs into a CH334P USB 2 hub. One downstream port goes to the target’s D+/D- (so DFU mode and any USB 2 device behave just like the Lite), and another goes to the dongle’s MCU (CH32X035G8U6).
- USB 3 (TX/RX) skips the hub completely. Each port’s two lane sets go into a CH9441P 2:1 muxMultiplexer: a high-speed analog switch that routes whichever side of a reversible USB-C plug is active onto one pair of board traces.. Each mux reads its own port’s CC1/CC2 lines to handle cable flip and connects the active lane set to its common side. The two muxes sit in the center of the board, wired straight together through a short corridor with no hub and no redriverAn active signal-conditioning chip that boosts and equalizes high-speed USB 3 traces to overcome cable and PCB insertion loss..
What Could Go Wrong
This sounded like it would work to me on paper, but there were a few things I thought could go wrong:
- Two passive muxes in series with no redriver. Every connector, ESD array, via, and switch adds insertion loss and reflections. I was hoping two CH9441P chips back-to-back would pass 5 Gbps. But hitting 10 Gbps is even better.
- Sharing the target CC lines. On the target port, the HUSB311 PD PHY actively drives the CC lines to send Apple’s SOP” DebugA USB-PD packet framing addressed to a debug accessory rather than a normal device, required for Apple's DFU commands. VDMsVendor-Defined Messages: custom USB-PD packets. Apple uses them to trigger DFU, reboot, and serial debug without touching the keyboard.. The target’s CH9441P is also reading the lines to steer its lanes.
- Host OS behavior. Even though it made sense in theory, I really wasn’t sure if a machine would happily enumerate a USB 2 hub on a port’s D+/D- lines while a separate USB 3.2 Gen 2 device negotiated directly with the same port’s SuperSpeed lanes.
On the Bench
When the boards arrived, I immediately plugged one into my mac, plugged an iPhone into the target port, and inspected the bus with system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType and ioreg -p IOUSB.
Here is what macOS sees on a single physical USB-C port (AppleT8132USBXHCI@01000000):
The raw system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType output shows both sides active at once:
0x01100000 is the USB 2 half of the physical port, and 0x01200000 is the SuperSpeed half of the same port. The iPhone enumerated straight through both passive CH9441P muxes at 10 Gb/s (USB 3.2 Gen 2), while the CH334P hub and Dongle-Pro-v2 MCU enumerate at 480 Mb/s and 12 Mb/s on D+/D-.
Companion Ports
Splitting the bus required one interesting change in the host SDK (restorekit).
On the Dongle-Lite, whatever device you plugged into the dongle always showed up as a child of the dongle’s hub. That made it easy to tell which target Mac belonged to which dongle when you plugged in several at once.
On the Dongle-Pro v2, that breaks whenever the target connects at USB 3. Just like iPhone@01200000 above, a SuperSpeed target bypasses the CH334P hub completely and shows up as a sibling directly on the host’s root hub.
Turns out the OS already tracks which USB 2 and USB 3 root ports share the same physical port and it exposes it directly:
- On macOS, the USB 2 port’s IORegistrymacOS's live kernel tree of hardware devices, ports, and drivers, which you can inspect with ioreg. entry has a UsbProtocolCompanion (3.x) property containing the path to its SuperSpeed twin.
- On Linux, the USB 2 port’s sysfsLinux's virtual filesystem at /sys that exposes kernel devices, USB hubs, and physical port peer links. directory has a port/peer symlink pointing straight to the SuperSpeed port.
So restorekit can still know with 100% certainty which 10 Gbps device is plugged into which dongle.
Cutting the Cost
I originally planned to have a Dongle-Lite and significantly more expensive USB 3 Pro, but that means having to maintain two hardware lines, so if I could cut the cost of the USB 3 version to be comparably priced to the original Dongle-Lite it felt like a no brainer.
After I removed the GL3510 USB 3 hub from the original design, I went through the rest of the board to see what else I could cut:
- SuperSpeed path: HD3SS3220 ($1.66) + HD3SS3212 ($1.55) + GL3510 ($1.23) came to $4.44 on Pro v1 for 5 Gbps. Two CH9441P muxes cost $0.47 total ($0.24 each) on Pro v2 for 10 Gbps. Pro v1’s SuperSpeed chips alone cost more than the entire Pro v2 BOM.
- MCU: Swapped the RP2354A + 3.3 uH inductor + crystal ($1.62) with a CH32X035G8U6 ($0.42), running off its internal 48 MHz HSIHigh-Speed Internal oscillator: an on-chip clock source that lets an MCU run without an external quartz crystal. with no crystal, no external inductor, and a built-in ROM USB bootloader.
- PD PHY: Swapped the FUSB302BMPX ($0.68) with a HUSB311BLA ($0.51).
- USB 2 hub: Swapped the CH334F ($0.53) with a CH334P ($0.31), which integrates the crystal load capacitors and drops two more passives.
- 1.2 V SBU UART level shifters: two 74AVC1T45 translators plus a dedicated TLV70212 1.2 V LDO ($0.79) became two HL2302 MOSFETs and a few resistors ($0.05) wired as common-gate level shifters.
- Unified ESD and passive discipline: swapped mixed USBLC6 + TPD4E05U06 parts for six H5VU25U flow-through arrays (JLCPCB Preferred Extended = $0 feeder fee), and limited the whole board to just three resistor values and three capacitor values.
Running the three BOMs against JLCPCB pricing:
(Parts and Extended feeder fees from JLCPCB’s catalog, excluding PCB fab and placement fees. V2 wins on fab cost too since it is 40% smaller than the Lite and 60% smaller than Pro v1, packing three boards into one 81 x 48 mm panel.)
These swaps resulted in a 72% BOM reduction from original Dongle-Pro while doubling the SuperSpeed link rate from 5 Gbps to 10 Gbps, and a 42% BOM reduction compared to the Dongle-Lite.
Conclusion
If you are building an inline USB-C tool where your MCU only needs a slow control channel and the host just needs fast passthrough to the downstream device, you might not need a USB 3 hub. USB-C gives you two independent buses in the same port.
Next up: A flash drive with USB 3.2 Gen 2 + 2 speeds?

- On Linux, the USB 2 port’s sysfsLinux's virtual filesystem at /sys that exposes kernel devices, USB hubs, and physical port peer links. directory has a port/peer symlink pointing straight to the SuperSpeed port.
So restorekit can still know with 100% certainty which 10 Gbps device is plugged into which dongle.
Cutting the Cost
I originally planned to have a Dongle-Lite and significantly more expensive USB 3 Pro, but that means having to maintain two hardware lines, so if I could cut the cost of the USB 3 version to be comparably priced to the original Dongle-Lite it felt like a no brainer.
After I removed the GL3510 USB 3 hub from the original design, I went through the rest of the board to see what else I could cut:
- SuperSpeed path: HD3SS3220 ($1.66) + HD3SS3212 ($1.55) + GL3510 ($1.23) came to $4.44 on Pro v1 for 5 Gbps. Two CH9441P muxes cost $0.47 total ($0.24 each) on Pro v2 for 10 Gbps. Pro v1’s SuperSpeed chips alone cost more than the entire Pro v2 BOM.
- MCU: Swapped the RP2354A + 3.3 uH inductor + crystal ($1.62) with a CH32X035G8U6 ($0.42), running off its internal 48 MHz HSIHigh-Speed Internal oscillator: an on-chip clock source that lets an MCU run without an external quartz crystal. with no crystal, no external inductor, and a built-in ROM USB bootloader.
- PD PHY: Swapped the FUSB302BMPX ($0.68) with a HUSB311BLA ($0.51).
- USB 2 hub: Swapped the CH334F ($0.53) with a CH334P ($0.31), which integrates the crystal load capacitors and drops two more passives.
- 1.2 V SBU UART level shifters: two 74AVC1T45 translators plus a dedicated TLV70212 1.2 V LDO ($0.79) became two HL2302 MOSFETs and a few resistors ($0.05) wired as common-gate level shifters.
- Unified ESD and passive discipline: swapped mixed USBLC6 + TPD4E05U06 parts for six H5VU25U flow-through arrays (JLCPCB Preferred Extended = $0 feeder fee), and limited the whole board to just three resistor values and three capacitor values.
Running the three BOMs against JLCPCB pricing:
(Parts and Extended feeder fees from JLCPCB’s catalog, excluding PCB fab and placement fees. V2 wins on fab cost too since it is 40% smaller than the Lite and 60% smaller than Pro v1, packing three boards into one 81 x 48 mm panel.)
These swaps resulted in a 72% BOM reduction from original Dongle-Pro while doubling the SuperSpeed link rate from 5 Gbps to 10 Gbps, and a 42% BOM reduction compared to the Dongle-Lite.
Conclusion
If you are building an inline USB-C tool where your MCU only needs a slow control channel and the host just needs fast passthrough to the downstream device, you might not need a USB 3 hub. USB-C gives you two independent buses in the same port.
Next up: A flash drive with USB 3.2 Gen 2 + 2 speeds?

articles.title: AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean in Less Than 10 Years
articles.body:
AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean In Less Than 10 Years, Up To 133x In AI
This month brought the availability of the new EPYC 9006 "Venice" SP7 Zen 6 server processors. We have seen excellent generational gains with the likes of the EPYC 9686F and EPYC 9996 over Zen 5 Turin CPUs as well as sharply outperforming the competition from Intel and NVIDIA. With the first-generation EPYC "Naples" processors having launched nearly ten years ago, I was curious to quantify AMD's server performance gains over the past decade. So up today is a look at how the EPYC 9996 and EPYC 9686F Zen 6 processors compare to the original EPYC Zen 1 flagship with the EPYC 7601 across real-world workloads for performance as well as power efficiency for some pretty epic gains.
The AMD EPYC 7601 launched back in June 2017 as the flagship of the EPYC Naples "Zen 1" processors. The EPYC 7601 was notable for its time with 32 x Zen 1 cores / 64 threads, 2.2GHz base frequency, 3.2GHz max boost frequency, and 64 MB of L3 cache. On the memory side was eight channel DDR4-2666 memory and for connectivity were up to 128 PCIe 3.0 lanes. The TDP of each EPYC 7601 processor is 180 Watts.
Now just shy of a decade later, the EPYC 9006 SP7 processors have begun shipping. With the AMD EPYC 9996 256-core flagship are 256 Zen 6C cores / 512 threads per socket, 2.55GHz base clock, 4.1GHz max boost frequency, and an incredible 1024MB of L3 cache. EPYC 9006 SP7 processors support DDR5 RDIMMs or up to MRDIMM-12800 memory at 16 channels. There is also 96 lanes of PCI Express 6.0. The EPYC 9996 has a 600W default power rating.
Or for the frequency-optimized flagship is the EPYC 9686F with 96 Zen 5 cores / 192 threads with a 4.05GHz base frequency and up to 5.3GHz maximum boost clock. The EPYC 9686F has a 384MB L3 cache size while also having a 600 Watt default power rating.
Over the past ten years of AMD EPYC there has been incredible architectural advancements too not reflected in the key specs alone such as AVX-512 with Zen 4 and further refined in Zen 5, security improvements to reduce the need for software-based security mitigations, and countless other architectural improvements each step of the way from Zen 1 to Zen 6.
For comparing EPYC Zen 1 to Zen 6, I dusted off the Dell PowerEdge R7425 server originally provided by AMD for EPYC Naples testing at Phoronix. Nearly ten years later, the Dell PowerEdge server with the dual AMD EPYC 7601 processors still fires up and runs reliably. The AMD EPYC 7601 2P was running with 16 x 32GB DDR4-2666 memory, Samsung SSD 860 SSD storage, and other stock components of this Naples review unit.
With the AMD EPYC 9686F 2P and EPYC 9996 2P testing was the Nigeria reference server with 32 x 64GB MRDIMM-12800 memory, and Micron MTFDMBQ7T6THM-1BP1JABDC PCIe Gen6 SSD.
The AMD EPYC Naples and EPYC Venice servers were tested on the same software stack with using Ubuntu 26.10 for a very up-to-date open-source software experience. Ubuntu 26.10 ships with the Linux 7.3 kernel and GCC 15.3 compiler by default.
In addition to the raw performance testing for EPYC Zen 1 vs. EPYC Zen 6, the CPU power consumption and performance-per-Watt were also compared using the exposed CPU PowerCap/RAPL sensors of 2P processor configuration.

articles.title: Mayo Clinic To Give Appointment Workers 5 Paid Minutes a Day To Boot Up Computers
articles.body:
Mayo Clinic To Give Appointment Workers 5 Paid Minutes a Day To Boot Up Computers (cbsnews.com) 46
			
		 	
				Mayo Clinic has agreed to pay more than $906,000 in back wages to employees who schedule patient appointments. An investigation by Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison found that employees were performing unpaid work before and after their shifts, including time spent booting up computers and finishing patient calls. Under the settlement (PDF), Mayo will stop rounding employees' work hours and give them five paid minutes at the start of each shift to boot up their computers. CBS News reports:  In a statement, Mayo Clinic said it reached the agreement to resolve concerns about "certain timekeeping practices" involving a group of the specialists. The clinic said it doesn't agree with the attorney general's position but decided that a resolution in which money went to its staff, rather than to defense fees, was preferable. Mayo said it is committed to paying employees accurately and appropriately and reviews its compensation policies regularly. Neither the announcement nor the statement says how many workers are covered or how far back the unpaid time goes.
"Under Minnesota law, workers need to be compensated for all the time they work," Ellison said. State law requires employers to pay employees for all time spent on duties connected to their jobs, including time on the employer's premises. Ellison said Mayo cooperated with the investigation and changed its policies on its own to pay workers for the time. He said other employers should take note: "they're on the clock and need to be paid" if they are on site or doing work duties. Ellison encouraged any worker who believes they're being underpaid to contact his office, saying it may be able to help co-workers as well.

articles.title: Heart attack and stroke risk detectable decades in advance
articles.body:
Scientists identified early patterns in a range of risk factors for cardiovascular disease – conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels – including high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney function.
They also revealed differences in the blood of those who went on to have a cardiovascular event, such as a heart attack or stroke, more than a decade beforehand.
The findings highlight a large window of opportunity to intervene to reduce cardiovascular risk and prevent the development of serious disease, experts say.
Disease risk
Cardiovascular disease kills one in four people in the UK. Traditional risk factors, such as high blood pressure and cholesterol, have been widely linked to the risk of disease. However, previous studies have typically focused on a single risk factor and don’t monitor long-term changes.
Other influences, such as kidney function and biomarkers in the blood, could also play an important role in establishing disease risk.
A research team, led by the University of Edinburgh, examined data from more than 100,000 people between 1985 and 2019 to explore the patterns of multiple risk factors in relation to cardiovascular events over time.
The research, funded by the British Heart Foundation, included data from four population studies across the United States, Norway and the United Kingdom.
Blood pressure
Systolic blood pressure – the pressure in arteries when the heart beats or contracts – was consistently higher in those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who were event-free, starting at 4 mmHg higher three decades before and increasing to 7 mmHg closer to the event.
Patterns were different between sexes throughout life. Younger women had lower blood pressure than younger men, but this switched around the age of 65, when female readings tended to be higher than males.
Other patterns
Researchers also identified important differences by age. Those who experienced a cardiovascular event at a younger age were more likely to have diabetes and a higher body mass index in the decades before the event.
Patterns in blood biomarkers also revealed early differences between those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who didn’t. Changes in the levels of a protein called NT-proBNP – used to monitor heart failure – could be seen up to 10 years beforehand.
Trajectories of other non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors, including physical activity and kidney function, also differed between individuals with and without cardiovascular events.
Predict risk
Tracking the course of risk factors over time may help to better predict serious cardiovascular events, experts say. Further research should also explore whether incorporating non-traditional risk factors could help to improve the estimation of cardiovascular disease risk, they add.
The study did not look at risk factors by ethnicity, and the team cautions that further research exploring potential differences in risk factor and biomarker trajectories across ethnic groups is needed.
