articles.title: Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg
articles.body:
Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.
Can I just add one more?
I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs, to make profile-guided optimization reproducible, and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.
Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.
What is the critical path?
The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.
If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲
I added a new rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached.11All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work. Kneel before Zod! 
  Aside: New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?
Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?
The usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep. 💤💤💤
§Where the time goes
Every rewind time starts with two numbers:
$ rewind time 7a29e716
libuv-1.51.0
    78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU    47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs            67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing
The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.
No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.
The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep.
A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis: look at where threads block, not only where they compute.
On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤
Here is the whole output for libuv:
$ rewind time 7a29e716
libuv-1.51.0
    78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU
    47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs
            67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing
The critical path by phase
    3.54 s  configurePhase  ██
    1.67 s  buildPhase      █
    42.0 s  checkPhase      █████████████████████
     99 ms  5 other phases
The critical path by process
   on path      pid  process, with what it started
    47.4 s       34  init › bash -e source-stdenv.sh default-builder.sh
    41.9 s     4076  ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash VERBOSE=y check
    36.4 s     4910  │  ├─ make › bash › lt-run-tests
    3.38 s     5412  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime  asleep in clock_nanosleep 3.38 s
    2.00 s     5013  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept  asleep in epoll_pwait 2.00 s
    1.62 s     5126  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watch_dir  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.62 s
    1.60 s     5103  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_event_close_in…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.60 s
    1.60 s     5508  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s, computing 600 ms
    1.24 s     6095  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests tcp_write_ready tcp_write_ready
    1.14 s     5510  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_t…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s
    1.10 s     5132  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_file_current_dir fs_event_wat…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.10 s
    22.6 s           │  │  └─ 279 more
    5.59 s     4077  │  └─ make test/run-tests
    2.22 s     4183  │     ├─ gcc -fPIC -fstack-clash-protection -O2 -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE …
    2.10 s     4189  │     │  └─ cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c
    3.35 s           │     └─ 20 more
    1.99 s       68  ├─ sh ./autogen.sh
    1.99 s           │  └─ 9 more
    1.67 s     2642  ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash
    1.67 s           │  └─ 5 more
    1.53 s      403  └─ bash ./configure --disable-static --disable-dependency-tracking…
    1.47 s              └─ 581 more
What would shorten it
    sooner      pid  if this took no time
    36.1 s           every lt-run-tests, 600 processes
    6.66 s           every cc1, 283 processes
    3.38 s     5412  75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep: lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime
    2.00 s     5013  2 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept
    1.76 s     4189  cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c
    1.62 s     5126  30 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watc…
    1.60 s     5103  16 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_ev…
    1.60 s     5508  lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time
    1.22 s           every perl, 9 processes
    1.14 s     5510  lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_thread
Look closer
  rewind time 7a29e716 --in PID             one process: its threads, sleeps and waits
  rewind time 7a29e716 --folded             the path for flamegraph.pl or speedscope.app
  rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F         every process on a timeline, for ui.perfetto.dev
The second table is the path as a tree of processes based on Gregg’s colony graph idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path.22A ps snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief. 
In this build, make check needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is lt-run-tests, libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds.
All of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers.
Drag can be less than time on the path.
The last table answers a different question: how much sooner would the run finish if this part took no time? The critical path method calls this drag.
For the truly magical part, we can jump to any part of the path and see what was happening, invoke gdb and fork the run at that moment. A profiler hands you a stack, sampled at some moment you can never go back to. Every frame in rewind time is a moment in a recording, and Rewind can replay the run to it.
--in looks inside one process,33It can take a pid, a program or a word of the command line.  so let’s dive into the hrtime test that spent 3.38 seconds asleep in clock_nanosleep:
$ rewind time 7a29e716 --in hrtime
lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime (pid 5412)
    3.38 s  on the critical path with what it started, 7% of the 47.4 s path
            100% asleep (clock_nanosleep 3.38 s), <1% computing
What would shorten it
    sooner      pid  if this took no time
    3.38 s           75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep
Look closer
  rewind where 7a29e716 115894 --pid 5412   the source line the first row's time starts at  rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F         every process on a timeline
Since this test spent 100% of its time asleep, the step provided on the last line is where it began. rewind where replays the run to that step and asks gdb where the thread was:
$ rewind where 7a29e716 115894 --pid 5412
process 5412 (lt-run-tests), thread 5412, at step 115894
#2 uv_sleep (src/unix/core.c:1869)
    1867
    1868    do
>   1869      rc = nanosleep(&timeout, &timeout);    1870    while (rc == -1 && errno == EINTR);
    1871
arguments:
  msec = 45
locals:
  timeout = {tv_sec = 0, tv_nsec = 45000000}
  rc = <optimized out>
  __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ = <error: Cannot access memory at address 0x7fb172519ae8>
called from #3 run_test_hrtime (test/test-hrtime.c:39)
called from #4 __libc_start_call_main (../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58)
🎯 We can see that the test is calling uv_sleep(45) from line 39 of test/test-hrtime.c, and that it is sleeping for 45 milliseconds.
It does that 75 times for a total of 3.38 seconds.44Turns out that the test sleeps on purpose: it is checking how far uv_hrtime moves across a sleep. There is nothing to optimize in this case. 
As the cherry on top: the run is deterministic, so step 115,894 is the same instruction every time you replay it. You can open rewind gdb at that step and investigate to your heart’s content.
The Rewind app’s Time tab shows the same answers. The path becomes a flame graph, colored the way Gregg colors his off-CPU flame graphs: computing is warm, asleep is blue, and a process shades from one to the other by how much of its time it slept.
Clicking a frame picks it and moves the playhead there, so the build log, the process tree and the files all show that moment; clicking a process again zooms into it. When you pick a blue frame, the app replays the run to that part’s longest sleep and shows the stack where it slept:
Under the stack, Show source opens the source panel at that moment on that thread, and Open gdb here opens gdb in a fork of the run at the sleep:
If you’d rather use tools you already know, rewind time can emit the data in their formats: folded stacks for flamegraph.pl and speedscope, or a Perfetto trace for ui.perfetto.dev.

articles.title: Worshipping at the Altar of Brendan Gregg
articles.body:
Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.
Can I just add one more?
I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs, to make profile-guided optimization reproducible, and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.
Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.
What is the critical path?
The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.
If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲
I added a new rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached.11All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work. Kneel before Zod! 
  Aside: New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?
Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?
The usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep. 💤💤💤
§Where the time goes
Every rewind time starts with two numbers:
$ rewind time 7a29e716
libuv-1.51.0
    78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU    47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs            67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing
The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.
No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.
The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep.
A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis: look at where threads block, not only where they compute.
On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤
Here is the whole output for libuv:
$ rewind time 7a29e716
libuv-1.51.0
    78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU
    47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs
            67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing
The critical path by phase
    3.54 s  configurePhase  ██
    1.67 s  buildPhase      █
    42.0 s  checkPhase      █████████████████████
     99 ms  5 other phases
The critical path by process
   on path      pid  process, with what it started
    47.4 s       34  init › bash -e source-stdenv.sh default-builder.sh
    41.9 s     4076  ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash VERBOSE=y check
    36.4 s     4910  │  ├─ make › bash › lt-run-tests
    3.38 s     5412  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime  asleep in clock_nanosleep 3.38 s
    2.00 s     5013  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept  asleep in epoll_pwait 2.00 s
    1.62 s     5126  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watch_dir  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.62 s
    1.60 s     5103  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_event_close_in…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.60 s
    1.60 s     5508  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s, computing 600 ms
    1.24 s     6095  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests tcp_write_ready tcp_write_ready
    1.14 s     5510  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_t…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s
    1.10 s     5132  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_file_current_dir fs_event_wat…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.10 s
    22.6 s           │  │  └─ 279 more
    5.59 s     4077  │  └─ make test/run-tests
    2.22 s     4183  │     ├─ gcc -fPIC -fstack-clash-protection -O2 -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE …
    2.10 s     4189  │     │  └─ cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c
    3.35 s           │     └─ 20 more
    1.99 s       68  ├─ sh ./autogen.sh
    1.99 s           │  └─ 9 more
    1.67 s     2642  ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash
    1.67 s           │  └─ 5 more
    1.53 s      403  └─ bash ./configure --disable-static --disable-dependency-tracking…
    1.47 s              └─ 581 more
What would shorten it
    sooner      pid  if this took no time
    36.1 s           every lt-run-tests, 600 processes
    6.66 s           every cc1, 283 processes
    3.38 s     5412  75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep: lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime
    2.00 s     5013  2 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept
    1.76 s     4189  cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c
    1.62 s     5126  30 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watc…
    1.60 s     5103  16 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_ev…
    1.60 s     5508  lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time
    1.22 s           every perl, 9 processes
    1.14 s     5510  lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_thread
Look closer
  rewind time 7a29e716 --in PID             one process: its threads, sleeps and waits
  rewind time 7a29e716 --folded             the path for flamegraph.pl or speedscope.app
  rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F         every process on a timeline, for ui.perfetto.dev
The second table is the path as a tree of processes based on Gregg’s colony graph idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path.22A ps snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief. 
In this build, make check needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is lt-run-tests, libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds.
All of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers.
Drag can be less than time on the path.
The last table answers a different question: how much sooner would the run finish if this part took no time? The critical path method calls this drag.

lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime (pid 5412)
    3.38 s  on the critical path with what it started, 7% of the 47.4 s path
            100% asleep (clock_nanosleep 3.38 s), <1% computing
What would shorten it
    sooner      pid  if this took no time
    3.38 s           75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep

$ rewind where 7a29e716 115894 --pid 5412
process 5412 (lt-run-tests), thread 5412, at step 115894
#2 uv_sleep (src/unix/core.c:1869)
    1867
    1868    do
>   1869      rc = nanosleep(&timeout, &timeout);    1870    while (rc == -1 && errno == EINTR);
    1871
arguments:
  msec = 45
locals:
  timeout = {tv_sec = 0, tv_nsec = 45000000}
  rc = <optimized out>
  __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ = <error: Cannot access memory at address 0x7fb172519ae8>
called from #3 run_test_hrtime (test/test-hrtime.c:39)
called from #4 __libc_start_call_main (../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58)

It does that 75 times for a total of 3.38 seconds.44Turns out that the test sleeps on purpose: it is checking how far uv_hrtime moves across a sleep. There is nothing to optimize in this case.

articles.title: New York Bans Subscription and Post-Purchase Fees on Cars
articles.body:
S.9348A/A.10411A Prohibits Car Companies from Charging for Built-In Features
Amid Rising Consumer Fees, New Law Increases Price Transparency and Puts Money Back in New Yorkers’ Pockets
Governor Kathy Hochul today signed a bill restricting motor vehicle manufacturers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees after they purchase a vehicle. Amid rising consumer prices, the new law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.
“New Yorkers are already struggling with rising prices due to Trump’s affordability crisis, and we’re not going to let harmful business practices increase the cost of living even more,” Governor Hochul said. “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets.”
S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.
New York Attorney General Letitia James said, “No one should have to pay recurring fees just to use features in a car they already bought. My office has secured millions of dollars for New Yorkers throughout the state who were charged illegal junk fees when purchasing a car. Unfair fees are fueling rising costs, and I am proud to work with Governor Hochul and the legislature to bring costs down.”
State Senator James Skoufis said, “People ought to know they’re able to use their already-installed remote start or heated seats during the winter without a monthly subscription. This new law will simply and clearly prohibit car manufacturers from ripping off New Yorkers who already paid for vehicle features when they purchased their car. It’s a common sense law and I’m grateful for the Governor and Assemblymember Magnarelli for their partnership enacting this legislation."
Assemblymember William B. Magnarelli said, "I thank Governor Hochul for recognizing the importance of this legislation, particularly as technology continues to evolve at a rapid pace. This law will help protect New Yorkers from unfair fees and ensure consumers aren’t paying extra for features already built into their vehicles.”
The law will take effect in 90 days on February 27, 2027.
This new law is the latest in Governor Hochul’s ongoing commitment to help address the cost of living by putting money back in the pockets of New Yorkers statewide. Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, she has:
- Secured reforms to lower auto insurance premiums for New Yorkers, battling fraud, limiting damages paid out to bad actors, and ensuring consumers, not insurance companies, are prioritized.
- Signed legislation requiring businesses to notify consumers of upcoming renewals and price changes as well as provide clear instructions on how to cancel subscriptions.
- Cut middle-class taxes to their lowest rates in 70 years.
- Tripled the Child Tax Credit, providing families up to $1,000 per child under the age of four and up to $500 for school-aged children, beginning in 2026.
- Made school meals free for every student, saving families $1,600 per child every year.
- Sent Inflation Refund checks to 8.2 million New Yorkers — up to $200 for individuals and up to $400 for families.
- Increased the maximum weekly unemployment benefit by $300 a week.

articles.title: Show HN: Mason – a lightweight Postgres read-replica, built on columnar storage
articles.body:
A lightweight drop-in replacement for your Postgres read replica.
Same SQL, same answers. But extremely fast for analytical queries.
AWS m7g.xlarge · 4 vCPU · 16 GiB RAM · EBS gp3
Why Mason
- Lightweight: Mason is a single Node.js process you can run anywhere. It keeps all its config and your synced data locally in the folder you run it in.
- Fast: Mason syncs your Postgres data into DuckDB's columnar engine, and rewrites your Postgres queries on the fly into the form DuckDB runs fastest.
- Postgres: Mason is built from the ground up to match Postgres's syntax and behavior (not DuckDB's), so you can point your existing Postgres queries at it with confidence.
- Read replica: You choose which tables and columns to sync from your Postgres database, and how each stays in sync: on demand, by polling or by logical replication.
- Built for AI agents: Add a user per agent, with role-based access control (RBAC) that limits the tables, columns and rows each one can read. Every query is logged with who ran it, the SQL they sent, how long it took and, if it was refused, how to fix it. Mason also has MCP support built in.
Try it out in minutes, run it anywhere
$ npm i -g @mason-data/cli
$ cd my-app
# tell Mason which Postgres database to sync from
$ mason init 'postgres://me:secret@db.example.com:5432/my_db'
# choose the tables to sync
$ mason add orders customers
# start Mason locally and wait for the first sync to finish
$ mason start && mason wait
# get a connection URL for your favorite Postgres client
$ mason user add me
# get results fast
$ psql "postgres://me:<password>@localhost:5433/mason" -c "SELECT country, sum(amount) FROM orders JOIN customers ON customers.id = customer_id GROUP BY country"
# or give it to your coding agent
$ claude mcp add mason --env MASON_URL="postgres://me:<password>@localhost:5433/mason" -- mason mcp
# done? stop Mason and delete its synced copy of your data
$ mason stop && mason destroy
Where Mason is fast, and where it isn't
Fast
Queries that read lots of rows, like counts, sums and group-bys over big tables. The kind dashboards, reports and AI agents run.
Not fast
Queries that fetch a few rows and many columns, like looking up one order by its ID. Mason is fastest when you're querying a lot of rows across a few columns.
From a cold start: each engine restarted and the page cache dropped before every run. 1 or 10 clients send the query at the same moment, and the time is until every client has its answer, the median of 3 runs. Actual results will vary, depending on the size and distribution of your data.
How it was measuredAWS m7g.xlarge · 4 vCPU · 16 GiB RAM · EBS gp3
Features
- Role-based access control: Mason gives each tool, AI agent or customer its own login, and its role decides which tables and columns it can read. You can add, disable or remove a user at any time, and the change takes effect immediately.
- Row-level security: You can limit each user to its own rows, such as the rows for one customer. Mason applies the same limit to related tables by following their foreign keys.
- Generated tables: These are like materialized views, but Mason keeps them up to date for you. They put no extra load on your database.
- MCP: Mason has its own MCP server, so AI agents like Claude Code and ChatGPT can look at your tables and run queries. Each agent can only see what its role allows.
- Monitoring: Mason works with the monitoring tools you already use. Prometheus and Grafana can read its metrics at /metrics, and uptime checks, Kubernetes and ECS can check its health at /healthz. It writes its logs to stdout, so Datadog or CloudWatch can collect them. You can also look back at every query, every sync event and how busy Mason has been, with mason logs and mason usage.
- IP allowlists and TLS: You can limit each user to the IP addresses it connects from. Mason can also encrypt every connection, with your own certificate or with one it makes for you.
- Web UI: Run mason ui to open a web page where you can add tables and users. The page also shows you queries, usage and sync events as they happen.

articles.body:
Between putting up decorations, entertaining guests, and meal prep, the holidays are busy enough without worrying about vacuuming. Thankfully, a proper robot vacuum can do the dirty work while you focus on more enjoyable things. And thanks to Black Friday, you can pick up some of the best we’ve tested for up to 60 percent off.
Dreame and Eufy are offering nearly 60 percent off robovacs for Black Friday
We’ve rounded up the best discounts on our favorite robot vacuums, including models that can mop on your behalf.
We’re seeing some excellent deals on a wide range of robot vacuums, including some of our favorite models from Roborock, Dreame, and Eufy. There are also rare discounts already available on premium models like the Matic and Matic Serene, which impressed us with their almost humanlike navigation, while midrange options such as the Eufy Omni C28 have dropped into budget territory. Whether you want a high-end model that cleans itself or something budget-friendly but still powerful, we’ve rounded up the best deals we’ve found so far.
Roborock Q10 S5 Plus
Despite lacking a multifunction dock, the budget-friendly robot vacuum and mop offers an impressive set of features for the price, including AI-powered obstacle avoidance, sonic mopping, automatic mop lifting, and a self-emptying dock.
Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow
Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design.
Matic robot vacuum
The Matic robot vacuum and mop is ideal for cluttered homes with pets, multiple floors, and a mixture of carpets and hardwood. It offers almost humanlike navigation, tackling high-pile rugs and mopping up wet spills. The quiet bot also requires less maintenance than many rivals thanks to its onboard water tank and dust bag. Read our review.
Eufy Omni C28
The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.
Dreame X60 Ultra
The Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets.
Narwal Flow 2
If you have all hardwood floors, the Narwal Flow 2 is an excellent option. A superb mop with a wide flat roller pad and an excellent vacuum, the Flow 2 also has top-notch navigation and obstacle detection. Its sleek base station is also less of an eyesore than most.
Roborock Saros 20
Roborock’s Saros 20 stands out for its ability to climb tall thresholds, avoid obstacles with impressive accuracy, and clean under low furniture thanks to its slim design. It also combines powerful 36,000Pa suction with great spinning mop pads, which is why we recommend it for homes with multiple floor types and tricky transitions between rooms.
Ecovacs Deebot X12 OmniCyclone
Ecovacs’ robot vacuum and mop can pretreat stains, keep carpets dry with a smart mop cover, and deliver powerful 22,000Pa suction. It also includes an all-in-one dock that automatically empties the dustbin, refills the water tanks, and washes the mop with heated, pressurized water.
Switchbot K11 Plus
The Matter-compatible SwitchBot K11 Plus is ideal for small apartments, bedrooms, and home offices. It can easily navigate around chair and desk legs and into tight spaces that most other bots miss. It also features a commendable 6,000Pa of suction power — which is great for this price point — and works well on both hardwood and carpet.
Dreame X50 Ultra
With high suction power, an improved brush system, and the ability to scale thresholds up to 6cm, the X50 Ultra stands out as a great robot vacuum-mop hybrid. While its 20,000Pa suction isn’t quite as powerful as the X60 Ultra’s and it can’t tackle especially high thresholds as well, it’s still an excellent option. Its edge cleaning also isn’t quite as effective as the X60 Ultra’s, but you’re otherwise getting many of the same features for a lot less.
Dreame L40 Ultra Gen 2
The Dreame L40 Ultra Gen 2 delivers powerful 25,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a self-cleaning dock that empties the dustbin, washes the mop, and refills its water tanks. Unlike the X50 Ultra, however, it lacks the ability to climb high thresholds or stairs.

articles.title: Who in Washington owns and trades Nvidia stock
articles.body:
Who in Washington owns and trades Nvidia stock
Every disclosed Nvidia stock trade by Trump and 37 members of Congress, around Jensen Huang's resignation and reinstatement.
Nvidia fell 48% from its October high to 20 November, through Huang's resignation and quarterly results. It rose 33% on 23 November, when the board reinstated him, citing input from senior levels of the US government (NBC News).
Trump's trades in Nvidia stock in 2026
28 purchases ($5.1M to $16.7M) and 15 sales ($4.4M to $12M), plotted on Nvidia's daily close. His latest report, released 19 Nov 2026, runs to 24 September.
▲ Purchase▼ SaleLarger: higher valueHuang outMay not be reported yet
Members of Congress who traded Nvidia stock since January 2025
192 trades by 37 members, largest totals first. The latest disclosed trade is from 28 October. Periodic transaction reports only.
▲ Purchase▼ SaleValue≤ $15K≤ $250K> $250KHuang outMay not be reported yet
About the data
- Holdings: Trump's annual report values his Nvidia stock at $12.5M to $58M on 31 December 2025, or 67,000 to 311,000 shares at that day's close.
- If he still held them, he lost $0.5 million to $2.2 million from 11 to 23 November. We can't tell whether he did: his 2026 trades are reported in ranges too wide to net.
- His accounts are run by independent managers, according to the Trump Organization (AP). The reports don't show who decided a trade.
- Trades can be reported up to 45 days late, so November's will appear by early January. We'll update the page then.
- Congress: periodic transaction reports only, including family accounts. Trades in annual or candidate reports, like those NOTUS found for Eric Swalwell and Ritchie Torres, aren't included.

articles.title: GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two
articles.body:
Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old “NotRexed,” has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two.
GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two
Modders are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC.
Leonida was designed to translate a leaked GTA VI Xbox build to run natively on Windows. Cyberleek, the leaker who posted multiple GTA VI gameplay videos over the summer, published a full Xbox build of the game earlier this week. The leak has kicked recompilation efforts up a notch, as modders race to reverse-engineer the game’s code and rebuild it into native PC code.
Some have managed to get the game to boot on PC, but recompiling the full game won’t be easy — even with help from AI tools like Claude. Take-Two is trying to slow this progress, and its IP enforcement team targeted the main GitHub repository for Leonida and more than 2,900 forks of it, claiming that it “infringes upon Take-Two’s copyrighted works and facilitates copyright infringement of Rockstar Games title, Grand Theft Auto VI.”
PortWatch VI is tracking the efforts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox build over to PC. At the time of publishing, the VIctory project and forks of it are leading the way. People are also trying to use XCL, a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X games on a Windows PC, to get GTA VI running.
At this point, it seems like Take-Two might not be able to avoid the inevitable here. The clock started ticking down to the release of the PC version last week, and if recent reports are true, we might see it in a few months. If GTA VI is close to being officially ready for PC, we could hear about a release before modders manage to get the game running on PC unofficially.

articles.title: Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
articles.body:
Tidal is officially banning AI-generated music on December 9th. As a result of this change, Tidal will delete around 29 million AI-generated songs and reject an estimated 80,000 to 85,000 tracks per day, according to Tidal music lead Robert Andersen.
Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
The music streaming platform estimates that it will delete 29 million songs as a result of the AI ban.
The move comes just months after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing tracks identified as 100 percent AI-generated. In a post on X, Andersen says Tidal needed to take a more “drastic” measure, as AI music made up 43 percent of the tracks distributed to the platform in the last 90 days. “We believe this will resonate with both artists and listeners alike, as 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays at all,” Andersen adds.
Bandcamp similarly banned AI music earlier this year, while other music streaming platforms attempt to address a flood of AI songs by applying new labels or removing them from user algorithms. Spotify recently announced that it removed 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from recommendations over the past year, and also launched new “AI persona” badges for artists that use an AI identity. YouTube has rolled out AI music labels as well, while Apple Music is planning to launch AI labels this year. Meanwhile, Deezer is giving users the option to filter out AI music.
“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” Tidal says in a separate post on X.
The platform is also going to ban music distributors from submitting AI songs, using the AI detection tool Ircam Amplify and metadata checks to reject submissions generated solely with AI. Tidal notes that it won’t ban songs made with the assistance of AI tools, as long as AI doesn’t make up the “sole output.”
